articles.title: Elon Musk says ASML and other critical semiconductor equipment suppliers will expedite shipments to Terafab — facility targets volume chip production by Q3-Q4, 2028, in 'highly aspirational' timeline - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: Elon Musk says ASML and other critical semiconductor equipment suppliers will expedite shipments to Terafab — facility targets volume chip production by Q3-Q4, 2028, in 'highly aspirational' timeline  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
"These are very aggressive dates, and we're very appreciative of ASML and all of our other suppliers in accelerating equipment deliveries in order to achieve this outcome," said Musk, CEO of both companies behind Terafab. SpaceX plans to manufacture its first experimental test chip at its research fabrication facility in Austin, Texas, around Q2 2027.
Aside from Terafab, Musk also outlined near-term ambitions for his AI companies during the broadcast, saying he expects them to have 2.5 to 3 gigawatts (GW) of computing capacity active by the end of 2026. He also stated he is highly confident about bringing an incremental 10 GW online in 2027, saying he "would be surprised" if they do not hit a total of 13 GW of AI compute by the end of 2027.
Meanwhile, the next-largest project by planned capacity, the now-restructured 10 GW Project Stargate, was expected to reach full capacity in the 2030s. Meta's 5 GW Hyperion also has a similar timeline. To achieve the 13 GW milestone, Musk revealed that SpaceX and xAI are aggressively procuring upcoming next-generation NVIDIA architecture. He announced plans to get a massive 440,000-GPU Nvidia "Vera Rubin" training cluster online by the end of Q2 2027.
Shifting back to Terafab, Musk also boasted that once fully scaled and operational, the sheer commercial value of Terafab's advanced chip output will place it within the top 20 global country GDPs from a single physical building. For context, the 20th country on the list is Switzerland, with a GDP of around $1.14 trillion. The facility is a planned multi-billion-dollar, vertically integrated chip factory in Texas, with an ambitious goal of manufacturing 1 terawatt (TW) of AI computing power per year. Terafab will fabricate logic, memory, and advanced packaging internal architectures in one place. The project's massive planned output has mandated various collaborations across the semiconductor supply chain. Terafab will utilize traditional extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems utilizing Intel's 14A manufacturing node technology.
Intel officially joined the Terafab venture in April 2026 to help co-develop and refactor silicon fabrication technology, providing access to its state-of-the-art 14A manufacturing process. ASML, the world's sole commercial supplier of the $400 million EUV lithography systems required for high-volume, leading-edge chip production, is perhaps the project's most critical partner. Terafab's first EUV tool was reportedly slated for delivery in mid-2027, according to unofficial sources. It remains unclear if this is the expedited timeline Musk referred to in the broadcast.
Other major suppliers include American equipment manufacturers Applied Materials, Lam Research, and KLA Corporation, as well as Japan's Tokyo Electron. These companies will provide front-end processing, metrology, and process control machinery. Tesla and SpaceX are also in talks with about 10 South Korean equipment makers, including Hanmi Semiconductor, known for advanced packaging equipment, and HPSP, a high-pressure hydrogen annealing equipment manufacturer, as well as firms providing specialized piping components and process valves.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Musk's announcement says that several of these suppliers are expediting supply to Terafab, even as capacity remains tight across the semiconductor supply chain. The facility, which aims to mitigate future shortfalls of cutting-edge AI processors from external foundries like TSMC, will supply the chips for Musk's xAI clusters, self-driving vehicles, Optimus humanoid robots, and SpaceX's orbital AI data center, as well as the broader AI industry.
However, many experts have questioned the validity of Musk's 1 TW Terafab ambition. For context, research firm Gartner estimates the total global AI-optimized data center capacity is roughly 44 GW as of late 2026, 4.4% of Terafab's planned output. Although global AI computing capacity has grown by roughly 3.3x to 3.4x per year since 2022, according to EpochAI.

articles.title: Chinese Semiconductor Equipment Manufacturers to Strengthen Hybrid Bonding: NAURA, Piotech, and AMEC Launch Offensive in 3D Integration｜Semiconductor Geek - note
articles.summary: Chinese Semiconductor Equipment Manufacturers to Strengthen Hybrid Bonding: NAURA, Piotech, and AMEC Launch Offensive in 3D Integration｜Semiconductor Geek  note
articles.full_text:
Summary (approx. 100 characters)
China's largest semiconductor equipment manufacturer, NAURA, is acquiring a hybrid bonding equipment company for approximately 405 million yuan. Piotech and AMEC are also advancing investments and acquisitions in related technologies, aiming to localize 3D integration equipment for HBM and chiplets and enhance their technical capabilities.
Keywords (5)
NAURA
Hybrid Bonding
HBM
3D Integration
Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment
Article Translation
Chinese semiconductor equipment manufacturers are accelerating their entry into the advanced packaging sector, driven by growing demand for technologies that support the integration of HBM and chiplets.
According to ETNews and Yicai, NAURA, China's largest semiconductor equipment manufacturer, is planning to acquire a company specializing in hybrid bonding technology, seeking to expand its business domain from existing areas centered on etching and deposition to 3D integration technology.
According to Yicai, Beijing NAURA Microelectronics Equipment, a wholly-owned subsidiary of NAURA, has signed an agreement with the Beijing Integrated Circuit Equipment Industry Investment & M&A Phase II Fund to acquire 100% of the shares of Beijing Nuohe Jianwei Equipment for approximately 405 million yuan in cash.
NAURA has already entered the hybrid bonding market. According to Yicai, the company announced the 'Qomola HPD30,' a die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding system compatible with 12-inch wafers, in March 2026.
According to NAURA's 2026 semi-annual financial report, the company's hybrid bonding equipment covers both wafer-to-wafer (W2W) and D2W methods, supporting wafer-level 3D integration and heterogeneous chip integration. It also reports that the D2W equipment has already entered the commercial introduction stage and that its hybrid bonding products have completed customer verification.
With this acquisition, NAURA's technical capabilities are expected to be further strengthened. According to Securities Times, Nuohe Jianwei has developed hybrid bonding equipment that achieves nanometer-level alignment accuracy and has already secured repeat orders.
On the other hand, the company's products are still in the stage of technical improvement and market introduction. Due to limited revenue and high research and development expenses, it recorded losses in 2025 and the first half of 2026.
This move indicates that Chinese semiconductor equipment manufacturers are attempting to increase their presence in a market that continues to be dominated by overseas companies.
According to industry analysts cited by Yicai, the Dutch semiconductor equipment manufacturer BESI holds approximately a 70% share of the global market for hybrid bonding equipment and possesses strong competitiveness, particularly in the field of high-performance equipment.
Within China, Piotech has also launched its first mass-production-ready hybrid bonding equipment and has secured repeat orders.
Chinese semiconductor equipment manufacturers expand their 3D integration technology product portfolio
Chinese semiconductor equipment manufacturers are also advancing the strengthening of 3D integration technology through acquisitions.
According to Securities Times, Piotech has announced plans to acquire Wuxi Shangji and its related holding companies for 2.5 billion yuan.
Through this acquisition, Piotech will incorporate the physical vapor deposition (PVD) equipment that Wuxi Shangji is mass-producing. By combining this with the plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD), atomic layer deposition (ALD), and gap-fill CVD equipment it already offers, the company aims to expand its product lineup for 3D integration equipment.
AMEC is also investing in bonding technology.
According to the Science and Technology Innovation Board Daily, AMEC has announced plans to invest up to 35 million yuan in iSABers through its wholly-owned subsidiary, AMEC Lingang. The investment ratio after the financing is expected to be 0.50%.
iSABers, also known as Qinghe Jingyuan, specializes in advanced semiconductor bonding technology and provides high-performance bonding equipment and production line services.
The company's product lineup includes wafer bonding equipment, chip bonding equipment, and surface treatment equipment.
Analysis: Hybrid bonding is the next main battlefield for China's semiconductor equipment industry
A key point of this article is that Chinese manufacturers have begun to seriously tackle the localization of advanced packaging equipment, which is essential for HBM and chiplets, in addition to traditional front-end equipment.
Higher performance in HBM creates new equipment demand
In HBM, DRAM dies are stacked vertically to increase data transfer bandwidth. As the number of layers and connection density increase in the future, the importance of technology to bond dies with high precision will grow.
Hybrid bonding is a technology that combines copper-to-copper bonding with dielectric-to-dielectric bonding, and it has the potential to achieve finer connection pitches compared to traditional micro-bump methods. This is expected to lead to improved connection density and better electrical characteristics.
However, not all generations of HBM will immediately transition to hybrid bonding. The actual timing of adoption will depend on factors such as yield, thermal management, bonding reliability, and manufacturing costs.

articles.title: Shader Compilation Stutter Begone: Nvidia's Latest GPU Drivers Finally Add Advanced Shader Delivery - Digital Foundry
articles.summary: Shader Compilation Stutter Begone: Nvidia's Latest GPU Drivers Finally Add Advanced Shader Delivery  Digital FoundryGeForce Game Ready Driver For Phantom Blade Zero & Call of Duty®: Modern Warfare 4® Released  NVIDIANVIDIA Releases GeForce 621.01 WHQL Game Ready Drivers  TechPowerUpNVIDIA Brings Advanced Shader Delivery To Call of Duty: MW4 & Gears of War: E-Day In Latest Drivers While Cyberpunk 2077 Updated To Support 2nd Gen DLSS AI Models  WccftechNvidi...
articles.full_text:
At the start of October, Nvidia announced that it would soon be adding Microsoft's Advanced Shader Delivery (ASD) technology to its RTX and RTX Spark graphics drivers in the continuing fight against the shader compilation stutter that has become increasingly commonplace in modern PC gaming. With version 621.01, released today, ASD support is now finally in place.
ASD is designed to prevent the momentary hitches experienced in games when a shader needs to be compiled on the fly, often when a new model or effect appears for the first time. Most modern games include a shader burn when you first launch a game (or update your graphics drivers), but it's still common for some shaders to be missed by this step. ASD works by downloading precompiled shaders from the cloud for your specific graphics hardware on Windows 11. It's a similar approach to the Linux-based Steam Shader Pre-Caching system established by Valve for the Steam Deck.
This normally "just works", with no user involvement, though developers need to specifically support the technology. If you want to test it out, two high-profile releases with support are Gears of War: E-Day and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.
As well as eliminating troublesome shader compilation stutter, the technology also massively speeds up that initial precompilation step - Microsoft says it is reduced by up to 95 percent. Given that this can take upwards of 20 minutes even on high-end systems in some games, that's a meaningful improvement.
However, this technology doesn't help prevent traversal stutter, another hitch-causing phenomenon related to data being loaded into and out of memory when passing an invisible boundary in the game world.
Nvidia also has a technology to prevent shaders from being wiped out following a graphics driver update called Automatic Shader Compilation, and the two technologies can be used in concert.
To benefit from Advanced Shader Delivery support, you'll need to be using Windows 11 24H2 or later and update to Nvidia's 621.01 driver via the Nvidia app or by manually downloading the installer - I had to opt for the latter as the driver wasn't showing as available in the app for my PC.
Note that ASD is already part of AMD and Qualcomm's graphics driver and is also set to arrive for Intel discrete and integrated graphics later this month, though an official release date or graphics driver version number has not yet been set.
[source nvidia.com]

articles.title: Microsoft: FSR 4.1 Coming "Very Soon" to Xbox Game Developers for Series X, Series S - Digital Foundry
articles.summary: Microsoft: FSR 4.1 Coming "Very Soon" to Xbox Game Developers for Series X, Series S  Digital FoundryAMD FSR Upscaling 4.1 Boosts Frames and Image Quality on More Devices  AMDWhen will Xbox Series X|S and Xbox Ally get FSR 4.1? Sooner than you think!  Windows CentralAMD is bringing FSR 4.1 to Xbox consoles and handhelds  The VergeAMD Software Adrenalin 26.10.1 WHQL Drivers Released  TechPowerUp
articles.full_text:
Xbox vice president Jason Ronald has confirmed that game developers on Xbox will get access to FSR 4.1 support "very soon", following up on AMD's announcement of its latest-gen FSR coming to five new platforms yesterday.
It's an important development for the Xbox platform, given that Sony has already released two versions of its PSSR machine learning upscaler for PS5 Pro and recently backported a lightweight version called QSSR to the base PS5. Now, Microsoft's ML hardware on the Xbox Series X and Series S might finally come in useful - despite launching with the consoles in 2020, we've not seen it used for upscaling thus far.
It's not clear exactly how Microsoft's FSR 4.1 implementation will work, but the language here suggests that it will be down to game developers to integrate the upscaling technology in their games, rather than Microsoft being able to provide a system-level override that automatically upgrades older FSR versions to FSR 4.1.
Either way, FSR 4.1 is capable of producing better results than the older FSR 3 model, and it'll be fascinating to see how it compares to the likes of FSR, Epic's TSR, and Sony's QSSR and PSSR in shipping games.
Microsoft has also worked with Asus and AMD to add FSR 4.1 support to Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X handhelds, which is now available. I'm working on a review of the Intel-powered Acer Predator Atlas 8 handheld right now, and it'll be interesting to compare how the Xbox Ally X with FSR 4.1 and Atlas 8 with XeSS 3 compare in terms of image quality and performance.
What games do you think are crying out for FSR 4.1 support on Xbox Series consoles? Let me know in the comments below.

articles.title: Navitas unveils UHV SiC power module for energy and grid infrastructure - Semiconductor Today
articles.summary: Navitas unveils UHV SiC power module for energy and grid infrastructure  Semiconductor Today
articles.full_text:
News: Microelectronics
21 October 2026
Navitas unveils UHV SiC power module for energy and grid infrastructure
Gallium nitride (GaN) and silicon carbide (SiC) power semiconductor firm Navitas Semiconductor Corp of Torrance, CA, USA has announced an ultra-high-voltage (UHV) SiC power module family for advanced energy and grid infrastructure.
The new G4H08MT23GB4 2300V full-bridge module family uses the industry-standard SiCPAK form factor and has what is claimed to be a class-leading RDSON (8mΩ).
It has been developed to enhance efficiency and power density in solid-state transformers, grid-scale battery energy storage systems, solar inverters, and electric vehicle (EV) megawatt charging infrastructure. These gains are enabled through its deployment of Navitas' fourth-generation GeneSiC Trench-Assisted Planar (TAP) architecture, with the launch extending Navitas’ 2300V and 3300V ultra-high-voltage SiC portfolio.
As grid-tied power architectures increasingly underpin next-generation AI data centers, Navitas says that its UHV SiC modules provide the medium-voltage building block for solid-state transformers that convert grid power directly into the high-voltage DC rails used inside AI data-center racks. This places the new module family at the center of Navitas' AI infrastructure portfolio, spanning AI data-center and energy and grid infrastructure alongside battery energy storage, solar, EV megawatt charging, hydrogen fuel cell electrolysis and DC–DC conversion, and industrial motor-drive and high-voltage power supply applications.
Advanced construction for high-reliability, high-power operation
The modules also integrate several construction enhancements that better meet the needs of demanding, high-power applications. For example, its aluminium nitride (AlN) active-metal-braze (AMB) substrate enables superior heat spreading and supports an isolation capability of over 5kV. Its epoxy-resin potting technology reduces internal stress distribution, limits moisture and contaminant ingress, and delivers 10x improvements in thermal conductivity versus silicone gel.
Additionally, the module’s high-current, press-fit pins have twice the current-carrying capability per pin versus standard press-fit connections. An optional pre-applied thermal interface material (TIM), which simplifies and standardizes heat-sink assembly, is also available.
Extended reliability testing validates long-term system lifetime
The new module family will be qualified to Navitas’ internal AEC-Plus reliability benchmark, which tests beyond AEC-Q101 and JEDEC standard requirements. The benchmark reflects Navitas' focus on system-level lifetime requirements for the demanding mission profiles found in energy and grid infrastructure applications.
The AEC-Plus qualification includes dynamic reverse bias (DRB) and dynamic gate switching (DGS) testing to represent stringent fast-switching application mission profiles; it also more than triples the duration of static high-temperature, high-voltage tests (HTRB, HTGB, HTGB-R). Additionally, it implements an extended power-cycling and temperature-cycling testing and delivers HV-H3TRB (HV-THB) qualification for power modules, discrete and known-good-die (KGD) devices.
“Our fourth-generation GeneSiC Trench-Assisted Planar architecture continues to push the limits of what's possible in ultra-high-voltage SiC,” says Paul Wheeler, VP & general manager of Navitas’ SiC business unit. “This new 2300V module delivers a leading RDS(ON) of any device using the SiCPAK form factor, giving system designers a proven, reliability-tested building block for the solid-state transformers and energy storage systems that are reshaping grid and AI data-center infrastructure.”
Samples of the G4H08MT23GB4(HC) family are available immediately, with options for pre-applied TIM and high-current variants:
A double-pulse test (DPT) system, EVB-UHVSIC-GB-E-DPT-1, is also available on request. This has been created to help engineers evaluate the device’s switching performance. A white paper on Trench-Assisted Planar technology is also available for download from the Navitas website.

articles.title: Four workers killed after fall at TSMC’s 2nm fab construction site — accident marks at least nine construction deaths since 2024, broken bolt on a steel connection plate suspected as cause behind tragic accident (updated) - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: Four workers killed after fall at TSMC’s 2nm fab construction site — accident marks at least nine construction deaths since 2024, broken bolt on a steel connection plate suspected as cause behind tragic accident (updated)  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
Update - October 21, 11:20 am ET: In an update, local media reports that all four TSMC workers involved in an accident at its 2nm Fab 22 site in Kaohsiung have died. Reports indicate the accident was caused by a broken connecting plate bolt. TSMC has suspended all steel structure work at the site and all of its new plants in Taiwan while it investigates the cause of the accident. The rest of the story remains below as first published.
Three contract workers died, and one more is in intensive care after an accident at the construction site for TSMC’s 2nm Fab 22 in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, reports Taiwan’s Central News Agency. The Southern Taiwan Science Park (STSP) Bureau suspects the cause was a broken bolt on a steel connection plate that sent the workers and steel components tumbling. Steel hoisting on the project has been halted, and the STSP has sent labor inspectors to investigate. The accident is not the first of its kind but rather follows at least a half dozen others since September 2024 at TSMC construction sites in Taiwan, according to local reports. Each of those earlier accidents killed one worker.
Local police said that the men were welding a steel beam on an upper floor and fell with it, while the STSP said the workers were performing steel-structure hoisting and installation when a third-floor connection-plate bolt apparently broke.
10 emergency vehicles were sent to the site with 22 personnel, and all four men involved in the incident were taken to the hospital. On-site medical staff gave first aid, but three of the workers died despite resuscitation efforts, and the fourth was moved to intensive care. The workers were employed by a contractor working on the fourth phase of the complex’s construction, and TSMC said the area was within that contractor’s scope of work.
According to the report, TSMC stopped the related construction work on its own and is working with authorities and supervising the subcontractor’s follow-up.
The Fab 22 complex, located in Kaohsiung’s Nanzi District, is part of the science park and is being built to accelerate 2nm manufacturing. TSMC entered high-volume 2nm, or N2, manufacturing in the fourth quarter of 2025, including at Fab 22. The complex has five phases planned, with a total investment TSMC puts at more than NT$1.5 trillion, or about $46 billion. The accident happened on the construction side, not in a producing fab. Kaohsiung’s deputy mayor said construction on Phase 4 began in August 2025, with operations expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.
Business Today reports that TSMC fab construction has increased, from four fabs a year in 2017–2024 to nine a year in 2025 and 2026. The deaths come as the company plans for 13 new leading-edge and advanced-packaging fabs in Taiwan, with company-wide capex of $60 billion to $64 billion this year.
The faster pace has encouraged the addition of a contractor’s safety record as a weight in selection and a plan for a Taiwan Semiconductor Construction Engineering Safety Association with construction partners. TSMC Chairman C.C. Wei said at last year’s shareholders meeting that safety cannot be compromised, and the company’s 2025 annual report said it will keep investing in fabs across several locations in Taiwan “with a strong emphasis on construction site safety.”
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Cliff Hou, TSMC senior vice president and deputy co-COO, told Business Today that increased worker count and overlapping construction have raised the risk, requiring careful supervision, and that TSMC’s contractor lost-time injury rate had fallen about 42% from last year’s high as of late May, when the publication toured the Nanzi site to see the overhaul. It’s too early to call the program a failure, with the cause as yet unknown.
The accident comes less than a week after an explosion killed two people at Intel’s chip plant in Israel, though that was an operating fab rather than a construction site. Both accidents come as chipmakers race to meet demand, with global chip sales passing $1 trillion through August, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association.
The STSP’s findings will determine what penalties, if any, will fall under Taiwan’s Occupational Safety and Health Act, while it assists the victims’ families. No date has been given at this time for that or for the Phase 4 steel hoisting restart. Nor has TSMC commented on any schedule impact.

articles.title: As Congress Deliberates, States Lead the Way on AI Regulation - National Conference of State Legislatures
articles.summary: As Congress Deliberates, States Lead the Way on AI Regulation  National Conference of State Legislatures
articles.full_text:
Setting AI guardrails has emerged as the rare issue on which many state lawmakers see eye to eye with peers across the aisle.
(herstockart/Getty Images)
Four short years after the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, AI is everywhere. As it seeps into every corner of the economy and everyday life, state legislatures are pursuing strategies to install guardrails and regulate the industry.
NCSL Vice President Natalie Wood opened a session on AI at NCSL Base Camp 2026 with a big question for legislators: “How do you govern a technology that is evolving faster than our full understanding of its consequences?”
For context, she cites Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, known as the “godfather of AI,” who spoke at NCSL’s Legislative Summit this summer. “Regulation isn’t the brakes,” she recalls Hinton saying, “it’s the steering wheel. So, the challenge for legislatures is not simply whether to or what to legislate on AI. It’s actually how to steer.”
Legislating AI: An Overview
NCSL Fellow Will Clark says state action on AI mirrors many of the actions also taken by the federal government.
“In 2025, we had 1,262 (state) bills introduced, 227 enacted and adopted,” he says. “And this year, we had 1,539 introduced and 280 enacted as of (early October).”
Of the introduced legislation, bills related to private sector use of AI topped the list in 2025, followed by bills on deepfakes and government use. “Though we’ve seen a lot of those categories persist into 2026,” Clark says, “we really saw some interesting shifts this year, No. 1 being that there was a great increase in bills related to notification, nearly a threefold increase. Essentially, that’s letting a user know that they’re engaging with AI.”
But the introduced bills don’t necessarily represent the ones that became law, he adds. Deepfake bills were the most common type of AI legislation enacted in 2026, typically regulating explicit content, political advertising and use of digital likenesses. Other subjects of this year’s enacted bills include AI in healthcare and education.
Only two comprehensive AI bills were enacted in 2026, one in Colorado (SB 189) and the other in Connecticut (SB 5). Legislation targeting the big players’ frontier models was more common, including an Illinois bill on mandated third-party audits (SB 315) and one in New York on safety and transparency requirements (SB 8828).
The federal government has been less active than the states, Clark says. Congress has deliberated several bills, including the Kids Online Safety Act, the App Store Accountability Act and the Great American AI Act. The last of the three “would require large AI developers to create, implement and publish plans addressing potential catastrophic risks from their models,” Clark says. “A lot of the same ideas that get a lot of focus from the states are now being seriously deliberated by Congress.”
He says NCSL tracks relevant bills in its AI Legislation Database and offers a policy toolkit and other resources.
Case Studies: Utah and Connecticut
Before embarking on a legislative career in 2024, Utah Rep. Doug Fiefia (R) worked in sales for Google. “A few years ago, I was sitting in conference rooms at Google watching AI get pitched to some of the largest organizations in the world, and I’ll let you in on a little secret: The demo always works, always,” he says. “Today, I’m on the other side of the table as a legislator, and my job is to ask the question that nobody asked during the demo, which is, ‘What happens when it fails? Who gets hurt, and who’s responsible?’”
To answer these and other questions, Fiefia endorses “a pro-human approach” to AI policy. “We’re not antitechnology,” he says. “I worked in tech. I still do. I believe that AI will do some incredible things for our economy, our schools, our government—and solve some of the world’s biggest problems. But the technology should serve people, not the other way around.”
“I believe that AI will do some incredible things for our economy, our schools, our government—and solve some of the world’s biggest problems. But the technology should serve people, not the other way around.”
—Utah Rep. Doug Fiefia
To that end, Utah has led the way on AI policy, establishing the state Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy and the AI Learning Laboratory, aka the “sandbox,” in 2024. “Simply, here’s how (the learning lab) works: A company with a promising AI product comes to the state and says, ‘Some of your rules weren’t written with this technology in mind,’” Fiefia says. “Instead of saying no or saying anything goes, the state works with them. We set guardrails, we watch closely, and the company gets some flexibility while it proves the product is safe. Think of it as a learner’s permit. You get to drive, but someone’s always in the passenger seat.”
He adds, “What I love about it is that we’re learning from real products in the real world, not guessing in a hearing room.”
Fiefia says his legislative agenda for AI is centered on child safety. “We have never in human history had to regulate a product that can act like a friend, a product that remembers your child’s name, asks about their day, tells them that it understands them better than anyone else,” he says. “That’s what AI companion chatbots do, and millions of kids are using them right now.”
Fiefia sponsored this year’s Companion Chatbot Safety Act, but it ultimately didn’t become law. “It tells users clearly that they’re talking to AI,” he says. “It puts real age assurance in place. It requires companies to report every year on what’s happening on their platform, and it gives a safe harbor to companies that follow the rules. So, we reward the good actors instead of only punishing the bad ones.”
Fiefia pledges to keep the issue front and center. “Most of us wish that we had acted on social media 10 years earlier, and this time we have a real chance to get ahead of it,” he says.
Connecticut Sen. James Maroney (D) calls himself “an AI optimist”—with a catch. “I don’t believe there’s zero risk, and I don’t think we’re going to see full adoption until people feel safe,” he says. “There is a big backlash against tech because there’s a trust problem.”
“Saying AI should only be regulated federally is to say it shouldn’t be regulated at all.”
—James Maroney, Connecticut Senate Deputy Majority Leader
To address the problem, Connecticut began legislating AI in 2023, continuing with measures in 2025 (SB 1295) and this year (SB 5 and others). The bills cover user safety as well as automated decision-making, privacy and other subjects.
Maroney echoes Fiefia’s concerns about children, adding, “I equally worry about seniors. They’re not digital natives, and many are lonely, with the loneliness epidemic in our country.”
The Connecticut General Assembly enlisted systems engineer Stephen Nichols, from the Connecticut Academy of Scientists and Engineers, as a technology policy fellow in 2025. Bringing Nichols’ technical expertise in to help when lawmakers were crafting the bills was invaluable, Maroney says. “If you are looking for a bill to start with, maybe start with a tech fellows bill.”
Understanding and collecting data on AI-related layoffs is another of Maroney’s priorities. “We’re working with UConn’s Institute for Municipal and Regional Policy to study that and recommend other data points we should be collecting so that we have good data to act on,” he says.
A Bipartisan Issue
AI has emerged as the rare issue on which many legislators see eye to eye with peers across the aisle. “I’ve been in a room where I’ve seen people who disagree on just about every issue start nodding and agreeing when you talk about child safety and AI,” Fiefia says. “It is a unique area where you are seeing bipartisanship.”
As an example, Fiefia and Maroney are collaborating on an unofficial working group to develop AI standards and best practices. “Sen. Maroney and I are from different parties, but we are very close friends, and we coordinate,” Fiefia says.
“In tech policy,” Maroney says, “it’s not as much a line as a circle, in that the ends arrive at the same point from different directions.”
Fiefia says the main sticking point is about who should ultimately regulate AI. “There’s a large argument on states’ rights and what the federal government should be doing versus what states should be doing,” he says “My personal opinion on that is, it’s probably a little bit of both. We have to work together in order to get this right.”
Maroney is more direct. “Saying AI should only be regulated federally is to say it shouldn’t be regulated at all,” he says. “We haven’t seen any major tech legislation out of the federal government since the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act in 1998.”
In his mind, that leaves regulation to the states. “The more we can work together,” Maroney says, “the better the services, and the better we’ll be able to help all of our constituents.”
Eric Peterson is a Denver-based writer and editor.

articles.title: Hyundai Mobis Targets 2029 for Hyundai, Kia Semiconductor Integration - 조선일보
articles.summary: Hyundai Mobis Targets 2029 for Hyundai, Kia Semiconductor Integration  조선일보
articles.full_text:
South Korea is a global leader in both automobiles and memory semiconductors. However, 95% of the automotive semiconductors purchased by Hyundai Motor and Kia, the country’s flagship automakers, are imported. During the 2021 global semiconductor shortage, this high reliance on foreign suppliers caused disruptions in automobile factory operations.
Hyundai Mobis, the world’s sixth-largest automotive parts supplier, announced last year its ambition to localize automotive semiconductor production to overcome these challenges. The company has taken the lead in forming an ecosystem by connecting domestic semiconductor firms—specializing in home appliances, mobile devices, fabless design, and foundry production—with the procurement needs of Hyundai Motor and Kia. This initiative, dubbed the ‘Automotive Semiconductor Localization Platform (ASK),’ aims to strengthen domestic supply chains.
On the 21st, Hyundai Mobis held the second Automotive Semiconductor Forum, ‘Auto Semicon Korea (ASK),’ at a hotel in Seongnam, Gyeonggi Province, to share progress and future plans. Approximately 90 attendees, including Hyundai Mobis President Lee Gyu-suk and Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan, participated in the event.
◇13 Domestic Semiconductor Varieties Under Development…First Vehicle Integration by 2029
Hyundai Mobis revealed that since the first forum last year, it has identified 19 collaborative projects with domestic semiconductor companies and initiated development on 13 of them. For nine of these, specific Hyundai Motor and Kia vehicle models for application have been selected. President Lee Gyu-suk stated in a press briefing, “Starting next year, controllers equipped with these semiconductors will be tested in the early stages of vehicle development.”
The domestic automotive semiconductor industry has long faced challenges due to high entry barriers and low profitability. Strict safety and quality standards are required, as semiconductors directly impact human lives, and the multi-product, small-volume production model makes profitability difficult. Meanwhile, as vehicles evolve into ‘moving computers’ with electric and autonomous driving technologies, semiconductors now account for a growing share of automotive costs.
To address these issues, Hyundai Mobis adopted a strategy of adapting existing semiconductor technologies from the domestic electronics industry for automotive use. As the primary collaborator and semiconductor design company, Hyundai Mobis defines the performance and quality standards required for automotive applications and oversees integration into vehicles.
Over the past year, tangible collaborations have emerged. Above Semicon is developing vehicle communication and control semiconductors using technology previously applied in washing machines. Global Technology is adapting TV display driver technology for automotive use, while Neurotac and LX Semicon are working on wireless communication chips for vehicle battery management systems (BMS).
Since last year, Hyundai Mobis has also collaborated with Samsung Electronics to co-develop network semiconductors responsible for data communication between in-vehicle electronic systems, with prototype evaluations currently underway.
◇Expanding Collaboration…SK Partnership for Power Semiconductors
Building on its experience in network semiconductor development, Hyundai Mobis is expanding into next-generation high-performance system-on-chip (SoC) semiconductors. SoCs act as the ‘brain’ of vehicles, integrating control of multiple functions.
Park Chul-hong, Executive Vice President of Hyundai Mobis’ Semiconductor Business Division, stated, “We are developing SoCs optimized for Hyundai Motor’s next-generation vehicle architecture, targeting completion by 2030 through collaborations with specialized companies.”
The company is also exploring the application of automotive semiconductor technologies in robotics. Motor drive and power management semiconductors required for robotic actuators—joint driving devices under commercialization by Hyundai Mobis—are a key focus.
To strengthen research and production capabilities for power semiconductors, Hyundai Mobis signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with SK Keyfoundry, four small-to-medium-sized fabless companies, and four supporting institutions.
To prevent stagnation in 8-inch wafer production capacity—widely used for automotive semiconductors—Hyundai Mobis proposed to the government the operation of a public-private vehicle semiconductor fabrication facility. The government, responding to last year’s forum, is already constructing a comprehensive support center for automotive semiconductors in Cheonan, South Chungcheong Province, with a completion target of June 2027.
Meanwhile, the ‘Automotive Semiconductor One-Team Task Force (TF),’ involving the Ministry of Industry, Hyundai Motor, Hyundai Mobis, LG Electronics, and 21 other companies and institutions, was launched. The TF aims to enhance collaboration from semiconductor design to verification and mass production, thereby improving supply chain independence for the domestic automotive industry.

articles.title: Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11205-zPinal, a 16-billion-parameter artificial intelligence model, designs functional proteins from natural-language descriptions, demonstrating experimentally validated activities and improved CO2-fixation product yields without iterative optimization.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Programming biological function—designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks—is a foundational goal of molecular engineering.
However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1,2,3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation.
Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function.
Trained on 1.
7 billion synthetically annotated protein–text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure.
In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs.
We applied Pinal to four distinct design tasks—a fluorescent protein, a polyethylene terephthalate hydrolase, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein—and experimentally observed the intended function in each case, including catalytic activity for both designed enzymes.
Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.
7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway.
These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.

The release of large-scale training resources for generative protein design requires careful consideration of potential dual-use biosecurity risks.
In developing Pinal, the large-scale structural component of the training corpus was derived from AFDB, whose released protein-structure collection does not include viral proteomes.
Accordingly, Pinal was not trained or intended for viral protein design.
Nevertheless, unrestricted public release of the full pretraining corpus together with the complete training pipeline could lower the barrier for adapting similar systems to sensitive biological datasets.
To mitigate this risk, these full-scale training resources were provided only under confidential access for editorial and peer review assessment.
Because they will not be publicly released in full, and to support transparency and reproducibility, we instead provide public access to the inference code, evaluation code, model usage instructions, trained model weights and the web server, in line with common release practices for large-scale protein foundation models such as AlphaFold69,74, ESM338 and ESMFold68.

articles.title: Donut Lab Puts Its EV Battery Through a –22 Degree F Cold Test - Autoweek
articles.summary: Donut Lab Puts Its EV Battery Through a –22 Degree F Cold Test  Autoweek
articles.full_text:
Donut Lab says its battery technology has cleared another round of testing, this time showing that a complete battery module retained 97 percent of its capacity after being frozen to –22 degrees F (–30 degrees C).
The Finnish technology company, which has been developing an unconventional solid-state battery architecture, commissioned Finnish research organization VTT to conduct the test on a 14-cell battery module. Unlike a test performed on an individual cell, the experiment was designed to evaluate the performance of an assembled module under extreme cold.
The results are potentially significant for electric vehicles, as cold-weather operation can sharply reduce available battery energy and charging performance.
For the test, VTT placed the 48-volt module in a temperature chamber at –22 degrees F for five hours, without insulation or heat. Sensors confirmed that the cells themselves reached and remained at the target temperature.
A baseline, established at 77°F, the module delivered 27.77 amp-hours, equivalent to 1,354 watt-hours of energy, when fully discharged. After the module was, the same discharge test produced 26.8 amp-hours—97 percent of the original capacity. Measured energy output, however, fell to 1,254 watt-hours, or about 93 percent of the baseline, because battery voltage naturally drops at extremely low temperatures.
In other words, the cells retained nearly all of their capacity in terms of amp-hours, but the extreme cold reduced the amount of energy they could actually deliver because of the lower voltage. Donut Lab says that effect should be less pronounced in a vehicle, where the battery would be enclosed in an insulated housing and would generate heat during operation.
That distinction is important because Donut Lab’s headline claim at CES 2026 was that its battery could retain 99 percent of its capacity at –22 degrees F. The latest test did not quite reach that figure, but the company says the results support the claim because the tested module deliberately lacked insulation and heating.
“Winter is the moment of truth for every battery,” Donut Lab CEO Marko Lehtimäki said.
The cold test is the latest in a series of evaluations performed by VTT on Donut Lab’s first-generation cells. The testing program also covered five-minute fast charging, exposure to temperatures as high as 212 degrees F (100 degrees C), self-discharge, repeated fast charging of a damaged cell, swelling and pressure, and energy density.
At CES earlier this year, Donut Lab also said its battery could charge from 10 to 80 percent in five minutes, although such claims remain considerably different from the performance of batteries currently used in mainstream EVs.
The company says the VTT testing of its Gen1 cells is now complete and that development is moving toward its next-generation technology. Among the areas Donut Lab is pursuing is a bipolar cell structure, which it says could enable further improvements at the system level.

articles.summary: Nvidia CEO encourages Europe’s lagging AI sector and offers tools to accelerate data center buildout  Taipei Times
articles.full_text:
Nvidia Corp CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) yesterday urged players in Europe’s lagging artificial intelligence (AI) industry to get going and touted a modular system to quickly build AI data centers with the massive computing capacity the continent’s developers need, but currently lack.
In an upbeat speech at the company’s GTC conference for developers and investors in Berlin, Huang also laid out tools to keep AI applications from running amok by confining them in a digital “sandbox.”
“Europe’s AI economy is starting, and it’s accelerating, and it’s great to see,” Huang, striding across the stage in his trademark leather jacket and sneakers, told about 3,000 developers, analysts and journalists at Berlin’s Tempodrom auditorium.
Photo: Reuters
Huang, whose company designs the computer chips and software used by AI developers such as Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, frequently name-checked European partner companies such as Siemens AG, Mercedes-Benz AG and Volkswagen AG’s Audi.
“Europe is building its AI economy” as the technology moves from language models to so-called physical AI in manufacturing, Huang said.
“Every company in the future will be an AI company,” he said.
Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kallenius, whose company is working on developing autonomous driving technology with Nvidia, said that the technology could reduce the number of auto fatalities caused by human error “down to zero... we will have safer streets once we have full autonomy.”
Nvidia’s design for the Vera Rubin DSK Pod, a ready-made modular computing center that is delivered in a shipping container-like box, would reduce the time needed to set up a data center from months to days, Huang said.
The pod “will change the way people build AI centers,” he said.
Nvidia has invested US$10 billion in European start-ups and partners in the past year, Huang said.
Building out data centers is key for Europe, which has only about 5 percent of the world’s AI computing capacity, compared with 75 percent in the US. Lack of the massive computing power, or “compute” in digital jargon, needed to train AI applications is a key obstacle for European developers.
“The big bottleneck is compute,” General Catalyst Partners LLC president and managing director Jeannette zu Furstenberg said ahead of the speech.
General Catalyst invests in AI companies.
Huang was briefly interrupted by protesters who stood up with a banner urging him to “clean up” his business.
Huang promised “to talk to you later” and urged security to avoid rough handling as they removed the protesters.
He also addressed concerns about safety by talking about the company’s OpenShell open-source software designed to exert external control over what AI applications are doing and block them if they contravene company policy.
The event is part of a tour through Europe by Huang, who has been signing deals with local companies and trying to persuade the continent’s political and business leaders that AI is safe. His trip comes at a delicate moment for the industry. AI stocks have been battered during the past two weeks, and the closely watched Philadelphia semiconductor index suffered its longest losing streak since 2008.
Nvidia, the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, has frequently cited supply chain constraints as an impediment to its growth. To combat that, Ibiden Co, Samsung Electro-Mechanics Co and Unimicron Technology Corp (欣興電子) are to help it get more substrates — the materials used to house other components. Amkor Technology Inc is to help increase the amount of chip packaging available by fourfold by the end of 2028. That material is used to encase semiconductors and connect them with other components. KYEC Microelectronics Co, a subsidiary of King Yuan Electronics Co (京元電子), is to increase testing capacity.
Nvidia is also helping to boost the availability of on-package optical connections, which would speed up communication between components.

articles.title: Smash Bros and Kirby creator Masahiro Sakurai says AI usage will lead to unoriginal and "unprofitable" games - PC Guide
articles.summary: Smash Bros and Kirby creator Masahiro Sakurai says AI usage will lead to unoriginal and "unprofitable" games  PC GuideMasahiro Sakurai Says Gaming Needs Originality Or It ‘Will Die Slowly’  KotakuSmash Bros creator Masahiro Sakura says AI will lead to “unplayable” games and “the vast majority will be direct copies of games we've seen before”  FRVRSuper Smash Bros. creator speaks out about the impact of artificial intelligence on the industry  GameGPUMasahi...
articles.full_text:
The use of AI in game development has become a controversial topic across the industry. Some studios are experimenting with the technology to speed up parts of the development process, while others have raised concerns about what greater reliance on AI could mean for creativity and originality. Super Smash Bros. and Kirby creator Masahiro Sakurai has now shared his thoughts, and he believes AI could contribute to an even bigger flood of games that players simply don’t want.
During an interview with Denfaminico Gamer, Sakurai discussed how difficult it has become for developers to create something genuinely original. He pointed out that many modern games are described by comparing them to something that already exists, making it easier for audiences to immediately understand what they are getting.
What does Sakurai think about generative AI in game dev?
Sakurai believes creating something original requires taking a different approach. Instead of simply making something similar to what players already know they enjoy, developers have to come up with ideas people may not even realize they want yet. The difficult part is not only finding those ideas, but also convincing a development team or publisher that they can work. AI, however, could make that problem even more noticeable as the number of games being released continues to increase.
Latest tech deals.
Prices correct as of October 9th, 2026.
For example, if Super Smash Bros. had followed the rules of a typical fighting game – 1-on-1 with guarding, attacking, and special moves, and a health system where the match ends with a KO – then I don’t think the first Super Smash Bros. would have even been released.
Even if it had been released, it would likely have been treated as a novelty item, and the history of Super Smash Bros. would have ended there.
Masahiro Sakurai, speaking to Denfaminico Gamer [translated]
Sakurai highlighted Steam as an example of how quickly the market has expanded. When the Game Designers Award was established in 2010, around 275 games were being released on Steam each year. That figure has now climbed to more than 19,000 annually, and Sakurai expects the number to grow further as AI makes it easier to produce games.
“AI will increase the number” of games, he says, but he also remarks that “I think most of them will become unprofitable titles”. The Kirby creator adds, “When it comes to things created with AI… or things mass-produced with poor quality, I think most of them will simply be reproductions of systems seen in various other games.” Hence, they lack the all-important originality.
Likewise, Steam’s latest Next Fest event (the October 2026 edition) is happening right now. The showcase is designed to feature upcoming games by allowing Steam users to access playable demos, but it’s plagued with even more generative AI than last time, with 36% of games coming with an AI disclaimer. In Japan, over 85% of game devs reportedly use AI in some way.
He believes many AI-made games could end up copying ideas and systems that have already proven successful rather than introducing something genuinely new. Sakurai used simple puzzle games as an example, pointing out how one successful concept can quickly lead to numerous similar games. AI could make producing those kinds of imitations even easier.
The game designer also used Fumito Ueda, known for games such as ICO and Shadow of the Colossus, to explain the difference between copying an existing style and creating something new. In Sakurai’s view, AI could potentially study Ueda’s previous games and produce something that resembles them. What it couldn’t do, however, is predict and create whatever entirely new idea Ueda himself might come up with next.

articles.title: EV Battery Technology in India: Trends and Growth - IBEF
articles.summary: EV Battery Technology in India: Trends and Growth  IBEF
articles.full_text:
Battery technology is emerging as a critical driver of India’s electric vehicle (EV) market. Due to the increasing popularity of EVs, technological developments in battery science and production costs have become more important in relation to vehicle affordability and performance, and creation of domestic EV supply chain.
Over the past few years, an increasing trend of registration of EVs in India has taken place starting from 0.456 million units in FY22 to 2.536 million units in FY26.The focus is now extending beyond EV sales to the development of a broader battery ecosystem. Investments in cell manufacturing, alternative battery chemistries, critical mineral processing and battery recycling are strengthening different parts of the value chain. In addition to government schemes like the ACC Production Linked Incentive, efforts to build domestic manufacturing capabilities have been strengthened.
Hence, batteries are becoming increasingly important not just for the development of India’s EV industry, but also for the country's clean mobility and energy storage ambitions in general.
Source: Vahan Dashboard, Note: * - Till August 2026
Batteries form a considerable part of the total cost associated with electric vehicles, implying that battery costs and innovations are fundamental factors determining the cost and adoption of EVs. Global lithium-ion battery pack prices fell to an all-time low of Rs. 9,413.28 per kWh (US$ 108 per kWh) in 2025, reflecting an 8% decline compared to 2024, according to reports published by BloombergNEF. This fall in the cost of lithium-ion batteries is because of overproduction, increasing competition, and the use of cheaper battery technologies like LFP batteries.
The Indian EV battery market is also forecasted to witness significant growth, increasing from Rs. 23,707.52 crore (US$ 2.72 billion) in 2025 to Rs. 1.50 lakh crore (US$ 15.90 billion) by 2034, which translates into a compound annual growth rate of 21.70%. It becomes vital for India to build its own domestic capability along the battery value chain to facilitate its burgeoning EV market.
There is growing focus on developing a domestic battery ecosystem through investments in cell manufacturing, battery components, and battery recycling. The PLI scheme for batteries, through the ACC, has helped develop domestic manufacturing of batteries, with at least 10 manufacturers planning their battery manufacturing capacity to about 178 GWh in the next five years.
A layered set of policies is trying to pull India's battery ecosystem in the same direction: cheaper cells, more of them made domestically, and a system for recovering critical minerals once batteries reach the end of their life.
Apart from the aggregated production capacity of the battery manufacturers, what is more pertinent for India is the battery chemistry and technology options that are trending, and the reasons behind the selection of these technologies being different from the rest of the world. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries have started gaining popularity all over the world due to cost savings and safety benefits of such technology. It was also stated that in the year 2025, the usage of LFP batteries in global EV batteries constitutes 55% of all the batteries. In addition, LFP batteries are 40% less expensive than NMC batteries. This makes the use of LFP batteries even more pertinent considering the fact that affordability of the batteries is very important in making the EVs affordable.
India is developing its battery cells manufacturing capacity as a part of the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cells (ACC). As of February 2026, at least 10 manufacturers have announced their production capacities of 178 GWh in the subsequent five years' period, helping to create the Indian battery industry.
India is exploring the opportunities of sodium-ion battery technology as a part of its energy storage and battery innovation ecosystem. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has conducted the assessment of the global sodium-ion battery market and its potential for applications in India in the framework of the India-UK ASPIRE programme. The use cases for sodium-ion technology include stationary battery storage and selected mobility applications.
The ACC PLI Scheme, budgeted at Rs. 18,100 crore (US$ 2.43 billion) aims to create 50 GWh ACC manufacturing capacity in India. Battery recycling becomes an important element of the ecosystem of critical minerals and clean energy in India. Within the framework of the National Critical Mineral Mission, the Government of India has approved a Rs. 1,500 crore (US$ 158.93 million) scheme to support recycling of critical minerals recovered from sources such as lithium-ion batteries. As of April 2026, 58 companies have become eligible for the scheme, taking the pledged recycling capacity to 850 KTPA and investments to around Rs. 5,000 crore (US$ 529.77 million).
India's battery ecosystem is expected to gain further momentum, supported by the continued growth of EV adoption and expanding domestic manufacturing capacity. EV registrations reached 25.36 lakh units in FY26, while the ACC PLI Scheme is supporting the development of 50 GWh of domestic Advanced Chemistry Cell manufacturing capacity.
Initiatives from the government such as PM E-DRIVE, investment in critical minerals and recycling of batteries have helped strengthen various sections of the battery value chain. Investments in cell production along with advances in new technologies like sodium-ion batteries and development of a recycling ecosystem are helping create an integrated industry in the field of batteries and energy storage in India.
India's EV registrations increased from 4.56 lakh units in FY22 to 25.36 lakh units in FY26, reflecting the rapid expansion of electric mobility in the country. Falling global battery pack prices, which reached US$ 108 per kWh in 2025, along with improvements in battery technology, have supported the growing affordability and adoption of EVs.
The Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) PLI Scheme, with an outlay of Rs. 18,100 crore, aims to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity. The scheme is supporting investments in cell manufacturing and helping strengthen India's battery manufacturing ecosystem.
India has negligible lithium reserves but is a major producer of soda ash, the key input for sodium-ion India is exploring sodium-ion batteries as part of its broader battery innovation and energy storage ecosystem. The technology offers opportunities for applications such as stationary energy storage and selected mobility segments, complementing India's growing battery technology landscape.
India's Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 establish an Extended Producer Responsibility framework for the collection and recycling or refurbishment of waste batteries. The Government is also supporting critical-mineral recycling, helping strengthen India's circular economy for battery materials.
Battery technology plays a central role in EV affordability, performance and safety. Technologies such as LFP batteries, along with growing investments in domestic cell manufacturing, advanced battery technologies and recycling, are supporting the development of India's electric mobility and energy storage ecosystem.

articles.title: China tech giants flood Nvidia with GPU orders to skirt US curbs - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: China tech giants flood Nvidia with GPU orders to skirt US curbs  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
China's ByteDance Ltd., Alibaba and Tencent are said to have ordered more than 3 million Nvidia graphics cards that meet U.S. semiconductor export controls. The order value tops $35 billion (about 47 trillion won), but China's total orders exceed Nvidia's expected output for next year by more than double, meaning actual supply is likely to be limited. Analysts say demand among Chinese corporations for AI compute semiconductors remains high despite U.S. controls on advanced chip exports.
On the 20th (local time), Reuters, citing three sources familiar with the matter, reported that China's three big tech firms ordered more than 3 million units of Nvidia's new graphics card, the "RTX PRO 5500." The product is priced at about $11,400 (about 15 million won) per unit, putting the list value of the order at more than $35 billion.
The RTX PRO 5500 is a workstation GPU installed in high-performance professional computers. Its compute performance is lower than Nvidia's cutting-edge AI accelerators used in large-scale data centers, but among products that comply with U.S. export rules to China, it ranks relatively high in performance.
Nvidia's Blackwell-based data center AI chip "B300" is currently banned from sale in China. The Hopper-based "H200" requires case-by-case review and export licenses from the U.S. government. As a result, Chinese corporations struggling to secure advanced AI Semiconductor chips are seen turning to the RTX PRO 5500, which faces relatively fewer export restrictions.
Chinese corporations plan to use the RTX PRO 5500 mainly for AI inference. Inference is the process by which a trained AI model answers user questions or generates content. It can be handled with comparatively less compute power than training a model on massive datasets.
Orders from Chinese corporations far exceed Nvidia's production plans. According to Reuters, RTX PRO 5500 orders from Chinese customers have surpassed 6 million units in total. By contrast, Nvidia has said it can produce up to about 3 million units worldwide in 2027. Orders placed in China alone amount to more than double next year's potential global output.
Nvidia has reportedly told customers and partners that it will be difficult to fulfill all orders. One source said Nvidia informed some partners they may receive only 5%–10% of their requested volumes.
The RTX PRO 5500 has similar performance to the "RTX 6000D," a China-bound graphics card Nvidia released last year. At the time, China's big tech firms held off purchases, judging the price high relative to performance. Expectations also played a role that, if U.S. export controls eased, they could buy more powerful AI Semiconductor chips.
But as controls dragged on and shortages of AI compute resources persisted, demand for the RTX PRO 5500 appears to have grown. The RTX 6000D is now discontinued, and its transaction price in China has reportedly doubled from the time of launch.
Nvidia's production strategy is also cited as a factor deepening the shortage. Starting next year, Nvidia is expected to allocate a significant portion of manufacturing capacity at TSMC, the world's largest semiconductor foundry corporation, to its next-generation AI Semiconductor platform "Rubin." With priority given to high-performance AI Semiconductor production for large data centers, expansion of RTX PRO 5500 supply could be limited.
Nvidia is expected to supply initial samples of the RTX PRO 5500 in December and begin commercial shipments in the first quarter of next year. Actual purchase contracts are also being signed in China. Tansun Technology, a Chinese fintech and AI computing services corporation listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, disclosed on the 13th that it signed a contract to buy 20,000 RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards. However, it noted that deliveries could be delayed or volumes reduced due to supply shortages and foreign technology controls.
Because of U.S. export controls, domestic corporations such as Huawei are increasing their share in China's AI Semiconductor market. According to market research firm IDC, Nvidia's share in China's data center AI Semiconductor market fell to 34% in the first half of this year. Huawei shipped 572,000 units for a 28% share.

Pete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada, says Canada made “a conscious decision” to move away from SpaceX, the company behind Starlink, as Ottawa puts billions of public dollars into Telesat’s Lightspeed satellite network instead.
Hoekstra made the comments on Tuesday at a space industry conference in Gatineau. That’s according to Tesla North, citing reporting from SpaceQ and The Globe and Mail. There’s some irony in Ottawa’s plan, since Telesat still needs SpaceX rockets to get those satellites into orbit.
Federal support for Lightspeed started with an $85 million investment in 2019. A year later, Ottawa committed up to $600 million for Lightspeed capacity that rural internet providers can buy. In September 2024, the federal government signed a $2.14 billion repayable loan with Telesat, and Quebec added a $400 million loan. Then on August 4, 2026, the Defence Investment Agency gave Telesat an Arctic military satellite contract worth about $2.3 billion to start.
Telesat booked 14 Falcon 9 launches with SpaceX back in 2023. Its release for the Arctic deal says the new satellites will be “launched by SpaceX on already-secured Falcon 9 rockets.” We covered that when Ottawa agreed to pay for Telesat’s Arctic satellites.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has been clear about where he stands. “Starlink, we will diversify away from, no question,” he told The New York Times in September, as we reported when Carney said he wants Canada off Starlink. Defence Minister David McGuinty said the Arctic contract is about “defending Canada’s sovereignty and security.”
Hoekstra said the US will plan around that choice, and he expects Elon Musk to find other partners. “If it’s not Canada, we’re moving forward; the space will be filled,” he said, according to the Globe.
SpaceX’s business keeps growing even as Ottawa moves away. In third-quarter results released Tuesday, SpaceX said Starlink had 13.6 million consumer subscribers as of September 30, up 1.6 million since June and nearly double a year earlier. The company posted net income of US$4.4 billion on revenue of US$14.6 billion, up 161 per cent from a year ago, making it SpaceX’s first profitable quarter since going public in June.
Ontario has its own mixed signals. The province cancelled its $100 million Starlink contract in 2025, yet the Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan has watched its SpaceX stake, bought for about $300 million in 2019, grow to nearly US$8.7 billion by June 30, according to the Globe. That jump came as SpaceX kept launching new Starlink satellites.
For now, Starlink is still sold to Canadian households, while Lightspeed’s military service isn’t expected until 2028.

articles.title: GM simulated 300,000 EV battery designs before building a single cell. Now comes the physical part - Fortune
articles.summary: GM simulated 300,000 EV battery designs before building a single cell. Now comes the physical part  Fortune
articles.full_text:
General Motors says it simulated more than 300,000 designs for its next EV battery before building a single physical cell. The run took 300 million CPU hours, or one computer running around the clock for 34,000 years, by GM’s math.
GM pitched the number Wednesday at its GM Forward event as proof it can halve the traditional four-to-five-year vehicle development process, to about two years. With the battery, the team went from first pack concept to formal program approval in one month.
Nearly every announcement ran on the same logic. GM’s self-driving software logs more than 3 billion simulated miles a day, against about 1 million real-world miles a month. Factory teams rehearse assembly in digital models.
Fortune reported Tuesday on the culture change gripping the top American auto-seller: engineers rewarded for missed stretch targets and a battery chief who says, “I want to see red.”
Sterling Anderson, the former Tesla Autopilot chief GM hired as chief product officer in 2025, recently told Fortune it’s “effectively the third phase in the evolution of product development for humanity,” built on “probabilistic, large data-requiring methods.” This is what he meant. That said, the battery won’t reach volume production until 2028.
A battery built on a long shot
The cells use lithium manganese-rich chemistry, or LMR, which GM says offers 33% more energy density than lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, the cheap chemistry China dominates, at comparable cost. They use roughly 30% to 40% nickel, battery engineer Andy Oury told Fortune, versus about 85% in today’s high-nickel cells. GM plans to build them with LG Energy Solution at their Ultium Cells joint venture in Spring Hill, Tenn.
“We’re not licensing this from China,” Kurt Kelty, GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, told Fortune. By his own account, most of the industry considers LMR a long shot, and GM made the call with perhaps 60% to 70% of the data. LMR has historically struggled with short cycle life and voltage decay, but GM believes it has solved that.
Proof will come from GM’s $900 million Battery Cell complex in Warren, Mich., due to be fully operational later this year and ramping toward a couple thousand cells a day.
The cone course
On Fortune‘s recent visit to Warren, Jason Fischer, a 28-year GM veteran who leads the AI push in engineering, demonstrated a digital car sliding off a cone course until engineers tuned it in simulation, work he said would take months with a real car. GM holds weekly “tall pole” reviews of whatever is slowing each job. “I’m convinced that we’re going to be able to do things just as fast as China,” Fischer said.
At GM Forward, the company said its fourth-generation EV platform should deliver about 20% more range per kilowatt-hour. It is expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter, with a 20% more compact pack and drive units with 40% fewer parts. In factories, GM’s PlantBrAIn platform has moved battery packs through assembly 30% faster, and Gen 4 vehicles will check their own wiring on the line. The platform will also carry an updated version of Super Cruise.
The brain goes into the Silverado
GM’s new central computer, with 40 times today’s processing power and 30% less wiring, debuts in 2028 on the Cadillac Escalade IQ, then spreads to GM’s highest-volume gas SUVs and trucks, three-row crossovers and Gen 4 EVs. It enables the other headline: autonomous highway driving, announced last year for the Escalade IQ, is coming to gas-powered full-size SUVs and light-duty pickups. Pre-production vehicles are testing on closed courses.
The driving software trains largely through self-play, with versions of itself playing the merging car and the surrounding traffic. Much of the method came from Cruise, the robotaxi unit GM absorbed in 2024. Rashed Haq, GM’s vice president of autonomous vehicles, told Fortune that GM kept “a lot of the methodologies” for the next-generation Super Cruise. Current Super Cruise customers have logged more than 1.2 billion hands-free miles.
The real-world miles come from hundreds of GM data-collection vehicles and from retail customers who have opted in to share data. GM says it has optimized its training enough that an improvement spotted in the software can reach the road within a single day.
An OnStar AI assistant arrives on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq via over-the-air update in the coming months. Anderson told Fortune a four-person team once had a voice prototype running in a Lyriq about 30 days after he asked for one.
Starting in 2027, a single OnStar app will replace OnStar Guardian and the separate Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet and GMC apps, adding cameras that automatically record incidents; GM says it can’t access the recordings. GM Fleet, about 20% of annual sales, gets its own AI assistant, and OnStar Fleet has more than 2.4 million subscribers, which GM says is twice its nearest competitor.
None of this is cheap. GM says it is investing more than $16 billion in U.S. R&D and manufacturing this year, after about $7.6 billion in EV-related charges last year.

articles.title: Here's how long it will take for quantum computing to become a reality - Invezz
articles.summary: Here's how long it will take for quantum computing to become a reality  Invezz
articles.full_text:
powered by
Buy QUBT. The CEO is tying the 2029 fault-tolerant target to a concrete error-correction milestone (Helios logical memory fidelity ~99.9995%). That de-risks the core bottleneck—keeping quantum information intact—so the market should re-rate the probability of Apollo hitting its timeline. This is the kind of technical proof that pulls forward customer and partner confidence.
Key Risk: Apollo’s error-correction results don’t scale to larger, fully integrated systems, pushing the 2029 timeline out materially.
Buy IONQ. If fault-tolerant progress is real, the whole quantum stack benefits: more credible timelines increase demand for quantum-ready algorithms, tooling, and hybrid workflows. Even before full fault tolerance, better error correction expands what can be run reliably, which lifts the value of quantum software and services across the sector.
Key Risk: The industry’s progress stalls (or competitors leap ahead), so fault-tolerant timelines slip and customers delay spending.
- Quantinuum CEO says quantum computing will be a reality by 2029.
- Rajeeb Hazra explained his view in a CNBC interview today.
- Quantinuum stock is currently down over 50% versus its YTD high.
Quantum computers already exist, but the race to make them reliably useful for demanding commercial applications has a more specific deadline: 2029, according to Quantinuum CEO Rajeeb Hazra.
Speaking with CNBC on October 21st, Hazra said a breakthrough in quantum error correction strengthens the company’s confidence in delivering Apollo, its planned universal fault-tolerant computer, that year.
“We are very confident now of realizing the vision in 2029,” he said.
That puts Quantinuum’s next major milestone roughly three years away, although translating laboratory progress into dependable business results remains a substantial undertaking.
Why this week’s error-correction breakthrough matters
Quantum computing’s promise depends on keeping fragile quantum information reliable long enough to complete useful calculations.
Errors can otherwise undermine results before a machine finishes its work.
Quantinuum’s October 19 announcement reported 99.9995% logical memory fidelity on its Helios computer, equivalent to approximately five uncorrectable errors per million error-checking cycles.
Crucially, that measures protected quantum memory rather than establishing that every operation in a commercial application achieves the same accuracy.
Hazra described the CNBC headline figure as “5 errors in a million operations.” The commercial significance lies in extending how much dependable computation a system can perform.
Hazra pointed to drug discovery, new materials and supply-chain optimization as intended applications, framing error correction as the bridge between quantum computing’s theoretical potential and customers’ practical needs.
What must happen before Apollo arrives in 2029?
Better accuracy is one requirement. Quantinuum must also manufacture larger systems, integrate its components, and preserve performance as computational demands increase.
“Our scaling path is very clear to us,” Hazra told CNBC, citing supply-chain preparations and strategic relationships with manufacturing partners.
He said that expansion draws on innovations familiar from microelectronics, including larger chips, increasingly complex packaging, optics and cryogenics.
The challenge is turning those ingredients into machines that customers can deploy and use consistently.
Importantly, 2029 remains a company target.
Quantinuum’s announcement acknowledges that experimental results might not translate to larger systems, logical computation, or commercial use, and that Apollo could miss its expected timeline.
The latest result strengthens the technical case for that schedule; it does not establish that the remaining engineering and commercial work is complete.
Quantum’s arrival could strengthen AI rather than replace it
Hazra’s vision extends beyond a standalone quantum machine. He sees quantum processors working alongside artificial intelligence and increasingly capable high-performance computing infrastructure.
“We actually see AI and quantum as very complementary,” he said.
In that model, AI could generate hypotheses while quantum computers help evaluate selected problems through more accurate measurements and simulations.
For businesses researching molecules or materials, the potential attraction is a tighter connection between proposing possibilities and testing their underlying behavior.
Those benefits still need demonstration in commercially valuable workflows.
Apollo’s arrival would therefore represent a milestone rather than an instant transformation across every industry.
As of October 21st, the clearest answer is that Quantinuum is targeting 2029 for its fault-tolerant system.
Whether that becomes a broader quantum revolution will depend on what customers can accomplish with it.
