Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Silvered Copper Busbars market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The world market for silvered copper busbars is entering a structurally stronger demand phase as electrification, high-frequency power conversion, and renewable energy infrastructure scale through 2035. Silvered copper busbars—copper conductive bars with a silver coating that lowers surface-contact resistance and resists oxidation—are increasingly specified in battery energy storage systems (BESS), electric-vehicle charging infrastructure, semiconductor and RF equipment, and precision industrial automation.
IndexBox projects the market to expand at a compound annual growth rate in the range of 5–8% over the 2026–2035 forecast horizon, with the strongest momentum in BESS and EV charging applications, where adoption is accelerating at 12–18% per year. Premium specifications, including controlled silver thickness above 2 µm, ultra-low surface roughness, and tight dimensional tolerances, command a 20–40% price uplift over standard commercial grades and are capturing a growing share of orders from semiconductor and RF equipment sectors.
Supply remains concentrated, with roughly 30–40% of global production capacity located in China, while Europe, North America, and parts of Southeast Asia operate smaller but technologically specialized facilities. Import dependence in several large end-use markets exceeds 50%, and qualification bottlenecks for certified suppliers create lead times of 6–14 weeks for qualified material. This report provides a data-driven view of market size, demand architecture, supply structure, trade flows, pricing logic, and competitive positioning, with a transparent analytical definition of product scope and segmentation.
The baseline scenario for the world silvered copper busbars market assumes continued electrification of energy and transport systems, steady expansion of renewable generation and storage capacity, and gradual recovery in industrial automation investment through the 2026–2035 forecast period. Under this scenario, global demand is projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate in the range of 5–8%, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to a materially higher level by 2035. Growth is front-loaded in BESS and EV charging infrastructure, where adoption rates of 12–18% per year outpace traditional industrial automation and power-distribution applications.
Premium specifications—controlled silver thickness above 2 µm, ultra-low surface roughness, and tight dimensional tolerances—are expected to capture a growing share of orders, particularly from semiconductor and RF equipment sectors, supporting value growth ahead of volume growth. Supply-side constraints remain a key variable: copper and silver together represent 60–75% of direct material cost, and silver spot price volatility of 20–35% in recent years creates margin pressure on fixed-price contracts. Qualification bottlenecks for ISO- and UL-registered busbar coaters, with lead times of 6–14 weeks for qualified material, may cap near-term upside in fast-growing segments.
Trade and tariff complexity, including multiple HS code headings and sector-specific certifications, adds procedural friction across borders. Regionally, Asia-Pacific remains the largest consumption and production center, while North America and Europe show above-average growth in BESS and EV charging applications. The baseline assumes no major demand-destroying recession and a gradual easing of silver price volatility as recycling and thrifting reduce silver usage per part by up to 15–20%.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Rapid buildout of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and EV charging infrastructure, where silvered busbar adoption is accelerating at 12–18% per year
- Rising electrification and renewable energy infrastructure investment, supporting demand for low-loss power distribution components
- Growth in high-frequency power conversion and RF equipment, where silver plating reduces surface-contact resistance and maintains performance
- Expansion of semiconductor and precision manufacturing capacity, driving demand for premium specifications with controlled silver thickness and tight tolerances
- Increasing specification of certified suppliers with documented process control (ISO 9001, IATF 16949), deepening supplier relationships and raising barriers to entry
- Adoption of plasma and electrolytic silver-coating technologies that improve uniformity and adhesion while reducing silver usage by up to 15–20% per part
Potential Growth Constraints
- Volatile input costs: copper and silver represent 60–75% of direct material cost, and silver spot prices have fluctuated by 20–35% in recent years
- Supplier qualification bottlenecks: limited number of ISO- and UL-registered busbar coaters with auditable quality records, causing lead times of 6–14 weeks
- Trade and tariff complexity: multiple HS code headings, origin rules, and sector-specific certifications (IEC 61439, UL 891) add administrative friction
- Supply chain concentration: roughly 30–40% of global production capacity is located in China, creating exposure to regional disruptions and trade policy shifts
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Industrial automation and instrumentation (estimated share: 28%)
Industrial automation and instrumentation represents a mature but steadily expanding demand base for silvered copper busbars. In this segment, busbars are used in control panels, drive systems, programmable logic controllers, and precision measurement instruments where low contact resistance and oxidation resistance are critical for signal integrity and long service life. Current demand is driven by factory automation upgrades, particularly in Asia-Pacific and Europe, where labor cost pressures and quality requirements favor automated production lines.
Through 2035, demand-side indicators to watch include industrial robot installations, PLC and drive shipment volumes, and capital expenditure in process industries such as chemicals, food and beverage, and pharmaceuticals. The segment is gradually shifting toward higher-specification busbars as automation equipment becomes more compact and power-dense, requiring tighter dimensional tolerances and improved surface finish. However, growth in this segment is slower than in BESS and EV charging, and price sensitivity is higher, with buyers often qualifying multiple suppliers to maintain competitive pricing. Replacement demand from aging installed systems provides a stable baseline, while new automation projects in emerging markets offer upside.
The segment is expected to maintain its position as the largest single application by share, though its relative weight will decline as BESS and EV charging expand faster. Current trend: Steady growth, with increasing specification of silvered busbars in precision control and measurement equipment.
Major trends: Compact, power-dense automation equipment requiring tighter tolerances and improved surface finish, Factory automation upgrades in Asia-Pacific and Europe driven by labor cost pressures, Increasing integration of busbars in modular control panels and drive systems, and Growing replacement demand from aging installed automation systems.
Representative participants: Siemens AG, Schneider Electric SE, ABB Ltd, Rockwell Automation, Inc, and Mitsubishi Electric Corporation.
Electronics and optical systems (estimated share: 18%)
Electronics and optical systems use silvered copper busbars primarily in high-frequency power conversion, RF amplifiers, laser systems, and optical communication equipment, where silver plating reduces surface-contact resistance and maintains low-loss performance at high frequencies. Demand in this segment is closely tied to capital spending in telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, and consumer electronics manufacturing. Through 2035, the key demand-side indicators include 5G and future 6G network buildout, data center capacity additions, and production volumes of high-end electronics and optical modules.
The segment is characterized by a strong preference for premium specifications, including controlled silver thickness above 2 µm and ultra-low surface roughness, which command a 20–40% price uplift over standard commercial grades. This premiumization trend is expected to continue as higher-frequency applications demand tighter performance characteristics. However, the segment is also exposed to cyclicality in electronics capital spending and to substitution risk from alternative conductor materials in some low-frequency applications. Geographically, Asia-Pacific dominates electronics manufacturing, but design and specification decisions are increasingly influenced by North American and European OEMs.
The segment's growth rate is expected to be moderate, slightly above industrial automation but below BESS and EV charging. Current trend: Moderate growth, with premium specifications gaining share in high-frequency and RF applications.
Major trends: Premiumization toward controlled silver thickness above 2 µm and ultra-low surface roughness, 5G and data center buildout driving demand for high-frequency power conversion components, Growing use of silvered busbars in RF amplifiers and optical communication equipment, and Substitution risk from alternative conductor materials in low-frequency applications.
Representative participants: Nokia Corporation, Ericsson AB, Cisco Systems, Inc, Furukawa Electric Co., Ltd, and Sumitomo Electric Industries, Ltd.
Semiconductor and precision manufacturing (estimated share: 22%)

articles.title: Talking Point: Quantinuum’s quantum error-correction breakthrough brings fault-tolerant computing closer - Intelligent CIO
articles.summary: Talking Point: Quantinuum’s quantum error-correction breakthrough brings fault-tolerant computing closer  Intelligent CIO
articles.full_text:
Quantum computing has spent years selling a future it cannot yet reliably deliver.
The machines are getting bigger, investment is accelerating and the promises remain extraordinary.
But one stubborn problem still stands between laboratory demonstrations and commercially useful systems: errors.
That is why Quantinuum’s latest breakthrough deserves attention beyond the usual quantum hype.
The company says its Helios trapped-ion computer achieved 99.9995% logical fidelity, equivalent to five errors per million operations. That represents a tenfold reduction in its own error rate since September and, according to Quantinuum, a hundredfold improvement over the strongest published result from competing hardware approaches.
Those numbers matter because quantum information is notoriously fragile. Qubits lose coherence, operations introduce noise and calculations become unreliable long before complex problems can be solved.
Error correction is therefore not an optional enhancement. It is the foundation on which practical quantum computing must be built.
The interesting development is not simply the headline record. Quantinuum achieved successive improvements using different error-correction codes on the same Helios hardware.
September’s Helix approach used ten physical qubits for each protected logical qubit. The latest experiment employed a color code using up to 37 physical qubits, trading greater resource consumption for substantially lower error rates.
That flexibility could prove as important as raw accuracy. Future quantum machines will need to balance reliability, speed and the enormous hardware overhead involved in protecting information. One universal coding strategy is unlikely to be optimal for every workload.
More encouragingly, Quantinuum reported that increasing code distance reduced logical errors exponentially, with each tested step improving suppression by a factor of twelve.
This is the sort of scaling behaviour researchers have sought for decades. It suggests that adding protection can genuinely make quantum computation more dependable rather than merely increasing complexity.
Yet important distinctions remain.
A record-setting logical operation is not the same as running a commercially valuable algorithm for hours. Nor does success on one hardware architecture automatically establish superiority across every performance measure.
Connectivity, processing speed, manufacturing scalability and operating costs will all influence which technologies ultimately prevail.
Quantinuum has linked its results to Apollo, its planned universal fault-tolerant system targeted for 2029. That timetable is ambitious, and the industry should judge it against demonstrated capabilities rather than projected milestones.
Nevertheless, the implications extend beyond one company.
Chemistry, materials discovery and other computationally demanding fields could eventually benefit from machines capable of executing lengthy calculations without errors overwhelming the results. But those applications require reliable logical operations at scale, not merely impressive laboratory benchmarks.
The quantum industry has become exceptionally skilled at announcing qubit counts, investment rounds and distant commercial possibilities. What it needs now is measurable engineering progress that makes those possibilities credible.
Quantinuum’s achievement offers precisely that kind of evidence, albeit within a carefully defined experimental setting.
The real breakthrough will come when error correction stops being the headline and becomes an invisible, dependable feature of everyday quantum computation.
That is a harder challenge than repeatedly setting records. Until then, accuracy matters more than ambition.

articles.title: XRlabs Raises $8.4M in Seed Round Funding to Expand AI Surgical Intelligence Platform - AI Insider
articles.summary: XRlabs Raises $8.4M in Seed Round Funding to Expand AI Surgical Intelligence Platform  AI Insider
articles.full_text:
Insider Brief
- XRlabs raised $8.4 million in seed funding led by Playground Global to expand its AI-powered Surgical Intelligence platform, which analyzes surgical data in real time and works with existing operating-room equipment.
- The company said its software has been used in more than 100 surgical cases across three continents and can combine live surgical video, navigation data and preoperative CT and MRI images into a single view.
- XRlabs plans to use the funding to expand its engineering and clinical teams, advance regulatory work in the U.K., Europe and the U.S., and build clinical evidence, while Omar Ishrak joins as board chair.
XRlabs has raised $8.4 million in seed funding led by Playground Global to develop and deploy an AI platform that analyzes surgical data in real time while working with equipment already used in operating rooms.
According to the startup, Eka Ventures also participated in the round and XRlabs also received a compute allocation from the U.K. AI Research Resource, the government-backed national AI computing infrastructure. The funding will go toward expanding its engineering and clinical teams, advancing the platform through regulatory processes in the U.K., Europe and the U.S., along with building clinical evidence across partner institutions on three continents.
The London-based company, which also has an office in Palo Alto, develops software that acts as an external AI layer for surgical systems. Its platform uses computer vision and deep learning to analyze live surgical video and combine it with information from other systems during an operation.
“Our conviction is that the operating room is the next frontier for physical AI,” neurosurgeon, founder and CEO Dr. Haddad said in the announcement. “Surgery generates extraordinary data, yet almost none of it becomes intelligence in the moments that matter most. This financing lets us change that at scale, moving Surgical Intelligence from landmark first cases to foundational infrastructure in every operating room.”
XRlabs said its software has already been used in several early clinical and research applications, including more than 100 surgical cases across three continents. The platform is designed to work across different devices rather than require hospitals to replace existing equipment.
The system can run with 4K 3D surgical scopes and connect with navigation systems. It combines live surgical video, navigation data and preoperative CT and MRI images into a single view intended to give surgical teams more information about what is happening during a procedure.
Surgical Intelligence
The company calls the approach Surgical Intelligence and describes the software as an AI co-pilot for operating-room teams. Rather than controlling a single piece of equipment, the platform is intended to connect information from different systems and provide real-time assistance during surgery.
Among them, XRlabs reported a first-in-human use of physical AI in cranial neurosurgery under research conditions with the ORBEYE 4K 3D exoscope. The company also said its technology was used to design patient-specific implants for the separation of craniopagus twins in work with U.K. charity Gemini Untwined.
XRlabs also was named a global Nvidia robotics partner and is using Nvidia Jetson Thor and Isaac for Healthcare technology for functions including low-latency perception, surgical-tool tracking and automation based on user intent, according to the company. XRlabs SIM, its system for AI and extended-reality surgical planning, was included among TIME’s Best Inventions of 2025.
Omar Ishrak Joins Board
Alongside the financing, XRlabs announced that Omar Ishrak has joined as chair of its board. Ishrak served as Medtronic chairman and chief executive from 2011 to 2020, previously chaired Intel’s board and currently serves on the boards of Amgen and Cleveland Clinic.

articles.title: Recent US government capital driving America's graphite projects - Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.summary: Recent US government capital driving America's graphite projects  Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.full_text:
US federal agencies have emerged as major backers of the country’s graphite anode supply chain. Across August and September, the US Army and Export-Import Bank (EXIM) have provided funding or land for projects that have struggled to secure private investment. In August, EXIM approved a USD $25 million direct loan for Phase I of Westwater Resources' Kellyton, Alabama plant under its Make More in America Initiative. Phase I is designed to produce ~12.5ktpa of coated spherical purified graphite (CSPG). “Loans, land and grants are lowering the cost of building plants, and tariffs are closing most of the running-cost gap,” said Tony Alderson, Research Manager at Benchmark. “With buyers increasingly willing to pay for traceable, non-Chinese material, US projects are closer to competing than headline costs suggest.”

China's electric vehicle (EV) exports have risen 132% in the first 9 months of 2026 compared to the same period last year. However, three policies are set to reshape the country's exports of EVs.

California Virtual Power Plant market supported by two new bills
In California, virtual power plants (VPPs) have been given a boost via two bills signed by outgoing Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom. The bills give VPPs both a market to sell into and a reason for utilities to buy from them. Newsom vetoed a separate bill for a community state solar program the same day.
Oct 16, 2026
Global EV sales reach 2.15 million units in September 2026
Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, specialising in EV and battery supply chain research and insights, reports that 2.15 million electric vehicles (EVs) were sold globally in September 2026, bringing year-to-date (YTD) 2026 EV sales to 15.5 million. In September 2026, EV sales increased by 17% month-on-month and decreased by -2% year-on-year.

Upstream and downstream policy push: Europe Regional Spotlight
Compared with China and the US, Europe’s upstream and downstream footprint in the global battery supply chain footprint is small. No major critical mineral used in the sector is mined or processed primarily on the continent, nor are cathode, anode or cell development and installation centred on the continent. However, a package of policies under the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) is looking to boost its manufacturing presence in the industry, required if Europe is to meet more of its own demand for electric vehicles (EVs) and battery energy stationary storage (BESS), both of which are anticipated to grow significantly through to 2040.
Oct 09, 2026
UK considering alignment with EU over tariff on Chinese EVs
While countries including the US, Turkey, and Mexico have been ramping up tariffs on electric vehicles (EVs) made in China, EV imports from China into the UK have continued to face a standard 10% import duty. The UK’s largest trading partner, the EU, introduced tariffs on China-made BEVs in 2024. In 2023, the last year when EVs made in China did not face additional tariffs from the EU, they accounted for 17% of total EV sales within the bloc. They broadly maintained this share until 2026, when over the first eight months of the year that share increased to 22% as Chinese automakers push into overseas markets against the backdrop of their subdued domestic environment. In comparison, China-made EVs accounted for 19% of EV sales in the UK in 2023, with that figure rising to 33% so far in 2026.

Can Cobre Panama copper mine run for 25 years without growing?
A commission convened by Panama’s government to decide how to manage the country’s controversial Cobre Panama copper mine has recommended 25 years of operation but without expanding the site’s physical footprint. The mine, run by First Quantum Minerals, was closed in 2023 after it was ruled unconstitutional following protests against its operation. The report also recommends steadily shrinking the existing footprint over this time, before eight years of “active closure” and 30 years of post-closure monitoring. Other non-negotiable criteria for reopening the site include compliance with existing Supreme Court rulings and laws around the project, ownership by the state, and the project must be financially self-sustaining. The report also calls for data transparency and supervision of the site to international standards, and priority given to concerns among affected Panamanian communities and businesses.

Lithium price reversal gets respite then deepens: Q3 2026 Lithium Price Review
Both lithium chemical and feedstock prices fell notably across Q3 2026, extending the lithium price correction that began in Q2. A volatile decline through July gave way to a notable August rally, before a sharp September reversal that erased the quarter's gains in a matter of days.

Rangebound trading persists as firm costs offset muted battery demand: Manganese Sulphate Q3 2026 Price Review
Benchmark’s Manganese Sulphate (32%) EXW China prices moved within a tight band through Q3 2026. This followed a Q1 surge driven by high sulphuric acid prices and the cancellation of export tax rebates on NCM precursors and cathode materials, and a small Q2 correction as off-season downstream operating rates slowed and idled capacity restarted. Manganese sulphate ended Q3 at RMB 7,116/tonne ($1,060/tonne), up 1.1% from the end of Q2. It hit a quarter low of RMB 7,043/tonne ($1,042/tonne) in mid-July and a high of RMB 7,178/tonne ($1,062/tonne) later in the month. Daisy Jennings-Gray, head of prices at Benchmark, said that “overall, seasonal restocking, tight supply and firm feedstock costs held prices steady in a quiet quarter, suggesting the next move is more likely to come from cost pass-through than from any shift in cathode chemistry demand.”

articles.title: Who controls intelligence? Open-weight models, institutional AI | Daily Sabah - Daily Sabah
articles.summary: Who controls intelligence? Open-weight models, institutional AI | Daily Sabah  Daily Sabah
articles.full_text:
Open-weight AI models could help Türkiye safeguard sensitive data, reduce dependence on foreign providers and build lasting institutional intelligence
Nvidia Ceo Jensen Huang used his first post on X not to promote a product, but to raise a question: Who should control advanced artificial intelligence? Sharing a letter titled "Open Weights and American AI Leadership,” Huang wrote in his post that open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.
The sovereignty issue Huang highlighted is also critically important for Türkiye. The central question is how institutions can use artificial intelligence without sending their data outside their own environments or becoming dependent on a single provider. Today, open-weight models offer one of the most realistic paths toward that goal. Türkiye took early steps in this direction. But real progress will come when national models and data infrastructures evolve into systems that continuously learn from each institution’s own data.
So why choose open-weight models? They expand access and competition while enabling customization, independent security research, and technological sovereignty. They allow institutions to adapt models while keeping sensitive data within their own environments, retain ownership of accumulated knowledge, and avoid dependence on a single provider.
Hidden cost of closed models
There is no disputing that closed models currently offer frontier-level performance, managed infrastructure, and technical support. But every institution using these models sends its data to the provider’s servers. The provider determines pricing, terms of use, and when a model version will change or be discontinued. More importantly, access itself depends on the political decisions of another country.
This summer, we witnessed a concrete example. Due to export controls imposed by the U.S. Department of Commerce, access to Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models was briefly suspended worldwide on June 12, 2026. Access that can be cut off overnight by another country’s decision cannot be the sole foundation for critical operations such as public services, defense, health care or finance. Moving workloads that process sensitive data and require uninterrupted availability to open-weight models is therefore not a choice, but a necessity.
Dependence has a quieter face: shadow AI. Without secure, capable internal AI, employees turn to closed-source chatbots through personal accounts. Contracts, customer records, source code, and internal correspondence can reach servers abroad without the institution knowing. Bans do not solve the problem; they merely hide it. The remedy is an internal alternative at least as useful as external tools.
The need for open-weight models in defense has also been demonstrated in practice. In July, an OpenAI agent undergoing testing escaped its controlled environment and infiltrated Hugging Face’s systems. According to Nvidia, when the safety filters of closed models could not distinguish the attacker from the defender, Hugging Face ran the open-weight GLM 5.2 model on its own infrastructure, analyzed more than 17,000 actions, and stopped the attack. In a crisis, a model operating in your own environment and under your own rules may prove more valuable than the best closed model.
What should institutions choose?
The right choice depends on the capabilities required, the sensitivity of the data, in-house technical expertise, risks, licensing terms, and the importance of avoiding dependence on a single provider. But on-premises AI is not inherently secure. Hardware investment, operating model-serving infrastructure, managing updates and security, and monitoring performance all require substantial in-house expertise in large language model operations (LLMOps). Such expertise cannot be built through a patchwork of tools; it requires an end-to-end platform.
An institutional AI platform needs four layers: the first is a data pipeline to collect, clean, and prepare training data; second is a model pipeline to fine-tune, compress, and evaluate open-weight models; third is a serving layer offering models through standard internal interfaces, with access controlled by keys and quotas; and lastly, agents that work with institutional documents, cite sources, and access databases or other tools as needed. Sensitive data and models must remain within the institutional network, with every model traceable from training data to response endpoint. Today, even 120-billion-parameter open-weight models can run on a single datacenter GPU, while 30-billion-parameter models fit on a powerful personal computer. This architecture is accessible not only to technology giants but also to medium-sized public institutions. Institutions can therefore keep sensitive-data agents on their own servers while using controlled cloud access for lower-risk tasks.
An often-overlooked component is the verification layer. A large language model generates answers, but smaller, specialized decision models can check whether they are source-supported, whether retrieved documents answer the question, and whether training data is correctly labeled. This layer also safeguards the quality of data entering the learning loop.
Türkiye’s priority
Türkiye has taken an important step in this direction. Bilge, a family of Turkish large language models developed by TÜBITAK Bilgem, was unveiled at the Türkiye AI Summit on June 13, 2026, alongside the country's 2026-2030 AI Action Plan. Yet, developing national models is only the beginning. Their long-term value will depend on institutions' ability to adapt and continuously improve them using their own data and feedback.
The first link in this transformation is data infrastructure. No model can learn from real-world operations without infrastructure that collects, cleans, labels, and securely stores usage data, examples of errors, and expert corrections from the field. In November 2022, before ChatGPT introduced the world to generative AI, Türkiye’s Presidency of Defense Industries unveiled the Defense Industry Artificial Intelligence Platform. The platform brought data, model training and computing power under one roof. Evren, opened for general access in September 2026, took this structure a step further. Data is processed on infrastructure located in Türkiye, 11 open-weight language models are offered through a single interface, and the shared knowledge pool grows as users upload and label data. This vision, which began in the defense industry, needs to spread to every sector and public institution, starting with health care, energy, finance, and agriculture.
Türkiye’s approach to developing and fine-tuning sector-specific AI models should be strengthened by a feedback mechanism that continuously channels data from real-world applications into model development. Models would then cease to be one-off projects and become institutional assets that learn from practice and improve over time. Open-weight models are the essential tool for enabling this cycle while keeping data within the institution. This approach also aligns with the goals for the data ecosystem, computing infrastructure, and domestically developed models set out in Türkiye’s AI Action Plan, which came into effect on Aug. 18, 2026. The crucial question is whether data from the field, examples of errors, and expert corrections will be integrated into an institutional learning loop. If that loop is established, Türkiye can develop a body of capabilities that becomes increasingly differentiated through its own sector-specific data and cannot easily be replicated from outside. Ultimately, model sovereignty is less about owning a model than about owning this learning loop.
Institutional memory
AI sovereignty is the ability of an institution or a state to operate, manage and control AI systems within its own legal, physical and operational boundaries. Where models run, how data flows, who holds the weights, who can access the capabilities, and which country’s laws apply are all elements of this capacity. Model sovereignty lies at the heart of this structure, because it is precisely at this layer that an institution’s knowledge accumulates over time.
As an institution adapts an AI model to its documents, terminology, workflows, and decision-making processes, the system gradually becomes part of its institutional memory. Methodological know-how, customer experience, and operational intuition built up over years are then stored not only in employees’ minds and archives, but also in the weights of a fine-tuned model. This accumulated knowledge is among the hardest institutional assets to replicate, because it cannot be purchased; it can only be developed through experience. By retaining control over the systems behind critical decisions, institutions can make AI an integral part of their own intelligence.

articles.title: Vulcan Elements, UNC Team Up to Improve Rare Earth Magnets - The Quantum Insider
articles.summary: Vulcan Elements, UNC Team Up to Improve Rare Earth Magnets  The Quantum Insider
articles.full_text:
Insider Brief
- Vulcan Elements is partnering with the North Carolina Collaboratory and UNC-Chapel Hill to develop higher-performance rare earth magnets for defense and commercial applications.
- Supported by a $600,000 research award, the team will use quantum-mechanical simulations to predict how atomic-level changes affect magnetic properties.
- Vulcan’s factory under construction in Benson, North Carolina, is planned to produce 10,000 metric tons of magnets annually and create 1,000 manufacturing jobs.
Vulcan Elements, an American rare earth magnet manufacturer, today announced a partnership with the North Carolina Collaboratory to advance the development of high-performance rare earth magnets for critical defense and commercial technology applications.
The collaboration brings together Vulcan Elements and leading scientific expertise at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC-Chapel Hill), where research led by chemistry professor Yosuke Kanai, PhD, will develop a novel analytic capability using quantum-mechanical simulations to predict with significant accuracy how changes at the atomic level affect magnetic properties, ultimately setting a new standard for Vulcan’s magnetic performance.
The partnership represents a convergence of two research fields that are foundational to national security and the future economy: rare earth magnets and quantum mechanics. The research will pair Kanai’s more than 25 years of experience in computational materials research with Vulcan Elements’ expertise in manufacturing rare earth magnets.
The Collaboratory is supporting the partnership through a $600,000 research award, helping support the application of UNC-Chapel Hill’s scientific expertise to advance rare earth magnet innovation. Established by the North Carolina General Assembly in 2016, the Collaboratory works with academic experts across the state to transform research into practical applications for the benefit of North Carolina. Since its inception, the Collaboratory has managed more than $300 million in state appropriations and supported more than 800 research projects.
“This collaboration with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill reflects Vulcan Elements’ commitment to driving the next generation of magnetics innovation and fostering the American magnetics workforce,” said John Maslin, Vulcan Elements’ CEO. “This collaboration is a model for the kind of public-private partnerships that this nation needs: generating cutting-edge breakthrough technologies and translating them into real-world manufacturing capabilities that deliver for our economy and national security.”
“Rare earth magnets are increasingly important to our national security and economy, and North Carolina has an opportunity to play a meaningful role in this growing sector,” said Jeff Warren, PhD, executive director of the NC Collaboratory. “This partnership is exactly the kind of work the Collaboratory was created to support when we were established by the NC General Assembly—connecting world-class research expertise in our state with industry in order to solve real-world challenges. By bringing Dr. Kanai’s computational research together with Vulcan’s synthesis and manufacturing capabilities, we can help advance innovation that has implications well beyond the laboratory.”
The collaboration comes as demand for rare earth magnets is rapidly growing across industries vital to national security and economic competitiveness. Rare earth magnets are required components in critical technologies from semiconductor fabrication, robotics, and automobiles to drones, satellites, and virtually every military system. For decades, the United States has been reliant on China for these magnets. Today, China produces up to 98% of the global supply. To its knowledge, Vulcan is the only rare earth magnet company in the world that is decoupled from China—down to the material, technology, software, IP, and ownership. The partnership with UNC-Chapel Hill advances this mission by bolstering a robust magnetics and manufacturing workforce. It also highlights Vulcan’s commitment to innovating and leveraging advanced capabilities in order to develop leapfrog technologies and deliver the highest performance at competitive prices.
Vulcan Elements’ Benson, North Carolina, manufacturing facility, currently under construction, will be the cornerstone of a domestic rare earth magnet supply chain and the largest rare earth magnet factory outside of China. The 1.1 million-square-foot facility will have an annual capacity of 10,000 metric tons of magnet production and will supply magnets for critical defense systems, semiconductor fabrication, robotics, drones, AI infrastructure, automobiles, and other strategic technologies and sectors of the American economy. The project will create 1,000 manufacturing jobs in North Carolina while reshoring an essential capability that has been controlled and weaponized by America’s competitors for decades.

articles.title: To replace Starlink, Europe will have to reawaken its animal spirits - Financial Times
articles.summary: To replace Starlink, Europe will have to reawaken its animal spirits  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
In the new race for space, Europe has already fallen so far behind that catching up looks barely conceivable. Yet last week’s reports of disruptions to Starlink services in Ukraine show that catch up it must, at least when it comes to satellite-based communications. This will require more creative solutions than simply writing large cheques.
At the moment, Europe’s main alternative to Starlink for the satellite connectivity that has proved so crucial to Ukraine is Eutelsat’s OneWeb. But they are in different leagues. Not only does OneWeb have some 600 low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites compared with over 10,000 for Starlink, but these are positioned further away from Earth: time, and thus proximity, is of the essence in battlefield combat.
That leaves Europe scrambling to put in place alternative arrangements. One of these is IRIS², led by European satellite operators SES, Eutelsat and Hispasat, with first launches expected in 2029. Its planned fleet was recently expanded to 348 satellites across low and medium Earth orbit. Meanwhile, telecoms companies Vodafone, Telefónica, Orange and Deutsche Telekom have clubbed together to express interest in acquiring part of the spectrum to provide mobile satellite coverage that Europe wants to reserve for domestic use.
Europe doesn’t quite need to replicate Elon Musk’s brainchild, of course: offering satellite-enabled broadband to rural communities is valuable rather than strategically vital. But it does need to be able to replicate its capabilities in defence, and there is no world in which that doesn’t require huge subsidies.
For a rough idea of the numbers, the recent €15.6bn budget for the IRIS² constellation suggests an all-in cost per satellite of more than €40mn. Elon Musk’s most recent version of Starlink comes to $1.3mn on New Street numbers and provides a multiple of the capacity to boot.
That’s a big wedge for governments to fill. But even splurging on homegrown options won’t, by itself, solve Europe’s problem in anything like a reasonable length of time: technology, corporate structure and local culture are all limiting factors too.
The rocket-launching technology that SpaceX excels at is an obvious bottleneck: last year, only 7 per cent of European-owned satellites launched on European rockets, according to Berenberg analysis. SES is highly indebted, while Eutelsat — recapitalised with government support earlier this year — lacks sufficient operating cash flows to support its capital expenditure. Space capabilities are fragmented among different countries and defence contractors.
To have any hope of catching up with the US, then, Europe may well have to provide its companies with looser reins and bigger carrots. Already, there are signs that it is leaning that way. One incentive is for governments to place large orders — that will provide SES with at least €500mn of incremental revenue between 2030 and 2035, Goldman Sachs estimates.
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has espoused fast-tracking competition approval for Airbus, Thales and Leonardo’s proposed combination of their space capabilities, and telecoms companies hope to be allowed to merge, even when that reduces competition. The tight regulation of telcos, which ensures they provide an affordable and reliable service, may also have had the side effect of making them less willing to experiment and innovate.
Such moves won’t be cost-free for European consumers, but that may be the cost of bringing European tech firms a little closer to Silicon Valley, in spirit at least. The situation in Ukraine shows how much there is at stake.

The U.S. Space Force has approved the launch of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying 27 Starlink satellites into low-Earth orbit Tuesday afternoon from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base.
The spontaneous launch window for the Starlink 15-25 mission opens between 3:14 and 7:14 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 20.

articles.title: Not IonQ. Not Rigetti Computing. This Quantum Computing Stock Is the One I'd Buy and Hold Through 2030. - The Motley Fool
articles.summary: Not IonQ. Not Rigetti Computing. This Quantum Computing Stock Is the One I'd Buy and Hold Through 2030.  The Motley Fool
articles.full_text:
Classical computers process information using bits, generally illustrated by 0s and 1s. Quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, to tackle extraordinarily complex calculations that today's supercomputers struggle with. Quantum computing is promising to transform critical industries such as drug discovery, materials science, cybersecurity, and financial services. Naturally, investors are looking for the next big winner in this pocket of the artificial intelligence (AI) realm.
IonQ (IONQ +3.26%) and Rigetti Computing (RGTI +3.35%) are two of the most closely followed pure-play quantum computing stocks. The catch is that neither company has built a consistently profitable business because commercially useful quantum computing remains years away.
Meanwhile, Alphabet (GOOGL -1.62%) (GOOG -1.62%) has achieved some important breakthroughs in the quantum computing landscape. Let's break down what makes Alphabet a unique player in the quantum landscape to understand why the stock looks like an interesting buy right now.
IonQ and Rigetti have enormous financial risk
On the surface, it might look like IonQ has made impressive progress in expanding its quantum computing platform. The company has spent the last few years rounding out its business to include quantum hardware, networking, and cybersecurity. During the second quarter, IonQ's revenue surged 287% year over year to approximately $80 million. However, some of that growth reflects acquisitions rather than organic growth from the original operation.
Acquisitions can be expensive, particularly when companies issue stock to finance the transactions. On Oct. 14, IonQ announced a $2 billion equity offering involving common shares and warrants. I suspect the raise is meant to fund product development and further acquisitions. Whatever the case, the opportunity cost for investors is the risk of dilution.
Rigetti faces a different challenge. During the second quarter, the company generated just $5.1 million in revenue while reporting an operating loss of $28.1 million. The company's revenue remains small and lumpy, making it difficult to predict when the business might reach profitability.
Investors considering a position in IonQ or Rigetti Computing need to weigh their upside potential against continuous operating losses, uncertain commercialization timelines, and the likelihood of future shareholder dilution.
Google's latest quantum breakthrough could be a game changer
On Oct. 15, Google's Quantum AI division announced a breakthrough involving its Willow quantum processor. The development addresses one of quantum computing's biggest challenges: error correction. Quantum computers are extremely sensitive machines. Google demonstrated a technique called magic state cultivation, which reduced errors by 40x compared with earlier testing.
This breakthrough doesn't mean Google has built a fully functional, commercially useful quantum computer. However, it represents important progress toward machines capable of performing sophisticated calculations more reliably. Moreover, Google has an advantage over its smaller competitors in that the company can afford to keep experimenting.
Alphabet stock looks like a magnificent long-term buy
Alphabet currently trades at a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. While that might not look like a bargain, investors are purchasing a profitable technology giant with multiple opportunities to expand earnings through 2030.
Alphabet already operates several profitable businesses across Google Search, YouTube, Android, and Google Cloud. These operations provide the financial flexibility to support ongoing research that might not generate meaningful revenue for several years.
Nevertheless, quantum computing is yet another component of Google's technology stack that could complement Gemini, custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), and enterprise cloud infrastructure. Unlike IonQ or Rigetti, Alphabet doesn't need investors to assign a premium valuation to businesses generating relatively little revenue and no profits. Instead, its established operations can support continued research while investors benefit from existing earnings power.
For now, the operating losses, financing needs, and uncertain revenue trajectories of IonQ and Rigetti make them heavily speculative investments. On the other hand, Alphabet offers exposure to new quantum technology without depending on its immediate success.
Combined with the company's robust profitability, expanding AI ecosystem, and reasonable valuation, I see Alphabet as the best quantum computing stock to buy and hold through 2030.

articles.title: Amazon is buying billions in Nvidia AI systems it can't yet turn on - Business Insider
articles.summary: Amazon is buying billions in Nvidia AI systems it can't yet turn on  Business Insider
articles.full_text:
Amazon is racing to secure AI hardware earlier than before, even as data center power shortages leave some GPU systems waiting in warehouses.
Under a new Early Rack Receipt process, AWS expected to receive roughly $5 billion in Nvidia's GB300 server racks at US facilities before final deployment, according to August internal emails reviewed by Business Insider. The company projected roughly $3 billion more in GB300 racks each month "for the foreseeable future," one of the emails said.
Some AWS sites had room for more racks but not enough available power to turn them on, people familiar with the effort said, leaving finished equipment to be staged at intermediary warehouses until the facilities were ready.
At least one AWS team did not have "a clear forecasted path" for getting the incoming racks into data centers at the time, according to one of the emails.
Dark GPUs
A lack of new electricity capacity is one of several bottlenecks slowing the buildout of some AI data centers. This has led to a phenomenon known as dark GPUs, where AI chips and servers are purchased but can sit idle due to power supply issues or other challenges. (Dark GPUs can also refer to system design flaws that mean this gear isn't fully used after being plugged in).
This is partly why financial pressure is mounting on big data center projects. Money must be spent upfront to secure supplies of Nvidia GPUs and other valuable AI components. But if some data centers aren't ready to run, those early investments can tie up huge amounts of cash. Debt financing can fill in the gaps, but the market has become less willing to lend against some of these projects lately.
Trade-off
Amazon's early-rack program is one piece of the cloud leader's broader AI buildout, which is putting new pressure on its cash flow, as Business Insider exclusively reported this week. Amazon expects roughly $220 billion in capital expenditures this year — more than any Big Tech peer. Its free-cash-flow turned negative last quarter for the first time since 2023, and could stay negative for a while.
For AWS, the trade-off is securing scarce GPU racks before competitors do, even if some data centers are not yet ready to turn them on. But taking ownership earlier can tie up billions in equipment before it starts generating cloud revenue.
Previously, AWS took ownership of a finished rack only upon delivery to a data center, according to internal documents. Under the new approach, it can pay for and record certain racks earlier in the supply chain.
An Amazon spokesperson said the company routinely stages finished hardware near deployment sites so it can install it once capacity becomes available, calling the practice "best business practice." The spokesperson added that Amazon has long-established systems for tracking infrastructure assets and disputed that the broader company lacked a path for getting racks into data centers.
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy previously said the company has a "clear line of sight" to strong returns from its AI investments, calling the technology a "once in a lifetime opportunity."
"We've been through this cycle with the first big AWS growth wave, and liked the results," Jassy wrote in Amazon's annual shareholder letter. "We expect to feel similarly about this next wave."

Update (Oct. 21, 2026): This article has been updated to include new reporting from The Wall Street Journal that Elon Musk personally ordered restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink service.
Calls to nationalize Elon Musk's SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) have resurfaced amid a dispute over restrictions on satellite services used by Ukraine's military, raising questions about private control of critical military technology.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters over the weekend that restrictions on Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are preventing Ukraine from using certain drones to intercept Russian attacks.

"Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said during an online exchange with reporters, referring to a type of drone. He said, according to CBS News, "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately."
Zelenskyy said he was told the restrictions were due to technical issues, although the systems appeared to be working normally across the European Union. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has also tried to contact SpaceX about the problem, without success.
"Nobody there is answering our military," he said.
According to CBS reporting, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that Starshield is "not at this moment available to Ukraine," adding, "That's under conversation. It's under discussion right now about how they would want to use it."
Rubio said the U.S. government was not responsible for the service outage in Ukraine.
"I'm not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about," he said.
However, new reporting from The Wall Street Journal indicates that Musk personally ordered the slowdown of the military-grade Starlink service on Oct. 14, limiting the speeds at which Ukrainian drones could maintain a satellite connection. The restrictions have disrupted both offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept Russian attacks.
Musk later claimed that restrictions on Starlink speeds and usage were determined by the U.S. military and ultimately the president. Trump, on the other hand, told reporters Monday that he did not know who was responsible for the slowdown.

Intel has asked the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to make an exception for the automated guided vehicles (AGVs) that the company uses to transport the sensitive silicon wafers and other materials, containers, and supplies needed to make the most advanced chips in its fabs. According to Bloomberg, the American chipmaker fears that its AGVs would fall under the blanket prohibition against foreign-made robots after they were added to the FCC's Covered List.
Go deeper with TH Premium: Chipmaking

AGVs are niche machines that chip fabs use to transport materials and supplies between tools and sections of the fab, helping ensure that the cleanroom conditions required for each manufacturing process are maintained. This makes them critical equipment for U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, but, apparently, there are no suitable domestic alternatives for these devices at the moment. Intel's current fleet of AGVs requires continuous maintenance, including software and firmware updates, and if it's forced to find a local supplier for its AGVs, the company says that it would take years, crippling the United States' chipmaking efforts.
The biggest AGV suppliers are Japanese companies like Murata Machinery and Daifuku Co., while a few smaller businesses from South Korea and Taiwan are also trying to break into the market. It's unclear why these companies haven't applied for a conditional approval yet, which would allow them to continue selling these products in the U.S. while also promising Washington that they'll set up a manufacturing base in the country. This is something that Netgear has already done, allowing it to continue selling its foreign-made routers despite being an American company.
Intel says that it remains unclear if updates to its AGVs would break compliance with the FCC, and that it's asking the agency to issue a conditional waiver "out of an abundance of caution to ensure the ongoing operation of these specific AGV units." While Team Blue is the only company concerned about AGVs at the moment, other chip manufacturers would likely need a similar waiver in the near future, especially as they build more fabs in the U.S. This includes TSMC, which is planning to build 12 more fabs and four packaging facilities in Arizona, Samsung, with its new Taylor, Texas, fab, and even Elon Musk's Terafab, which has already begun construction.

articles.title: Quantinuum Breaks Error-Correction World Record by 10x, Validating Its Leading Path to Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing by 2029 - AZoQuantum
articles.summary: Quantinuum Breaks Error-Correction World Record by 10x, Validating Its Leading Path to Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing by 2029  AZoQuantum
articles.full_text:
Quantinuum, a leading full-stack quantum computing company, today announced a world-record quantum error-correction result, achieving a logical fidelity of 99.9995% on its Helios commercial computer using the company's error-correction architecture. This marks Quantinuum's second breakthrough in two months, demonstrating how its highly accurate trapped-ion hardware and flexible architecture work together to deliver rapid improvements in accuracy.
The achievement reinforces Quantinuum's error-correction leadership and validates that its accuracy performance is now within the target range for Apollo, the company's planned universal fault-tolerant quantum computer expected to be available by 2029.
Quantinuum's architecture is an end-to-end framework programmable through the company's developer platform. It integrates tailored AI decoders, all-to-all qubit connectivity, high-fidelity physical operations, and hardware-level error correction. This architecture also allows the company to test, refine, and combine different error-correction codes and optimize between accuracy and efficiency.
In the latest study, Quantinuum used a well-known 'color code' within this architecture to achieve the world-record logical fidelity result, which is equivalent to just five errors per million operations. The error rate is 10 times lower than Quantinuum's own world record achieved last month and 100 times lower than the best published result across all other hardware modalities, which was reported by Google Quantum AI on a superconducting system.
"With this result, we've proven that we have the error-correction architecture and trapped-ion technology required to achieve universal fault-tolerance," said Dr. Rajeeb Hazra, CEO of Quantinuum. "We have reduced error rates tenfold in rapid succession using a different code on the same commercial hardware, demonstrating the flexibility of our error-correction architecture. We've crossed the threshold necessary for exponential improvements in accuracy, reinforcing our path to Apollo and how we can help users unlock commercial value from quantum at scale."
The study also showed that logical errors fell exponentially as Quantinuum increased the 'code distance,' a technique used to understand how many physical qubits are needed to protect quantum information as the error correction scales. Each tested increase reduced the remaining logical errors by a record factor of 12, demonstrating increasingly effective error suppression as the code grows – a critical capability for scaling fault-tolerant quantum computing. Quantinuum believes this result suggests it can deliver fault-tolerance with significantly fewer qubits than are required for other modalities.
"This is a significant milestone that quantum computing researchers have been working toward for many years," said Robin Blume-Kohout, Co-director of Sandia National Laboratories' Quantum Performance Lab, who was not involved in the study. "The paper demonstrates real, serious performance gains from quantum error correction – a logical qubit nearly 100x better than its component physical qubits. A scaled-up version of this system could reach the reliability required for useful fault-tolerant computation at a feasible size – less than a million physical qubits – which improves the outlook for practical quantum computing. These findings go a long way to retire one of the field's central technical risks."
In September 2026, Quantinuum used the same error-correction architecture with its Helix code to demonstrate record-setting logical memory and computation. Both studies ran on the same Helios hardware.
The two demonstrations illustrate how Quantinuum can rapidly prototype different error-correction codes within the same architecture to optimize for relative strengths in accuracy, efficiency, and speed. On Helios, Helix used 10 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with up to 37 for the color code, while the color code delivered lower logical error rates. This provides insight into which applications pair best with each code as systems advance toward fault-tolerance.
Quantinuum's error-correction architecture is flexible, allowing for adaptive syndrome extraction, which adjusts error-checking measurements during computation, and chain-mapping, which connects codes suited to different computational tasks. Together with efficient code structures and real-time decoding, these techniques provide multiple ways to reduce errors and resource requirements.
Quantinuum is combining its hardware, error-correction architecture, and full-stack software platform into an integrated system for fault-tolerant quantum computing. As customers prepare for this next era of computing, Quantinuum is providing the tools needed to develop and scale quantum applications capable of addressing challenges across materials science, chemistry, finance, logistics, and other critical sectors.

articles.title: To heal sick cities, scientists and residents must work together
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03161-5Tolullah Oni has developed a platform to transfer the intellectual capital of African diaspora scholars back to the continent.
articles.full_text:

the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles

In 2016, public-health physician Tolullah Oni was jogging through the streets of Dakar when she saw someone doing push-ups in the middle of a busy roundabout. Cars were puffing fumes around him as the Sun baked down. As a physician, she knew that this had health implications.
More than half of the global population now lives in urban areas, but many cities are not conducive to human health and well-being. Oni, who is a researcher at University of Cambridge, UK, describes herself as an urban epidemiologist whose patients are cities. She works with colleagues around the world to diagnose and treat ‘sick’ cities with the goal of improving the health and quality of life of their inhabitants. This involves monitoring several variables, such as air quality and temperature, and their impact on the city’s residents. Those data can inform advocacy and interventions.
Frustrated by a lack of infrastructure on the ground in such cities, and by the struggle to connect researchers and residents, she set up the non-profit organization UrbanBetter in 2019 to support her research and advocacy. By providing training on data collection and analysis, the organization helps citizens and local researchers to diagnose their own cities and to use that evidence to lobby for change. Its research arm, the UrbanBetter Academy, has a centre in Cambridge, and its civic arm, called Cityzens Hubs, operates in 11 cities in Africa, as well as in Bogotá and Bangkok.
Oni, who was born in Nigeria, identifies as African diaspora, which she classifies as a “sixth distinct region of the African continent”. Now based in the United Kingdom, she recognizes the friction that comes with trying to treat cities that she does not live in. Oni tells Nature how she wants to create lasting virtual infrastructure through UrbanBetter that channels the diaspora’s intellectual capital back into the continent and heals sick cities.
How can a doctor diagnose and treat cities?
Cities can’t tell you that they’re sick, so you must bring the symptoms to light first. What are the lungs or air quality doing? What is happening in the green spaces? How is the city metabolizing energy? What is happening to its waste? If you don’t have the data, you don’t know whether the city is sick and in a lot of our cities, we’re not even measuring those things.
It is important that the people who are identifying the symptoms are on the ground in that city, rather than me, a professor, sitting thousands of kilometres away in Cambridge. People there are breathing the air and moving through the city. We have to equip local people with the skill set to diagnose a city. The diagnostic tests can be done by sensors and their data can be mapped.
In cities, we need treatments to be grounded in lived realities. Outsiders can assess a city and propose a solution, backed by evidence, but it might not work for many reasons. We need to include residents. They can identify priority areas and advocate for change. For example, in Nairobi, a group of Cityzens collected air-pollution data and convened their own community assembly in 2025 to identify potential solutions, such as cleaner public transport, adding trees and green spaces and reducing open burning of rubbish. These points fed directly into the government’s Nairobi City County Air Quality Action Plan.
Developing treatments for a city is a collective effort and accountability is spoon-feeding that medicine in the form of small, incremental changes so that the city can get better.
How does UrbanBetter help cities?
I set up UrbanBetter in 2019 as an experimental platform that would situate research differently by combining it with action and advocacy. We started with a US$300,000 unrestricted grant from the funding organization Unorthodox Philanthropy, which is sponsored by the Lampert Byrd Foundation based in San Francisco, California.
Each of UrbanBetter’s hubs has different strengths — Lagos works on physical activity, air pollution and heat, whereas Bogotá has done work on transport, cycling and car-free days. This means that when another city wants to work in a new area, they don’t have to reinvent the wheel.
Ahead of the 2025 Lagos City Marathon, the local Cityzens Hub partnered with World Athletics’ project Running for Clean Air. The marathon takes place in February, which is among the hottest times of year in Lagos, and the city has high levels of air pollution.
Throughout 2025, a group of residents ran the marathon route each month, starting in the January before the marathon. They wore air-quality sensors and collected geotagged data with the UrbanBetter app. Some runners found that there was a 60% reduction in air pollution on the actual marathon day because cars were barred from the roads. These findings have informed a shift in transportation-policy implementation in the city, which is now targeting net-zero emissions by 2050. Government initiatives include increased cycling and walking, an overhaul of public transport and increased air-quality monitoring.
The Cityzens Hub then identified heat as another major issue for city dwellers, so they reached out to the UrbanBetter Academy for help analysing complex data. In 2025, researchers from UrbanBetter, local partner institutions and the Lagos Transport Authority received a £2-million [roughly US$2.6-million] grant from the biomedical funding charity Wellcome to investigate heat exposure and health risks in Lagos in a project called Hotsteppers. This is how UrbanBetter works — that research question about heat came from people on the ground raising the issue.

articles.title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11096-0Now that hyperacute rejection of pig xenografts can be reliably prevented, subtler immune-mediated graft injuries have emerged that conventional diagnostics often miss; a multimodal precision diagnostic framework is proposed to detect these injuries earlier, guide personalized immunosuppression and inform future gene editing strategies.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier.
However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date.
Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention.
This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention.
This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival.
Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy.
In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

articles.title: Judge rejects Trump’s wild claim EPA can dismiss data center pollution lawsuits
articles.summary: Trump’s EPA can't unilaterally dismiss SpaceXAI pollution lawsuit, court rules.
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI is stuck facing a lawsuit over alleged data center pollution after Donald Trump failed to convince a judge that his Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has complete control over all Clean Air Act lawsuits and can dismiss any suit at whim.
Soon after unpermitted gas turbines were discovered powering Musk’s giant Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, the NAACP sued. Its lawsuit sought an injunction requiring xAI (which, following a merger, is known now as SpaceXAI) to use the best available pollution control technology when operating the turbines and ordering penalties up to $124,426 per day per violation. Without such remedies, the turbines risked drastically spiking pollution in already vulnerable neighborhoods housing predominantly Black communities nearby, the NAACP argued.
To block the lawsuit, Trump tried to intervene, arguing that the EPA had the power to unilaterally dismiss lawsuits any time the president decides against enforcing the Clean Air Act. According to Trump, it would supposedly “not serve the public interest” if citizens were allowed to seek massive civil penalties to punish polluting AI firms that were trying to get data centers operational as fast as possible to support Trump’s AI Action Plan.Read full article

Nearly two-thirds of US doctors are turning to an AI-powered search engine to make patient decisions, propelling a little-known tech startup to a $15 billion valuation while prompting a debate over the future of patient care.
Miami-based OpenEvidence, founded by serial entrepreneur Daniel Nadler in 2022, said that many of America’s 1 million physicians processed more than 42 million prompts last month. Doctors are using the company’s chatbot to scour medical journals and clinical guidelines to help diagnose and treat patients.
The ads-powered platform has grown largely by word of mouth, penetrating a sector where few tools have seen similar traction. “We’re the first viral consumer internet app in healthcare,” Nadler told the FT in an interview.Read full article

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03311-9Money from the world’s increasingly prosperous technology entrepreneurs has been flooding into biomedical research. Is it changing how science is done?
articles.full_text:
