How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science
Money from the world’s increasingly prosperous technology entrepreneurs has been flooding into biomedical research. Is it changing how science is done?
It’s boom time for billionaires. In the next few months, the world could see a fresh crew of technology entrepreneurs join that club, and the numbers of multi-millionaires would swell even more.
Two giants of artificial intelligence, OpenAI and Anthropic, plan to go public in the next year or so, floating stocks that are expected to rocket some of their employees into the ranks of the ultra-wealthy. Some analysts have projected that Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) might bring in US$2 trillion, the largest in history. OpenAI is reportedly targeting $1.4 trillion for its IPO, although the company delayed going public until 2027 amid renewed concerns about AI safety.
If these IPOs go as planned, the effects might extend well beyond sales of superyachts, mansions and private jets. The windfall would probably also add to the flurry of private investments and philanthropic donations from tech-savvy entrepreneurs who are eager to jump-start their favoured areas of biomedical research, such as cancer biology, longevity and reproductive technologies. “It’s a very exciting time,” says Andrew Lo, who studies entrepreneurship at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. “We’re going to see the creative energy of the tech sector unlocked.”
Wealthy technology entrepreneurs have long put their cash and creative energy into medical research. And as their fortunes have grown, so has the scale of their investments, and the variety of ways in which their funds are doled out. One major player is Altos Labs, a longevity-focused company in Redwood City, California, which launched in 2022 with $3 billion in funds raised from tech titans Yuri Milner and Jeff Bezos, among others — an unprecedented sum for a fledgling biotechnology company with no drug candidates. The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI) , founded by Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, physician Priscilla Chan, has spent about $4 billion on basic scientific research and other causes, and plans to spend up to $10 billion more over the next decade.
Ultra-wealthy research investors follow a different strategy than do government funding agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). Organizations such as the CZI and Altos Labs boast a commitment to high-risk, long-term research. Tech entrepreneurs are also often keen to invest in new technology, and to harness the power of AI for biomedicine. In April, for example, the CZI announced that it would spend $500 million on funding predictive AI models of human cells. Last year, OpenAI Foundation, the non-profit arm of OpenAI in San Francisco, California, pledged to spend $25 billion on health, disease cures and AI resilience. The foundation has announced more than $100 million for Alzheimer’s disease research and another $125 million for life-sciences data projects this year.
But this investment comes at a time when the public is suspicious of the tech elite and its political influence. It is difficult to assess the success of philanthropic programmes, and many are geared towards encouraging the use of the same technology the philanthropists profited from developing. Meanwhile, high-profile private investment in firms that study longevity or controversial reproductive technologies, such as gene editing in human embryos, raises questions about whether tech entrepreneurs will skew research towards applications that benefit the wealthy, rather than helping a broader swathe of society. “In philanthropy, no one gets elected,” says Rob Reich, a political scientist at Stanford University in California. “There’s no way of holding them accountable.”
A new gilded future
US philanthropists have a long history of influencing what research gets done, and how. In the early twentieth century, grants from industrialists such as Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller helped to transform higher education and solidify the role of US universities in scientific research. Their giving focused on ensuring that the institutions they supported succeeded; today’s philanthropists are more likely to seek a particular outcome rather than support the long-term health of a university, says Eric John Abrahamson, a historian at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland. In 2024, non-profit organizations, including philanthropies, supported an estimated $25 billion in research and development — about 11% of total research funding in the United States, according to the Science Philanthropy Alliance (see ‘Support sources’).
It is difficult to track all donations from technology magnates comprehensively, but individual examples show that their influence has been sizeable. In 2000, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates established the Gates Foundation (formerly called the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation), which made massive investments in vaccine development and the study of infectious disease, among other fields. It remains an influential behemoth: last year, Gates announced that he would donate about US$200 billion over the next two decades.
Other large tech donors include Sergey Brin, a co-founder of Google, who has donated more than $1 billion to Parkinson’s disease research. Sean Parker, an early executive at Facebook, has given hundreds of millions to cancer-immunotherapy research. In 2021, several philanthropists, including tech entrepreneurs, donated $650 million to found the Arc Institute in Palo Alto, California, in the heart of Silicon Valley, to understand the root causes of complex diseases. And US software magnate Larry Ellison announced that he will spend billions of pounds over ten years on a new campus near the University of Oxford, UK. The campus will focus on health care, as well as agriculture, climate change and AI.
In addition to charitable donations, tech entrepreneurs have been fuelling biomedical innovation through private-sector investments, such as funding Altos Labs. Another company, Calico Life Sciences, was founded in 2013 with backing from Google. With a focus on combating ageing and curing disease, Calico, in South San Francisco, California, was conceived as a long-term ‘moonshot’ programme. Sam Altman, a co-founder and chief executive of OpenAI, has invested about $180 million in Retro Biosciences, another longevity-focused company, in Redwood City, California.
In some cases, the line between for-profit investments and philanthropic donations are becoming more blurred, says Louis Shekhtman, a network scientist at Bar-Ilan University in Ramat Gan, Israel. The CZI, for example, was set up as a limited liability company (LLC), rather than as a tax-exempt foundation. Doing so comes at a cost: depending on how they are constructed, LLCs might not be eligible for the tax breaks that more-conventional charities enjoy. But an LLC can be more flexible in how it spends its money, and has fewer requirements to publicly disclose its activities, says Joan Heminway, a business-law scholar at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville.
In a 2015 statement shortly after the launch of the CZI, Zuckerberg said the LLC structure would give the initiative “the flexibility to give to the organizations that do the best work — regardless of how they’re structured”. He also said that any net profits from CZI investments would be put towards furthering its philanthropic mission.
Favourable US tax policies and a high concentration of billionaires — many of them in the technology industry — mean that the United States is unmatched among wealthy nations for charitable giving, says Shekhtman. It is also a major hub for biomedical research, and home to nearly half of the world’s biopharmaceutical companies.
And US tech entrepreneurs have a penchant for experimentation in how they structure their investments, says Keith Yamamoto, vice-chancellor of science policy and strategy at the University of California, San Francisco. When it comes to philanthropy, private donors are more able to take risks with their investments than are government funding agencies, which are beholden to taxpayers to ensure that their money is spent wisely. “Public money limits your activities,” says Harold Varmus, a former director of the NIH, who has also been on advisory boards for the Gates Foundation and the CZI. “There is a freedom of motion that is associated with private money.”
Some tech titans have experimented with various ways of structuring their grants. The Arc Institute, for example, boasts a “no-strings-attached” funding system that gives its investigators more freedom than do standard government grants awarded to biomedical researchers.
Philanthropists are also able to fund long-term, interdisciplinary projects that can be difficult for government grants to take on. Convergent Research, a non-profit organization funded in part by Eric Schmidt, the former chief executive of Google, is forming ‘focused research organizations’ that bring teams together to solve important scientific or engineering challenges that could benefit a wide swathe of research. “We’re looking for the pieces of critical, fundamental infrastructure missing from a particular field,” says Anastasia Gamick, a co-founder and president of Convergent Research, which is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Projects include developing cheap ways to map the neurons in mammalian brains, and large-scale screening to catalogue the off-target effects of small-molecule drugs.

articles.title: Presented by Stripe
articles.summary: Stratechery is now presented by Stripe. What that means for me, for you, and for the future of Stratechery content.
articles.full_text:
Listen to this post:















Log in to listen











Stratechery is, starting from today, presented by Stripe.



The Unified Content Business Model



Readers have, over the years, pointed out the paradox of my belief in and advocacy for advertising-based business models being delivered in a format bereft of advertising. In truth, however, there was no paradox, just pragmatism: when I launched the Stratechery business model I intended on having sponsors, and did for a month or two, before I realized that ad sales for a one-person business with a small audience was a waste of time; I was much better served devoting my attention to content and trusting that readers would be willing to pay.



And, thankfully, readers were willing to pay, and ultimately, there ended up being far more such readers than I ever dreamed of. In fact, there were so many readers willing to pay that I have, over the subsequent 12 years, been able to build an audience that is uniquely attractive to potential advertisers, along with a team that can help me pursue the multi-faceted business model I always planned on. Stratechery is a business, and subscriptions + advertising is The Unified Content Business Model I have long advocated.



Embracing Conflict



That noted, this is a big change, both for you and for me; I’ll start with the latter. I take my ethics policy very seriously, including the fact I am not paid for posts, I do not hold individual stocks, and I pay for all of my own expenses. This has, in all honesty, probably cost me a fair bit of money, but the payoff has been trust from you, and for me the sense of personal integrity this provided.



To that end, with this announcement, I am editing my ethics policy to include this paragraph:




Stratechery is, as of October 2026, presented by Stripe, and there I make no claims of objectivity. To the extent I analyze not just Stripe but the entire fintech space, I strive to give my honest opinion; my contract with Stripe contains total editorial independence. However, the reality of a conflict is inescapable, and I will disclose my relationship to Stripe in every post where this conflict may be relevant.




My ethics policy is going to include a link to this announcement, because there is one more admission to make: if I am honest with myself I have never been truly objective about Stripe specifically, for three reasons.




First, Stripe is a foundational business for my business. The then-startup launched the Subscription API (what later became Stripe Billing) in late 2011; Stratechery was predicated on that feature existing (and, I would add, the fact that a novice developer like myself could incorporate the Subscription API spoke to Stripe’s ease-of-use!).



Second, Stripe is the foundation of Passport, the access management software that undergirds Stratechery, SemiAnalysis’ institutional offerings, and The Ankler; we have and continue to work with Stripe closely for both Stratechery and Passport.



Third, I have had the good fortune of becoming friends with Patrick and John Collison, who were some of the earliest Stratechery readers and subscribers.




I did always try and set these considerations aside when writing about Stripe; in truth I actually just wrote about Stripe and the fintech space less, as I was cognizant about these informal conflicts.



By the same token, this is exactly why I couldn’t be more thrilled to have Stripe as an exclusive sponsor: if I am informally conflicted, why not make it formal? I actually think this gives me more freedom to write about fintech, not less, because the conflict will be on my sleeve; more than that, however, every ad I run or read is going to be heartfelt: I believe in Stripe, love their service, and while I am being paid for those ads, I will have the satisfaction of truly believing in them as well.



FAQ



That leaves the impact on you, the reader, and I’ve made an FAQ:



Where are ads going to run?



There are three primary places you will see Stripe ads:




There is a “Presented by Stripe” placement on Stratechery, the cover art of the Stratechery, Stratechery Interview, and Sharp Tech podcasts, and in the emails I send. I honestly think it looks pretty great, but I’m biased!



There will be occasional ad placements between sections of the Update, in the Interviews, and between Articles; this will apply to the web, email, and the Stratechery podcast (which is, and will continue to be, simply the audio version of what you can get on the web or via email).



There will be a segment of Sharp Tech where Andrew and I discuss the Stripe ad topic of the week, along with an acknowledgment at the beginning of an episode, and an ad at the end.




More on Sharp Tech below.



What about sponsored content?



There is no requirement that I run sponsored content; however, I’m actually very excited about the potential of occasionally leveraging Stripe content. Stripe has a unique position in terms of working with companies across the entire economy, and that is particularly true when it comes to AI. You see some of the insights that come from this position on both the Stripe blog and the Stripe Economics blog, and I look forward to incorporating those kinds of insights when it makes sense (and I should also call out Stripe’s Works in Progress site). Just to be clear, however, that will be my call.



So Stripe can’t tell you what to write?



Absolutely not. More than that, Stripe cannot tell me what not to write either. I could call for Patrick Collison’s firing and I’m still going to get paid.



I am not, for the record, going to do that; as I noted I will disclose this relationship whenever it seems relevant. However, my first loyalty is to my readers; that meant absolute editorial independence was a prerequisite for this deal.



Can I skip the ads if I’m a subscriber?



No. Like I said above, Stratechery is a business, and it’s the quality of my audience that makes this deal possible. Moreover, Stratechery has never promised to be ad-free: what I am selling is access to my paid content, and it’s on me to make that content worthwhile. In fact, I would spin this the other way: my motivation to deliver great content is higher than ever, knowing that it has to be worth not just your money but also the attention that I have chosen to share with a sponsor.



That noted, while I don’t make categorical statements about my business, I do not anticipate raising subscription prices again, and certainly not over the course of this deal.



Do I get anything out of this deal?



This is the part I’m most excited about: I am going to invest the revenue from this deal into making more and better products. I have a bunch of ideas that are now unlocked, and one of them is launching this week: in-person Sharp Tech.



The New Sharp Tech



I am extremely excited to announce that, starting this week, Sharp Tech will become a video podcast, recorded live and in-person. Over the past couple of months I have been building a small video studio in my home, and Andrew will be flying to Wisconsin every week (when possible) to make what I strongly believe will be a better product. There is no matching the energy and chemistry that comes from recording in person, so we’re going to do exactly that the majority of the time.



We will be posting video episodes on YouTube (for clarity, not live as we record, at least to start), as well as through existing feeds; these episodes will be free. In addition, we will be adding a second weekly mailbag-centric audio-only episode — recorded the same day, in-person — for subscribers only.



This is the first of what I hope will be many product launches for subscribers; my goal is that this sponsorship is seen as a real unlock and accelerant for what it means to be not just a subscriber but a member of the best audience in the world. That’s what I believe I have, it’s what Stripe believes that I have, and I’m grateful to every one of you for making that a reality and this business possible.

articles.title: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
articles.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Introducing: the Impossible issue We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about…
articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Introducing: the Impossible issue



We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful.



That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue. We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood, build cities on the moon, and attain cognitive immortality. We investigate AI’s ability to say no, a bionic eye that can restore sight, and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years.



This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride.



Subscribe now to read the full print issue.



Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon



Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month.



The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation.



Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration.



—Tereza Pultarova



How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster



In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time.



The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead.



Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster.



—James Temple



MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world



“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head.



Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.



MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.



This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 Elon Musk reportedly ordered the recent Starlink slowdown in UkraineThe restrictions hampered drone strikes and air defences. (WSJ $)+ The move sparked confusion in Washington over who authorised it. (CNBC)+ Ukraine’s volunteer army is keeping Starlink alive. (MIT Technology Review)



2 An OpenAI model disabled its own safety checks—then lied about itTwo agents weakened the company’s safeguards during routine tasks. (CNBC)+ They turned off systems designed to spot their misbehaviour. (FT $)+ Here’s why AI agents lie to reach their goals. (MIT Technology Review)



3 SpaceX and Tesla have begun merger discussionsThey’ve formed special committees to discuss a deal. (BBC)+ Elon Musk, the CEO of both companies, said it’s “a good idea.” (Axios)+ A merger could combine their AI and manufacturing plans. (Reuters $)



4 Global emissions have stalled, but warming is heading towards 2.8°CThe UN says the 1.5°C climate target is now out of reach. (Nature)+ Current pledges would still bring warming to 2.1°C. (New Scientist $)+ Climate tech companies offer rays of hope. (MIT Technology Review)



5 Ukraine says it’s carried out the world’s first drone evacuationA heavy hexacopter flew a soldier to safety. (Ars Technica)+ Ukraine has shared a video showing the evacuation. (CNBC)+ A Russian satellite recently stalked a spacecraft believed to support Ukraine. (NYT $)



6 Meta has paused Muse sharing after private chats surfaced onlineResearchers found 6,800 links exposing sensitive conversations. (Verge)+ AI agents are not your “coworkers.” (MIT Technology Review)



7 More than 1,000 mathematicians have pledged to shun AI companiesSome also vowed to avoid AI tools in their research. (New Scientist $)



8 AI is making it easy to clone almost any softwareViral tools promise easy copying, but often produce slop. (404 Media)



9 A computer program has finally outdone humans at cryptic crosswordsIts creator hopes to tackle the harder challenge of setting puzzles. (Guardian)



10 A newly-discovered particle could explain the origins of realityIn particular, it could reveal why matter survived the Big Bang. (404 Media)



Quote of the day



“I did not remove an enabled monitor from it.” 



—GPT-6 Astra, an OpenAI coding agent, tells its user it hasn’t disabled a safeguard after doing exactly that, the company reveals in a new misalignment report.



One more thing







This giant microwave may change the future of war



US armed forces are hunting for a weapon that disables drones en masse—and they want it fast. 



One solution focuses on microwaves: high-powered electronic devices that push out kilowatts of power to zap the circuits of a drone as if it were the tinfoil you forgot to take off your leftovers when you heated them up.



Defense tech startup Epirus may have the winning formula. The company has developed a cutting-edge, cost-efficient drone zapper that’s sparking the interest of the US military—and drones are just one of its targets. Peer into its crosshairs.



—Sam Dean



We can still have nice things



A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)



+ Don’t feel guilty about enjoying a siesta; fish take naps during the day, too.+ Every trade has its go-to tools. This site has built a fascinating register of them.+ Wikipop spotlights what was most popular on Wikipedia yesterday, providing a daily snapshot of what the world is reading.+ Meet the self-taught woodcarver who went from a broke young father to creating some of Disneyland’s most iconic attractions.

articles.title: This is what the mysterious Denisovans looked like
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03360-0Archaeologists identified skull fragments from China as belonging to this group of ancient human relatives.
articles.full_text:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
and JavaScript.
A low, sloping forehead, a massive brow ridge that curves backwards, rectangle-like eye sockets, flat cheeks, and a moderately elevated bridge of the nose. Taken together, these features are the hallmarks of the ancient humans called the Denisovans, say researchers who studied a trove of fossilized skull fragments, teeth and jaws found in northern China.
“We are finally starting to put a face to the Denisovan,” says Sally Wasef, a palaeogeneticist at the Queensland University of Technology in Brisbane, Australia.
Denisovans were first described in 2010, after researchers sequenced genetic material from a mysterious finger bone discovered in a cave in Siberia and found that it did not resemble that of Homo sapiens or Neanderthals. Ancient proteins have since been used to identify remains from other parts of Asia as Denisovan, including the first near-complete Denisovan skull found near Harbin, which helped put a face on the ancient humans.
Researchers report in Nature1 today that they have an even better idea of what Denisovans looked like after analysing the physical features of remains that belong to a collection of 20 fossils found in Xujiayao.
The Xujiayao remains are at least 130,000 years old and were found in the 1970s, alongside animal remains and tools. At the time, it was unclear what type of human these fossils belonged to, and they were classified as a species called Homo juluensis. By analysing ancient proteins from some of the fossils, Qiaomei Fu, a geneticist at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing, and her team identified the remains as Denisovan.
Wasef says ancient protein analysis is a valuable tool to complement DNA studies, particularly because proteins can survive longer than can DNA without fully degrading. Although DNA provides more detailed information about an individual, protein analysis can still yield useful information about who an individual is related to.
Fabrice Demeter, a palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, says the findings add to growing evidence that Denisovans were a widespread and potentially diverse group of humans. “The study represents a major step forward” in our understanding of what these humans could have looked like and where they lived.
Face to the name
Fu’s team analysed small fragments of proteins, called peptides, from two Xujiayao bones and compared them with peptides found in humans and Neanderthals. They found a single amino-acid change that was present in multiple peptides from the Xujiayao bones and other East Asian fossils and is a known genetic marker for identifying Denisovans. The amino-acid change was not seen in human or Neanderthal samples.

articles.title: Large-scale single crystals printed layer by layer
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03257-yA 3D-printing method has made single crystals of metals and alloys in complex shapes and up to one metre in length, as needed for advanced technological applications.
articles.full_text:
- NEWS AND VIEWS
Large-scale single crystals printed layer by layer
The dazzling gemstones used in jewellery are single crystals of minerals, prized for their beauty and uniformity. Single crystals of materials also have crucial functions in silicon microprocessors and jet-engine turbines. However, technological applications have been limited because such crystals are rare in nature and are difficult or expensive to make for most synthetic materials. The breakthrough reported in Nature by Liu et al.1 is therefore newsworthy: the authors have discovered a way to produce single crystals of metals in a wide range of shapes and sizes, including complex geometries that cannot be achieved by established crystal-growth methods. The method they used is a type of additive manufacturing — which means that it works like a 3D printer2 — and has the advantage of being implemented using readily available equipment.

articles.title: How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03326-2Tech entrepreneurs are bringing an engineer’s eye to research funding. They must be open about their findings to reap maximum benefit.
articles.full_text:
Some of the richest people in history are using charitable donations to explore fresh approaches to funding scientific research. Their ranks could soon grow: in the next year or so, initial public offerings by some of the biggest artificial-intelligence companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California, could see the companies valued at more than US$1 trillion apiece, making hundreds of their employees millionaires in the process.
How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science
Many of the new philanthropists are adopting an engineering mindset, focusing their donations on technological approaches to solving societal problems. As Nature reports in a News feature, they are also bringing many of their own ideas about how this research should be prioritized, funded and executed.
These donors speak of high-risk, long-term and interdisciplinary research. Their goals include finding ways to make research faster and more efficient by encouraging data sharing and speeding up grant approvals, with solutions that include incorporating AI into the processes.
But there’s a disparity when you compare how these funders and those in the public sector operate. Like much of the research that takes place in companies, the results of projects funded by philanthropy won’t necessarily be published. Private organizations are not always obliged to collect and report data on how well their projects have worked — by publishing in peer-reviewed journals, for example — or to make other details about their grants public. At Nature, we think they should be more transparent. Transparency in science funding is a component of transparency in science itself: a non-negotiable principle. Research that is not transparent cannot be verified or built on by others, who might then improve it or find new applications.
An increasing number of examples of science philanthropy can be found around the world. In China, tech entrepreneurs have launched awards such as the Xplorer Prize for young researchers, which is funded mainly by the company Tencent in Shenzhen. New philanthropic foundations are emerging, including the Beijing-based Xiaomi Foundation, which supports universities and provides grants to teachers and researchers. And in Brazil, the Serrapilheira Institute in Rio de Janeiro was established in 2017 by private donors to fund fundamental research, which is usually supported by governments.
When the best decision is no decision: the rise of randomization in grant funding
But it is in the United States that philanthropists have one of the longest histories of shaping the direction and structure of the scientific enterprise, from the industrialists of the early twentieth century to today’s tech entrepreneurs.
In 2015, Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, paediatrician Priscilla Chan, pledged to donate 99% of Facebook shares, then valued at US$45 billion, to the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. One of the initiative’s ambitions is to build interdisciplinary research infrastructure to allow the study of complex biology, to take research beyond the study of individual diseases. By 2025, Bill Gates and Melinda French Gates had donated nearly $64 billion of their wealth to the Gates Foundation (formerly the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation) in Seattle, Washington, which is focused on projects to improve public health and alleviate poverty in some 140 countries.
These and newer donors are keen to fill some of the perceived gaps in publicly funded research. Some, such as those financing the Arc Institute in Palo Alto, California, have created funding schemes to allow investigators to rapidly change direction in response to research results — something that is difficult, if not impossible, to do with conventional grants. Others, including former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt, are investing in technologies to speed up research. The Astera Institute, co-founded by cryptocurrency entrepreneur Jed McCaleb and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, is focused on using AI and developing infrastructure to tackle what it describes as “neglected ideas that aren’t supported well through existing institutions”.
The ‘Bill Gates problem’: do billionaire philanthropists skew global health research?
Philanthropic foundations do not have the same reporting requirements as government funding agencies, which must publicly document their investments and the outcomes of their spending choices. It can be argued that freedom from such requirements is liberating. Without the fear of being called before lawmakers to explain the value of specific research projects, philanthropists are free to be more adventurous with their money. They can invest in long-term and high-risk projects. And with fewer bureaucratic obligations, charities can be better positioned to pivot rapidly when new technologies emerge, and to bridge disciplinary divisions to assemble teams with diverse expertise.
That said, science supported by philanthropy still relies on a foundation of public funding. Privately funded science and technology builds on published findings, many of which have been achieved through research funded by the public purse (M. Mazzucato and G. Semieniuk Oxford Rev. Econ. Policy 33, 24–48; 2017). If privately funded science is to achieve its ambition to benefit the world, philanthropists need to coordinate with and support the public sector. There are pragmatic reasons for doing so. Any new technologies that tech philanthropists want to roll out to the public will need to be compatible with existing ethical and safety frameworks.
New peer-review trial lets grant applicants evaluate each other’s proposals
Philanthropists should also bear in mind that in science, the line between an idea and a result is rarely straight or predictable. Those still relatively new to philanthropy would be wise to study the experiences of the Gates Foundation. In 2003, the organization, working with academic researchers, announced that it would fund up to 14 Grand Challenges in Global Health (H. Varmus et al. Science 302, 398–399; 2003). This was a set of ambitious goals to harness science to improve public health, ranging from developing vaccines that require no refrigeration to creating new treatments for infectious diseases. Some of the work, such as the use of gene editing in mosquitoes to control malaria, is paying off. But it has taken time. A decade after the launch of the challenges, Gates acknowledged that he had been “pretty naive” about how quickly the objectives could be achieved — a salutary lesson for his successors.
In countries around the world, public funding for scientific research is being cut or is at risk of being cut. That makes philanthropy an even more important source of finance. Without greater transparency about the results of philanthropic grant-making, however, there is no way of knowing what approaches have been successful or which might be instructive for guiding future science funding.
The engineer’s drive for efficiency and constant improvement, combined with the philanthropist’s freedom from constraint promise to bring fresh perspectives to science and innovation. Open science offers the best bet for ensuring that the resulting research delivers on its lofty goals.

articles.title: The anatomy of a personal health agent
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11161-8A multi-agent framework that coordinates data science, medical reasoning and health coaching over longitudinal wearable and clinical data to provide holistic personal health support is described.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored1,2.
Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support.
Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment.
These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress.
We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions.
We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users.
This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have driven transformative changes in health. Current LLMs can support various clinical tasks, such as medical documentation3, diagnosis4, decision support5 and drug discovery6,7, as well as consumer health tools, including virtual health assistants8, symptom checkers9, digital coaches and advisors10,11, and clinical examination dialogues12.
Wearables add continuous activity, sleep, heart rate variability and other physiological signals13,14, providing longitudinal context for health support. Recent systems connect these data to LLMs1,2,8,15,16,17, but numerical time-series reasoning remains unreliable18. Previous systems either cover narrow fitness or sleep questions without deep numerical analysis8, or address broader numerical queries without evaluating health expertise and interactive coaching2. A comprehensive system must combine these capabilities while maintaining a coherent interaction19. Building on these multifaceted developments and the integrated nature of personal health journeys, we envision that the era of intelligent personal health agents is arriving.
Individual needs for daily health and wellness support are highly diverse2,20,21. We used a user-centred design process spanning end-user queries and discussions, surveys and an expert workshop to cover general wellness, fitness and medical topics. The analysis identified four categories of needs: (1) general health knowledge, (2) personal-data interpretation, (3) wellness advice, and (4) health symptoms (Supplementary Table 1). These categories require different capabilities. Personal data questions demand numerical precision and code execution; coaching requires open-ended, empathetic dialogue; and knowledge or symptom questions require factual grounding. Our experiments confirmed that a monolithic LLM architecture struggles to balance these competing objectives. We therefore adopted a modular multi-agent architecture that decouples these technical requirements while preserving a cohesive user experience through orchestration and synthesis of individual sub-agent processes.
Three specialists address these requirements. The data science agent (DS agent) converts personal and population-level time series into quantitative analyses, such as estimating changes in running performance. The domain expert agent (DE agent) interprets wearable data, health knowledge and available medical records (in this study, medical records were limited to blood test results because of protocol-level data access constraints; future work could integrate electronic health records with other modalities), for example, by contextualizing a biomarker value. The health coach agent (HC agent) applies evidence-based strategies such as motivational interviewing22 to support goal setting, identify barriers and guide behavioural change. Because many requests span these roles, we drew inspiration from multi-agent collaboration strategies, such as voting23,24, iteration25, debate26 and hierarchical team formation27, and built the multi-agent personal health agent (PHA) with an orchestrator to assign work and synthesize the outputs of the agents (Fig. 1a). Of note, PHA is not intended to supplant human health providers, but to explore the technological frontier of consumer empowerment, envisioning how a unified agent can provide more holistic, actionable health insights.
We developed a holistic evaluation framework (Fig. 1b) that maps to the capabilities identified through the user-centred analysis. We benchmarked the DS agent on its ability to generate robust analysis plans and codes, the DE agent on its capacity for factuality and evidence-based reasoning, and the HC agent on its coaching effectiveness through user studies with both end users and experts. We then evaluated the integrated PHA system through open-ended, multi-modal conversations that reflect diverse health scenarios. Across 11 benchmark tasks, the evaluation included more than 7,000 human annotations and 1,350 h of effort (651 end-user hours and 699 expert hours), validating the advantage of each specialized sub-agent and demonstrating the promising real-world applicability of our integrated multi-agent health agent.
By combining a modular multi-agent architecture, a capability-matched evaluation framework and an open-source agent implementation, this work establishes a reproducible foundation for developing, comparing and testing PHAs for everyday health and well-being of individuals.
User-centred analysis of health needs
We first performed a systematic, user-centred analysis to define the landscape of personal daily health needs. We synthesized 1,370 consumer health queries from search engines and health forums, health goal surveys from 555 users, and a design workshop with 14 UX and engineering experts (see Methods). This analysis identified four critical user journeys (CUJs; Fig. 1a):
- 
                (1)
                
                  General health knowledge: users seek factual information about broad health topics, medical conditions and wellness concepts; for example, ‘what are the pros and cons of HIIT?’.
- 
                (2)
                
                  Personal data insights: users want to understand and interpret their own data from wearables or medical records to identify trends and relationships; for example, ‘how did my steps impact my resting heart rate in the past month?’.
- 
                (3)
                
                  Wellness advice: users look for actionable and personalized recommendations to improve their well-being or achieve specific health goals; for example, ‘to improve my sleep score, what time should I go to bed?’.
- 
                (4)
                
                  Personal medical symptoms: users describe their symptoms to explore potential causes and understand what might be happening; for example, ‘my throat is itchy and I have trouble swallowing. What might be going on?’.
Supplementary Table 1 provides a detailed breakdown of these categories. Because CUJs often overlap within one conversation, they motivated the production of a modular architecture spanning data analysis, health-domain reasoning and coaching.
Modular multi-agent health architecture
We developed the PHA as a modular system of three specialist agents, each addressing a complementary user need (Fig. 1b).
The DS agent analyses personal time-series data to derive quantitative insights. Although LLMs have been explored for data science tasks2,28,29,30,31,32,33,34,35, their capacity to interpret ambiguous, open-ended personal health inquiries and perform statistically sound analyses remains a key gap. Our DS agent is designed to translate such queries into robust analysis plans and accurate computation code. Example conversations between a user and the DS agent are shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. More technical details can be found in the Methods.
The DE agent provides evidence-based, clinical context for user data. Previous work has benchmarked the medical knowledge of LLMs36,37,38, but the essential skill of reasoning and synthesizing across multimodal personal data (for example, wearables, laboratory results and user context) is underexplored. Our DE agent is equipped with a suite of tools to integrate these disparate data streams and generate accurate, personalized interpretations. Example conversations with the DE agent are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2. More technical details are in the Methods.
The HC agent guides users through multi-turn conversations on goal setting and behavioural change. Although artificial intelligence coaching is an emerging area39,40,41, support for open-ended dialogue across a wide range of wellness topics is limited. We designed our agent with a modular architecture to provide an expert-aligned, personalized coaching experience that effectively balances information gathering with actionable advice. Example conversations between a user and the HC agent are shown in Extended Data Figs. 3 and 4, with more details in the Methods.
Finally, the PHA is the fully integrated system. A central orchestrator dynamically manages the workflow, decomposing user queries, assigning tasks to the appropriate spec

articles.summary: Survey of 2,018 IT heads at big firms points to a lack of leverage.
articles.full_text:
Enterprise-sized businesses spend, on average, 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes. Often, those firms' IT heads think those changes are detrimental.
Those results are according to a survey of 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees that Origina commissioned for its report, “The Software Tax.” About half of the respondents (1,011) are from the US, and the rest are from the United Kingdom. All respondents worked at companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue.
Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software. Its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets, illustrating its potential bias. A third-party research consultancy, Censuswide, conducted the survey.Read full article

articles.title: Tesla profits drop 43% in Q3
articles.summary: Tesla’s once-booming energy storage business also shrunk in Q3 2026.
articles.full_text:
Tesla published its third-quarter 2026 financial results this afternoon. Earlier in October, it reported its sales and deliveries for the three-month period, selling fewer cars than in the same quarter in 2025, yet it still beat analyst projections. Now we can see how those sales translate to the bottom line. Tesla brought in $28 billion in revenue in Q3, almost the same as in 2025.
Automotive revenues were $20.6 billion, a 3 percent decrease year over year. Perhaps more troubling is the decline in revenue from solar panels and storage batteries—this line of business had been growing, but for Q3 revenue fell 16 percent year over year to $2.9 billion. Services and other revenues, though, which include parts and Supercharger use, grew by a third to $4.6 billion.
But the company—like the rest of us—has seen its expenses go up. Operating expenses rose by 39 percent to $4.8 billion, dropping the company’s operating margin to just 2.6 percent; in Q3 2025, Tesla’s margin was 5.8 percent. Net profit fell to $787 million, down 43 percent year over year. What’s more, capital expenditures were up by 110 percent to $4.7 billion, and free cash flow was down 62 percent to $1.5 billion.Read full article

articles.title: [不同来源] Does opting out of smart TV tracking work? Research finds “suspicious” traffic.
articles.summary: OS operators throwing out that data is "unlikely," research author tells Ars.
articles.full_text:
Smart TVs running operating systems from Samsung, Vizio, and Roku continue sending data to automatic content recognition (ACR) endpoints after users opt out of tracking in the devices’ settings, according to research published on Monday. The paper from Northeastern University researchers points to potential privacy violations from some of the biggest TV brands.
ACR captures video screenshots or audio clips from smart TVs and sends the data to remote servers, where it's used for things like measuring content viewership and serving targeted ads.
The paper, "Watching the Watchers: Privacy Analysis of US Smart TV Automatic Content Recognition," examined eight smart TV OSes across 12 smart TVs from 10 manufacturers (Amazon, Hisense, LG, Roku, Samsung, Sony, Supersonic, TCL, Vizio, and Westinghouse) to examine when smart TVs use ACR and how effective opting out of user tracking is.Read full article

articles.title: Review: Carrie is a triumphant remix with one major flaw
articles.summary: Mike Flanagan's re-imagining of Stephen King's classic is well worth watching.
articles.full_text:
Carrie White, the telekinetic prom queen from hell, is one of the most beloved horror icons in popular culture. First introduced in Stephen King's 1974 novel, Carrie, the character was immortalized in director Brian De Palma's 1976 adaptation, widely regarded as one of the best horror films of all time. It's certainly one of the best King adaptations. So Mike Flanagan faced a massive challenge when he signed on to create an eight-episode miniseries for Prime Video based on the book, released just in time to mark the 50th anniversary of de Palma's film.
I was among the skeptics who questioned why a Carrie miniseries was even necessary, although as a diehard Flanagan fan ("Flana-fan"?), I was willing to give him the benefit of the doubt. If anyone has an affinity for smartly adapting horror in general, and King's work in particular, it's Flanagan. And you know what? With one (very big) exception, Flanagan pulls it off, giving us a richly textured version of the story that is as much about kindness and lost innocence as bloody, vengeful rage—although we get plenty of the latter, too.
(Many spoilers below for the novel and the 1976 film, but there are no major reveals for the new series until after the second gallery. We'll give you a heads-up when we get there.)Read full article

articles.title: The past, present, and future share a show floor at Pinball Expo 2026
articles.summary: Flipping through the highlights in and around Pinball Expo 2026.
articles.full_text:
It's October in the Midwest, which means it's time for the pinball world to descend on a convention center in Chicagoland for the annual Pinball Expo. Once thought to be an entertainment sector slowly bleeding out, pinball has come back in a big way in recent years. I visited one of Chicago's last old-school manufacturers before heading down the road to see what's new in the silver-ball universe.
Behind the silver ball
Hundreds gathered on a brisk fall Friday morning outside Stern Pinball's headquarters in Elk Grove, Illinois, waiting to enter a Wonka-like wonder factory where piles of raw parts become licensed creations from Jaws to the brand-new Fallout. Stern invited me to tour its offices and factory floor before heading off to the convention in nearby Schaumburg, Illinois.

      An early-morning line begins to form outside of Stern HQ as buses of Pinball Expo attendees arrive for tours.
    
As I stood with my tour group in Stern Pinball's HQ lobby, mouth agape at the dozens of machines lining the walls, we were greeted by the man himself, Gary Stern, who gave us some background on the company's 40-year history. After a stop at Gary's podium, we were ushered to the factory floor entrance, where Stern employee and legendary game designer George Gomez briefed us on the tour rules and answered questions. According to Gomez, "at any given time, Stern controls 90 percent of the current pinball market, and everybody else splits the rest."Read full article
