articles.title: We can do impossible things
articles.summary: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”  I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker:…
articles.full_text:
I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.” 



I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.)



My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine. 



If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now. 



We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious. 



Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing. That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular. 



We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with. 



It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible. 



Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker. 



So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no.



I hope you enjoy the ride.

articles.title: Nuclear-powered spaceships
articles.summary: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era…
articles.full_text:
Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.



The sticking points



Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not. The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites. And experts say there aren’t any major technical obstacles to making nuclear space propulsion happen. “I think it’s a very doable technology,” says Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute.“I’m happy to see them finally doing this.”



Still, developing space propulsion using reactors has been slow going. The US has started—and terminated—several programs looking into it over the past 75 years. The latest casualty was DRACO, a collaboration between NASA and the Department of Defense, which ended in 2025. The project was canceled because of high experimentation costs, an inability to compete with conventional rocket propulsion on price, and difficulty ensuring that ground tests could be performed safely and effectively. (You are creating an incredibly powerful nuclear reaction, after all.)



The progress



After much wavering, it now appears that nuclear-powered interplanetary travel is a $2 billion bet NASA is willing to make. The agency is pursuing an approach called nuclear electric propulsion, which uses the neutrons produced in a self-­sustaining, uranium-­atom-splitting reaction to create heat and ultimately electricity. The electricity is used to ionize a gas, which is blasted out of the spacecraft with the help of magnetic fields, generating thrust. The approach “is very low thrust, but very efficient,” says Sebastian Corbisiero, the US Department of Energy’s national technical director of space reactor programs. “So you can use it for a long period of time.”



What might such a rocket look like? A presentation by Steve Sinacore, program director of NASA’s SR-1 program, offers some clues. So far, the concept art makes the craft look like a colossal fletched arrow. The back will house the power-and-propulsion system, while the tip will hold a uranium-filled nuclear reactor with a capacity of at least 20 kilowatts. (For context, a typical nuclear plant on Earth is about 50,000 times more powerful.) The “fletches” on SR-1 are large fins that help cool the reactor by radiating heat into space.



Like many other pieces of space hardware, the reactor will need to be put through its paces on the ground before it’s cleared for the rough rocket trip to space. “Going through the launch safely is going to be a challenge,” says Middleburgh. “You are being shaken, rattled, and rolled.” For safety reasons, the reactor will be switched on around two days post-launch, when it’s comfortably far from Earth. Uranium isn’t tremendously dangerous by itself, but that can’t be said of the waste products that emerge when the reactor is running. If SR-1 works as planned, its journey to Mars will take about a year. 



Will this novel form of space propulsion actually reach the Red Planet by 2029? It’s possible. NASA says the Idaho National Laboratory, which is building SR-1’s reactor, is making progress and is on target for a late-2028 launch. “Procurement of major components is underway, and integration work on the power and propulsion element is advancing steadily,” Sinacore told MIT Technology Review. The outlook will get even sunnier if the Artemis program, which aims to start laying the foundations for a base on the lunar south pole by the decade’s end, keeps to its own bold deadline. 



“It’s an aggressive timeline,” says Lindsey Holmes, who is vice president of advanced projects at Analytical Mechanics Associates, an aerospace company in Virginia. She suspects the push is being driven partly by China’s and Russia’s own deep-space nuclear ambitions. The two countries have spoken about plans to place a reactor on the moon’s surface in the mid-2030s to power a jointly operated lunar base. Whether it flies or fails in space, SR-1’s development should help NASA put its own reactor on the moon; the technology involved in the two projects is broadly similar, given that the lunar surface, like space itself, is a vacuum. If an interplanetary nuclear-powered spacecraft works, a nuclear reactor on the moon should too.











Progress meter . . . . . . . . . . . . 6







Most of the technology for SR-1 already exists; it’s going to come down to piecing it all together and then seeing how it performs in space.

articles.title: Exercise in a pill
articles.summary: We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who…
articles.full_text:
We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness. 



The sticking points



It will take a lot of experimentation to untangle the myriad pathways by which exercise promotes health. But IDing the cascade of hormones, enzymes, and other molecules related to physical activity is just the first step. Scientists need to figure out how to turn that knowledge into safe and effective drugs. That’s a tall order: More than 90% of treatments that enter human studies fail.



There are regulatory hurdles too. The FDA approves medications to treat diseases, not to enhance wellness, says Thomas Burris, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida whose work focuses on diseases that respond to exercise, like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dementia.



The progress



There may never be a pill that delivers all the benefits of exercise, but research could lead to new medicines that mimic some aspects of working out. Scientists have already identified many important exercise-related signals and have even developed compounds to regulate them. (Some preliminary results have been so promising that doping authorities have proactively banned the compounds.) 



Burris and his colleagues are focused on a receptor that’s always switched on, even without exercise. Working out appears to boost that receptor in muscle cells, which in turn helps bolster endurance over time. Burris’s lab has spent years designing a drug that cranks up the receptor’s activity directly, and mice treated with the drug ran longer and farther than mice that weren’t. They “become marathon mice without having to do any type of exercise,” Burris says. There are even indications—also in mice—that the compound mimics some of the cognitive benefits of exercise and could help treat heart failure. Burris founded a company called Pelagos to carry the work forward into a clinical trial.



Other workout-mimicking drugs have already entered human studies. In June, the biotech firm Cambrian Bio reported that its experimental drug ATX-304 boosted metabolism and reduced liver and belly fat in people with obesity and prediabetes. It activates a metabolic switch that helps cells sense when energy supplies dip and coordinates the production of more fuel—the same switch that helps us sustain long sessions jumping rope or swimming laps. Cambrian hopes it will help people lose weight without losing muscle, a common concern with GLP-1 medicines.  







Progress meter ………… 5







Our understanding of how exercise benefits the body is still coming into focus, and drug development is prone to failure.

articles.title: Interspecies communication
articles.summary: Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think,…
articles.full_text:
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think, who have hopes and dreams of their own,” says Con Slobodchikoff, the founder of Zoolingua, a company working on dog-to-human speech.



The sticking points



Teasing all this out is complex. To decipher howls, squeaks, and clicks, researchers must match the creatures making sounds with what’s happening around them. Prairie dogs, for example, utter a different series of yips when a coyote approaches than when a hawk is nearby. It’s painstaking work, especially for difficult-to-­observe species, like deep-diving whales or subterranean mole rats.



There are other hurdles. Many animals communicate not just through sound but through visual cues, touch, pheromones, or a combination of signals, some of which might be difficult for us to perceive. And without a multispecies Rosetta stone, it’s hard to know if translations are accurate. 



The progress



Over the past 50 years, a growing arsenal of devices has made it easier to observe the sophisticated ways animals communicate. Hydrophones at the bottom of the ocean can capture humpback whale song, and tiny wearable “biologgers” can record a bat’s every squeak. 



In the last decade, advances in AI have leveled up our ability to make sense of it all. The technology can detect different calls, distinguish which sounds belong to which animal, and spot patterns. Researchers at the Earth Species Project (ESP), a nonprofit founded in 2018 to decode animal communication, recently used machine learning to detect vocalizations of carrion crows and determine which bird made which call. 



They suspect that more advanced AI could translate critters’ chatter. Large language models like Claude and ChatGPT excel at finding relationships between words, explains Sara Keen, one of ESP’s behavioral ecologists. ESP hopes its own NatureLM—trained on human speech, music, and animal sounds—will be able to interpret the vocalizations of a variety of species. 



That promise, however, is still theoretical. Yossi Yovel, a neuroecologist at Tel Aviv University, worries that these models will put too much emphasis on acoustic similarities and make mistakes—like lumping together similar sounds that have different meanings. 



As for a two-way convo? It’s not clear when—or whether—that will happen. Still, “a lot of animals have an evolutionary structure that is similar enough that we should be able to understand what they’re saying,” Slobodchikoff says. 







Progress meter ………… 4







Researchers have amassed heaps of data on animal communication, but they’re still trying to figure out how to decipher it all.

articles.title: Cleaning up PFAS
articles.summary: Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. They are known for a strong bond…
articles.full_text:
Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. They are known for a strong bond between carbon and fluorine, which the environment struggles to break down. 



The sticking points



PFAS are everywhere: They spew from factories and slough off products and into water with normal use. Scientists have found them in everything from human blood to Antarctic snow. One 2022 report found that 89% of the US population had PFAS in excess of two nanograms per milliliter of blood plasma, a common threshold for potential adverse health effects, and 9% of the population had passed the riskier level of 20 nanograms per milliliter.



The PFAS monster is also a moving target. New compounds are still being created and used. There are more than 12,000 of them, and much of the cleanup research focuses on only a small handful. 



The progress



Cleansing PFAS-contaminated soil is a project in its infancy, but it is possible to prevent more buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems. There are two ways to handle this: trap or destroy. Some scientists have found reverse osmosis—a process that pushes water through supertight filters—useful in point-of-use cases, like water filters at kitchen sinks. 



Other techniques in the pipeline might be more suitable for large-scale removal—for example, at water treatment facilities. One, called foam fractionation, generates bubbles that capture PFAS. More approaches, like ensnaring the chemicals in nanothin layers of charged metal, are also under investigation. 



Trapping, though, is imperfect. You’re left with PFAS-filled brine, which if not properly destroyed (an expensive and energy-sucking endeavor) can still end up in the environment. 



Jack Huang, a professor of crop and soil sciences at the University of Georgia, is working on destruction. He’s testing a method called electrochemical degradation, which uses electrodes to break down the bonds that hold PFAS together. The product destroyed more than 90% of PFAS mass in tests and has already been licensed by the engineering consulting firm AECOM. 



Ridding life of PFAS is also a policy challenge. There are alternatives; we just need the push to use them. And we’ve had success before: The EPA’s 2010/2015 PFOA Stewardship Program has helped slash the release of water-repellent perfluorooctanoic acid by 95%. More recently, Minnesota, Maine, and New Mexico have passed bans on PFAS in products like cookware and dental floss. 







Progress meter ………… 6







Scientists are making strides toward removing and destroying PFAS—but it’ll be all for naught if we don’t turn off the tap.

articles.title: Solid-state batteries
articles.summary: The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing and pumping out energy by moving charged lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte soup has…
articles.full_text:
The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing and pumping out energy by moving charged lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte soup has its drawbacks, not least that the batteries have a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer, creating power packs that charge faster, last longer, cram more energy into smaller spaces, and (crucially) run cooler. A new generation of companies aim to bring such batteries to market, and if their bets pan out, the tech could substantially ease the shift away from fossil fuels. 



The sticking points



Solid-state batteries have been “just a few years away” for more than a decade now. In laboratories, the technology works. But there have been challenges. In designs that pair the solid electrolyte with a lithium-metal anode (the side of the battery that releases electrons into an electrical circuit), needlelike filaments called dendrites tend to grow during charging, and they eventually push through the electrolyte and short the cell. Solid electrolytes are supposed to physically block the formation of dendrites, but many of them crack as the treelike projections break through like roots in a concrete foundation. 



Then there’s the problem of manufacturing at scale. Mass production requires large quantities of defect-free sheets of ceramic-like material to make the electrolytes as well as dry rooms for assembly, since those electrolytes have a tendency to react with water. Would-be manufacturers quote a range of potential prices for solid-state batteries, but most expect them to fall in line with lithium-ion packs sometime in the mid-2030s. 



The progress



Nascent as the technology is, solid-state batteries have already seen high-­profile missteps. But one of America’s most advanced solid-state-battery companies says it’s closing in on being able to bring its product to market. The Bill Gates–backed QuantumScape launched in Silicon Valley in 2010 and built its battery around a class of ceramic materials that it says is compatible with lithium—meaning no dendrite formation. “We spent, then, like 10 years learning how to process it to satisfy all of the other requirements,” says Tim Holme, QuantumScape’s cofounder and chief technology officer. In 2025, the startup announced a proprietary, large-scale manufacturing method for quickly producing and heat-treating the ceramic electrolytes used in its batteries. “Nobody has ever done this in the field of ceramics before,” Holme claims. For 10,000 years, producing ceramics has involved slowly cooking the starting materials in an oven over the course of days. “We figured out a way to shorten that down to several minutes,” he says. 



Plenty of other companies are pushing the tech forward as well. Toyota, the world’s biggest automaker, launched a research program on solid-state batteries way back in 2010. It’s now partnering with the global energy and petroleum company Idemitsu Kosan on a pilot plant, promising cars that can travel up to 745 miles after charging 10 minutes or less—a huge leap, if it works out. In China, CATL, the giant behind roughly 40% of the global battery market, is aggressively pursuing solid-state batteries too, pumping nearly $2.6 billion into a research program in 2024 alone. Mercedes, meanwhile, equipped one of its EQS sedans with solid-state batteries last fall; after driving nonstop for 750 miles, the car still had some range to spare. 



Will the tech gain traction? Investing in vehicle batteries makes sense given the size of the potential market. But any little uptick in cost typically gets passed on to buyers, so the first solid-state EV batteries will inevitably be more expensive. 



Grid storage buyers, who are working to meet the increasing demands posed by data centers, may also hesitate to purchase new technologies that still haven’t come down the cost curve. Then again, the promise of energy storage that lasts longer than lithium-­ion’s typical eight hours could make them easier to persuade. 



Some companies are taking a page from a playbook employed by outfits pursuing fusion: Focus on near-term markets with better margins to help fund development and bring down costs. Solid-state firms including California-based Solid Energies and Arizona-headquartered Sion Power are looking at selling batteries to the aviation industry or the military. “Those are sectors that are less sensitive to cost, and they typically require lower volumes as well,” says Evelina Stoikou, head analyst for battery technologies and supply chains at the consultancy BloombergNEF. “It’s a good way to prove your concept, then go through and fund the pilot plant where you can make that and eventually scale up.”







Progress meter ………… 7







The technology works, the capital is there, and demand is not far behind. But as with anything in manufacturing, unknown unknowns remain.

articles.title: Eliminating traffic deaths
articles.summary: Every year, traffic crashes kill more than one million people, and they’re the leading cause of death for children and young adults. In the US, 100 people a day lose their lives this way, in many cases not on highways but on rural and local streets. “Traffic deaths are a leading cause of preventable death,…
articles.full_text:
Every year, traffic crashes kill more than one million people, and they’re the leading cause of death for children and young adults. In the US, 100 people a day lose their lives this way, in many cases not on highways but on rural and local streets. “Traffic deaths are a leading cause of preventable death, yet we treat it like it’s inevitable,” says Leah Shahum, founder and director of the Vision Zero Network, a nonprofit focused on making streets less deadly. 



The sticking points



The causes of a crash can be muddy. Drivers make mistakes like speeding or getting distracted, but infrastructure fails them too: Perhaps they were on a road built for speed and not safety, in a screen-filled vehicle, or at an intersection where pedestrians, cyclists, and other cars aren’t visible. 



Cheap and proven traffic-calming opportunities abound—from using planters to tighten intersections to lowering speed limits—but government logjams and red tape can be speed bumps. “There’s so many moving parts,” says Laura Sandt of the University of North Carolina Highway Safety Research Center. “On the flip side, it shows that we have so many opportunities for injury prevention.” 



The progress



The total number of traffic deaths has increased over the last century. And though the US rate has dipped from a peak of 30.8 deaths per 100,000 people in the 1930s, the past decade has seen a concerning jump in deadly pedestrian incidents. At the same time, communities are waking up to the essential role of traffic safety policy, Shahum says. 



One success story is Hoboken, New Jersey, which hasn’t had a traffic fatality since 2017. This is due to a combination of efforts like boosting investment in public transit, promoting walkability by extending curbs, and using cameras to identify crash-prone intersections in need of a redesign. But even there, obstacles remain. If an intersection hasn’t been proved to be deadly, for example, it can be an uphill battle to argue for removing parking spaces to widen curbs. “You’re kind of selling insurance through these improvements, and that’s not always easy,” says Greg Francese, the city’s acting director of transportation and parking.



There’s also no silver bullet that will work everywhere. Situated directly across the river from New York City, Hoboken is a highly transit-oriented city of less than 60,000 people. Success there might not translate to traffic-death hot spots like Memphis or Dallas. But it’s not impossible. Take Edmonton, Alberta, a sprawling, car-centric Canadian city of around one million people: Between 2015 and 2020, it cut traffic fatalities by 63% and serious injuries by 40% by adjusting speed limits and improving signals at crosswalks. 







Progress meter ………… 6







We know how to tweak intersections and adjust traffic signals. Getting the funding and will to roll out those changes is the big red light.

articles.full_text:
If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process.
This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong:

On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...]
As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.

This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure:


August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.
August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.
August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team.
September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix.
October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available.
October 21, 2026: Public disclosure.



    Via Hacker News


    Tags: open-source, php, security, ai, ai-security-research

articles.full_text:
Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say:


  When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out?

  I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you

  So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to


In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post.

But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them?

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code. Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut.

In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation:


  Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts.


One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at


  having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed.


She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data.


  Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier.


The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug.


  The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control


A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments.

With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses.

The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution.


  Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies.


This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans.


  A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent


Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on.

And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent


  In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to


While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

articles.title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11317-6De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts
articles.full_text:
Abstract
The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis.
Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.
1–5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds.
In this study, we show that generative protein design6–8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9.
The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes.
Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity.
These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

articles.title: Teen depression and anxiety predicted by childhood brain development
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03357-9Analysis of nearly 30,000 brain scans yields detailed timeline of how the brain matures — and hints at the consequences of disrupting it.
articles.full_text:

the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
and JavaScript.
The speed at which regions of the brain mature during early adolescence can forecast the emergence of mental-health conditions up to four years before symptoms develop, according to a study of nearly 12,000 young people in the United States.
By tracking the brains of adolescents over six years in nearly 30,000 scans, researchers mapped how the brain’s outer layer, the cerebral cortex, thins as children grow into teenagers. The team observed that sensory areas of the cortex thinned, or matured, first, followed by regions responsible for complex thought.
The findings, posted on 11 October on the preprint server bioRxiv1, ahead of peer review, challenge the theory that psychiatric disorders are caused by defects in specific brain circuits. Instead, they indicate that vulnerability to mental-health symptoms could involve disruption of the brain’s developmental timeline and could be set in motion by genes that are active before birth.
The work “provides one of the clearest pictures yet of how the cortex develops from childhood into adolescence”, says Avram Holmes, a systems neuroscientist at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey, who was not involved in the study. “It makes you think about the timing of brain development, not just the location [in the brain], when we look at psychiatric symptoms,” he says.
But he cautions that the population-level patterns found in the study — trends that become visible only when averaging data across large numbers of people — are subtle and cannot yet be used in the clinic to forecast the mental-health trajectory of an individual child.
Pruning the brain
During childhood and adolescence, the cerebral cortex thins. Neuroscientists attribute this process to the pruning of unused connections between neurons, which helps the brain to operate efficiently.
Researchers have long suspected that disruptions to cortical thinning contribute to mental illness, because psychiatric conditions such as depression are often diagnosed during late adolescence, when the thinning process is winding down. But proving that link has been difficult because brain-imaging studies have historically relied on small sample sizes or single snapshots in time.
To overcome these hurdles, study co-author Jacqueline Clauss, a child psychiatrist at the University of Iowa in Iowa City, and her colleagues turned to data from a massive project that is tracking nearly 12,000 children from around the age of nine. Participants’ brains are scanned every two years and their parents complete surveys about their children’s mental-health symptoms annually.
When analysing the data, Clauss and her colleagues found that rather than thinning at a steady rate, brain regions change following a distinct trajectory that fits an S-shaped curve. Thinning of a region of the cortex initially accelerates, then proceeds steadily before decelerating as the region nears maturity.

articles.title: Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03355-xThe United Nations’ latest climate report is a stark reminder that limiting warming to the safest levels is now likely out of reach.

Despite a possible plateau in global greenhouse-gas emissions last year, average temperatures are set to hurtle past 2 °C of warming around mid-century barring a major acceleration in emissions cuts, finds the United Nations’ latest report on climate change.
“The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5 °C limit, and the consequences are already devastating,” said outgoing UN secretary-general António Guterres in a press briefing announcing the report — an annual accounting of progress towards tackling climate change published by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) on 21 October. Guterres pointed to extended heat waves, massive wildfires and deadly floods that have disrupted much of the world in 2026. He called for faster action from governments to cut emissions by transitioning away from fossil fuels, expanding clean electricity and reversing deforestation.
Under current policies, scientists estimate warming of 2.6 °C to 2.8 °C above pre-industrial levels this century — substantially exceeding the 2 °C upper limit of the 2015 Paris Agreement targets to avoid the most dangerous consequences of climate change. There is also a smaller, 10% chance of warming exceeding 3.4 °C on the current trajectory, which researchers say would be catastrophic. Even under a scenario where countries achieve all existing emissions pledges, the report projects 2.1 °C of warming.
Although the 1.5 °C goal is out of reach — 2026 is projected to be the second year in which temperatures have surpassed that level of warming — the report maintains it might be possible to “overshoot” that target, then bring temperatures back down through rapid decarbonization combined with a massive expansion of carbon dioxide removal.
UNEP’s assessment comes ahead of November’s COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, where governments will take stock of efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change. “The emissions gap is now a leadership gap. And the world is running out of time and excuses to close it,” Guterres said.
Bright spots
There is some good news in this year’s report. Initial estimates show that global greenhouse-gas emissions in 2025 were about the same or slightly lower than in 2024. That was mainly due to a decrease in emissions from land use, particularly those from wildfires after unprecedented blazes in 2024.
That would be the first decline seen since the COVID-19 pandemic, and it could represent the start of a plateau or even a peak in emissions (see ‘Have emissions peaked?’). But researchers caution that a single year is not enough to determine if this is a lasting shift.
“Global emissions will have to fall several per cent before there can be any certainty that they have peaked,” says Lauri Myllyvirta, a researcher at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a research organization in Helsinki. “Until then, one particularly hot summer or other cyclical development can cause a jump above the preceding peak, even if the structural trend is downward.”
Another encouraging trend is the rapid expansion of renewables. Clean-energy capacity has increased around three times faster than anticipated since 2015, and solar energy has expanded seven times faster than expected as costs have fallen.
Myllyvirta points out that even if this year doesn’t represent an emissions peak, the report projects a 5–8% drop by 2030 relative to 2025 levels. “The door to a much larger reduction than this over the next five years is open,” he says, as clean energy accelerates, fossil fuels become costlier, and because of the potential for China and India to overachieve their promised emissions cuts.

articles.title: Huge mapping study reveals how your brain tracks what your body is feeling
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03334-2Signals in the insula region, deep in the brain, can make people feel hot, tingly and nauseous.

Scientists have mapped one of the most mysterious parts of the human brain in unprecedented detail1. Their results detail how this region, the insular cortex or insula, is organised to support the brain’s processing of bodily sensations such as pain. The mapping also details a pathway that allows for the cortex — the seat of higher-order cognition — to work with the insula to affect bodily perceptions.
One region of the insula is responsible for the feeling of pain in certain parts of the body. Another region generates sensations, such as nausea, felt by the internal organs. A third region, at the front of the insula, ‘talks’ to other brain areas involved in cognition and emotion, suggesting it influences not only sensations, but also how the brain interprets them.
Contrary to previous thinking, the insula is “not just reading the body. It is partly influencing the story about how the body should be felt,” says study co-author Josef Parvizi, a physician-scientist at Stanford University in California.
The study is “quite a feat”, says Lucina Uddin, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. It’s also one of the most comprehensive studies on the insula and how it produces bodily sensations, she adds.
The findings were published today in Nature.
Buried in the brain
The insula has been notoriously difficult to study in detail because it’s located deep in the brain. Previous studies have suggested that this hard-to-reach region is involved in receiving signals — such as pain or pressure — from various parts of the body, then processing them into sensations that we experience. But most research on the human insula has relied on brain-imaging techniques to capture what happens in the insula when various sensations arise, Parvizi says.
To build a more detailed picture, Parvizi and his colleagues needed to find a way to send electrical signals to various parts of the insula in people and assess the bodily sensations that occur as a result. But implanting electrodes deep in the brains of healthy people would be unethical. So, the researchers turned to 87 people who’d had electrodes implanted in their brains for medical reasons.
In experiments that spanned more than a decade, Parvizi and his colleagues sent electrical currents through the electrodes into a variety of sites in the participants’ insulas.
Stimulating the rear of the insula produced pain, heat and other sensations — including tingling and numbness — in specific areas of the participants’ bodies, such as the arm or leg. Meanwhile, participants experienced more ‘visceral’ sensations, including nausea, pressure and feelings of fullness in their chest, when the researchers sent electrical currents to the middle of the insula.

articles.title: The Bursar
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03110-2A good way to learn?
articles.full_text:
The Bursar shook Cerise’s hand with firm confidence. “We don’t expect you to be familiar with procedures,” he said. “Orientation for our new parents is standard. Don’t be embarrassed to ask questions.”
“I suppose when Lorelei is my age the parents will take it for granted.” Cerise smiled in self-deprecation.
The Bursar nodded. “Of course, we expect our system to progress a great deal more by then. Now, your daughter Lorelei — she’s five?”
“Five in June,” Cerise agreed. “A normal, happy little girl, we’d like to think.”
“Our programme will help keep her that way.” The Bursar gestured for Cerise to follow him. The halls were bright and spacious, decorated with printouts of student artwork.
“Lorelei will have her own cubicle, kindergarten through graduation,” said the Bursar, gesturing at one of the dim nooks off the bright hallway. “One advantage of our programme is decreased contagion — although that’s not its main appeal.”
Read more science fiction from Nature Futures
Cerise peered in at the tiny, still form. She felt like a voyeur into this strange industrial transformation of sleep. She forced a laugh. “A far cry from showing me the gym and the art room, isn’t it?”
The Bursar pursed his lips. “Our students do experience those things. In some ways the virtual environment is superior — you and I didn’t see a new gymnasium remodel more than once, if ever. Lorelei will never experience anything but. No matter how the state of the art changes, our experience changes with it.”
They finished the tour in silence — not much to see except for the nurse’s office, which didn’t look much like the nurses’ offices of Cerise’s childhood except for its antiseptic gleam. Satisfied, the Bursar escorted her back to his office.
“We used to think that children just had to take whatever life threw at them,” he beamed, relaxing into his leather chair and leaving Cerise to perch on a wooden one. “What a terrible idea, raising children on random trauma! Then we reversed course and over-restricted them until their prefrontal cortexes developed.” He shook his head. “Lunacy. Learning requires error.”
“Of course,” said Cerise stiffly, one of that protected cohort herself.
But the Bursar was giving his favourite speech and could not be distracted. “Our calibrated experience will allow Lorelei to only experience the proper amount of error, conflict and pain. We can’t do what some of the upper-end models do, but at your budget … I think you’ll be pleased with her educational experience.”
“What about external … problems? Obviously we try not to have any,” Cerise hurried to explain. “But what if Lorelei has a grandparent with cancer, or something traumatic like that?”
“It’s crucial for you to report to us regularly. Even small trauma — she twists her ankle playing at the park — is used to customize her programme. We’d substitute a nurturing experience in for a challenge there. We’ll assess her reactions constantly, fitting her challenges to her means of addressing them, but our weekly report from parents is crucial. Just think what would happen if we were giving her scenarios like fighting with a friend at recess on top of her parents getting a divorce! Disaster.”
“We’re not getting a divorce,” Cerise blurted defensively, and then made herself add, “I know, you just meant … for example. But to take your example, can she really have fights with friends at recess? Do you connect the children’s simulations to each other?”
“Absolutely not!” snapped the Bursar. “Children are chaotic! You might as well send her to traditional school if that was all you cared for her brain development.”
“But … doesn’t that mean she won’t share childhood memories with anybody?” Cerise thought about the time Lucy Meisner threw up on a field trip to the zoo, the time she and Tony Azar got in trouble for hiding at the end of recess and how it made them laugh decades later.
“Many adults don’t remain close with their classmates from traditional schooling, either,” said the Bursar stiffly. “We feel the trade-off is well worth it.”
“I understand.” Cerise sighed. “So I expect you’ll have the fee structure to go over.”
His face closed disapprovingly. “I will direct you to that department on your way out.”

articles.title: Can plants defend coasts against storms?
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03063-6Salt-marsh plants can protect inland areas against huge waves — but seemingly only up to a point, and big storms cause progressive damage.
articles.full_text:
- NEWS AND VIEWS
Can plants defend coasts against storms?
Plants and other organisms can reduce the erosion of coasts by winds and waves. The physical structures of sand-dune and wetland plants, seagrasses, oysters and macroalgae can slow the flow of water and wind, capture sediment and modify soil. Over time, these organisms can also build land, store greenhouse gases, provide habitats for other species and beautify beaches and wetlands1. In some cases, they can be used as a nature-based solution in place of engineered structures. But coastal engineers and planners are often hesitant to incorporate them into construction projects, because their ability to perform in extreme conditions is unknown. Writing in Nature, Willemsen et al.2 determine the limits of coastal protection that salt-marsh plants can provide.

articles.title: A single antimatter particle in a cage opens door to ‘revolutionary’ physics
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03342-2Physicists trap and cool down positron for months to measure its ‘magnetic moment’ with extraordinary precision.

Physicists have now suspended a single positron — the antimatter equivalent of an electron — in mid-air and cooled it to its lowest possible energy state.
The set-up will enable researchers to study magnetic properties of the positron with unprecedented precision. Physicists hope to spot subtle differences between matter and antimatter that could shed light on one of physics’ greatest mysteries.
No one knows why the world is made overwhelmingly of matter. Today’s best theory of particles and forces, the standard model, suggests that just as much antimatter should have been created during the Big Bang.
But when they come into contact, matter and antimatter — which have the same mass but are opposite in properties such as charge — disappear into a burst of energy. If they had been created in equal amounts, “all the matter and antimatter would annihilate and there’d be no Universe left”, says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, who led the work.
Finding a mismatch in measurements between matter and antimatter “would be revolutionary in physics”, says Gabrielse. The standard model has proved maddeningly accurate at predicting experimental results despite being known to be incomplete. It cannot, for example, explain the apparent existence of dark matter, a substance thought to interact mainly through gravity.
The experiment, detailed in Physical Review Letters on 21 October1, is a “remarkable achievement” that will provide “a powerful probe for physics beyond the standard model”, says Barbara Maria Latacz, an antimatter physicist at CERN near Geneva, Switzerland. “I cannot wait to see their first precision measurements,” says Stefan Ulmer, a physicist at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU) in Germany.
Spot the difference
Since the 1960s, physicists have studied antimatter in ever-finer detail, hoping to find discrepancies with matter. They have observed a slight preference for matter in the behaviours of a handful of particles, but nowhere near enough to account for the world’s composition.
So far, exquisitely detailed comparisons of protons and antiprotons haven’t uncovered any such differences. Now, Gabrielse’s group hopes to compare a property that can be measured with 10,000 times greater precision in electrons and positrons: their ‘magnetic moments’, which determine how particles wobble on their axis in a magnetic field.
Pin a positron
To do their experiments, the team first faced a significant challenge: capturing a positron. They started with fast-moving positrons emerging from radioactive decay and slowed them down by scattering them off atoms in a crystal of tungsten. Although many were annihilated, the team skimmed off the slowest of the survivors and fed them into a trap.

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03375-7Researcher and policy adviser who championed tests and treatments for genetic diseases.

Kay E. Davies is Dr Lee’s Professor of Anatomy emeritus at the University of Oxford, Oxford, UK. She was a research fellow with Williamson at St Mary’s Hospital.
Robert (Bob) Williamson was a geneticist who dedicated his career to the identification of disease-linked genes and the diagnosis and treatment of single-gene disorders. He was concerned about the ethical implications of population-wide genetic screening and using stem cells in research. Williamson was one of the first to use DNA markers to locate the position of important human disease-associated genes on chromosomes. He mapped the location of genes linked to cystic fibrosis (CF) and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). This led to the development of genetic tests to identify people who carried DMD-related gene alterations, extending the range of counselling provided to affected families.
He was an astute politician, bringing together people from across the field of health care — from genetic research to the bedside — and working closely with patient advocacy groups and the UK government. After moving from the United Kingdom to Australia, he became interested in national science policy and medical and scientific ethics. There, he advised several premiers and ministers.
Williamson was born in Cleveland, Ohio, and spent his childhood in New York City. When he was 16 years old, his family moved to London. After doing undergraduate and graduate degrees in chemistry at University College London, Williamson moved to the University of Glasgow, UK, in 1963 to become a lecturer in developmental biology. There, his research focused on globin genes, which encode the protein components of the oxygen-carrying haemoglobin molecule. His group showed that blood disorders known as thalassaemias were often caused by deletions in the genes encoding α-globin and fetal haemoglobin. He later collaborated with others to develop prenatal diagnosis and testing methods for carriers of these disorders.
His work on haemoglobin synthesis in immature red blood cells led him to study the control of gene expression. Puzzled about unexpected free-floating DNA fragments that hindered his work, he reported in 1970 that this cell-free DNA was released by the nuclei of cells that had died during development (R. Williamson J. Mol. Biol.51, 157–160; 1970). In the same paper, he described the ‘nucleosome ladder’, a gel-electrophoresis pattern that reflected how DNA was organized in chromosomes. Williamson was particularly proud that these observations were recognized; his paper was published three years before the biological importance of nucleosomes was realized and several decades before cell-free DNA became a valuable diagnostic tool for cancer and other conditions.

articles.title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11145-8Salt marsh platforms resist erosion under extreme waves, but vegetation damage reduces wave attenuation; substantial wave attenuation by vegetation is mainly limited to low-energy marsh coasts with waves below 1 m.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Salt marshes protect coastlines by attenuating wind waves with their elevated marsh platform and above-ground vegetation1. Confidence in the persistence of this service under a changing climate requires knowledge on how extreme storms damage the platform and vegetation; however, a comprehensive, quantified understanding of salt marsh–wave interactions under extreme events is lacking. A unique experiment was conducted by transferring intact salt marsh to one of the world’s largest wave flumes, and subsequently exposing it to increasingly higher waves that reach up to 2 m significant wave height. We show that marsh substrates can persist with negligible erosion, despite cumulative wave exposure. By contrast, the vegetation was progressively damaged during continued wave exposure, gradually reducing vegetation-related wave attenuation. Results emphasize that vegetation was most effective in attenuating waves at low-energy marsh coasts (up to 1 m), where attenuation exceeded 10% (up to 50%), whereas attenuation at high-energy marsh coasts (wave height > 1 m) does not exceed 10%. Our global assessment supports the differentiation between low- and high-energetic conditions resulting from the flume experiment. Our results suggest that the marsh platform remains stable under extreme wave events and that substantial wave attenuation by marsh vegetation is limited to low-energy marsh coasts.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
In coastal regions characterized by high flood risk, people and assets are commonly protected from flooding by dikes, dams and sea walls; so-called grey flood protection. These engineered structures are increasingly challenged by changes in local and regional climate conditions, such as sea level rise, land subsidence and increased storm exposure, and may become unsustainable1. Hard engineering structures are static and do not adapt to a changing environment2. Therefore, so-called green–grey flood protection—which combines traditional grey-protection with green-ecosystems—is increasingly considered a more sustainable strategy for keeping coastal regions safe from storm events with extreme waves3.
Green–grey flood protection uses the natural capacity of ecosystems to buffer extreme wave events and consequently reduce flood risk. Specifically, salt marshes with unique salt-tolerant vegetation4, often located in the temperate climate zone at muddy coasts, serve to attenuate large waves during storm surge events5.
Salt marshes attenuate waves by dissipating wave energy due to (1) the elevated bed6, and (2) the drag and roughness of the vegetation growing in the marsh7,8,9,10,11. Both are expected to change during extreme wave events, thereby decreasing the wave-attenuating capacity. Studies so far have indicated that marsh substrates remain stable under moderate storms (significant wave height under 1 m), whereas stability under extreme wave exposure (wave height exceeding 1 m) has not been tested. At the same time, above-ground vegetation breaks and detaches from the marsh surface during moderate storms5,12. Modelling studies extrapolating field evidence highlight that nearly all vegetation is broken after exposure to waves up to 1 m (ref. 13), inevitably leading to decreasing wave attenuation5,13,14. Overall, there seems to be a relationship between wave forcing and vegetation loss: as a storm lasts longer, above-ground vegetation is progressively damaged and wave attenuation diminishes.
In several regions, future storm surges are expected to exceed the water levels that have been assessed in laboratories so far (maximum of 2 m)5,15 ; for example, the UK16 and the Netherlands15. Such surges are also predicted to occur with a 25-year return period in the Yellow Sea and East China Sea (China); the Gulf of Carpentaria (Australia); the Bay of Bengal (Bangladesh); and the Gulf and East coast of the United States17. Surge levels are expected to increase even further in the coming decades18. There is a lack of quantified knowledge explaining progressive vegetation damage and potential substrate erosion under these conditions, and the efficacy of damaged marsh vegetation in wave attenuation during extreme wave events (>1 m).
Based on flume experiments and projected storm simulations at a global scale, here we aim to quantify the persistence of the marsh substrate and address the progressive vegetation damage and associated reduced wave attenuation under extreme storm conditions, by assessing:
- 
                I.
                
                  The stability of salt marsh substrate under extreme wave events.
- 
                II.
                
                  Progressive vegetation damage and associated wave attenuation under extreme events.
- 
                III.
                
                  The global contribution of progressively damaged salt marsh vegetation to wave attenuation that proceeds from results of the flume experiments.
Natural marsh in a large-scale flume
A 306-m2 salt marsh with intact above-ground biomass and marsh substrate was installed in the Delta Flume, a 300-m-long, 5-m-wide and 9.5-m-high wave flume (Deltares, Delft, the Netherlands), enabling a full-scale test. A winter-state salt marsh was transplanted to two cross-shore transects using the first 200 m of the flume (Fig. 1). The marsh, fronting the dike, was characterized by a high density of marsh vegetation species, dominated by Elymus athericus (E. athericus), but with Atriplex prostrata present at lower densities (Methods). Such vegetation is present at a high elevation in the tidal regime, which makes it effective in attenuating waves14,15.
Extreme conditions were simulated over the marsh (Fig. 1). The water depth above the salt marsh surface ranged between 1.5 m and 4 m, and the hydrodynamic conditions reproduced depth-limited waves, with maximum significant wave heights (Hm0) set to half of the local water depth. Offshore significant wave heights ranged between 0.75 m and 2 m. The marsh was exposed for a total duration of approximately 29 h, of which 21 h included above-ground vegetation, whereas the last 8 h occurred without above-ground vegetation, but with largely intact below-ground biomass (see Methods and Supplementary Table 1 for the testing programme). The lower end of this range is equal to field observations and past flume experiments, with wave heights of 0.85 m (ref. 12) and 0.90 m (ref. 5). The upper end of the range represents extreme events, for example, in the Western Scheldt (the Netherlands) and Chesapeake Bay (United States)14,19.
Marsh substrate under extreme storms
Whether salt marshes effectively contribute to wave attenuation primarily depends on the stability of the marsh substrate.
When the substrate erodes, below- and above-ground vegetation biomass might also be (partly) removed.
Elevation measurements at 32 fixed locations at the salt marsh show, on average, a decreasing marsh surface over the total experimental time of 21 h with damaged vegetation (7 mm; 0.
33 mm h–1), which is in the same order of magnitude as previous studies with smaller wave heights (4.
4 mm surface lowering; 0.
16 mm h–1)5,20, and smaller-than-typical length scales of the marsh microtopography (Methods).
The presence of below-ground biomass and roots in the marsh substrate is known to enhance soil stability.
A clear root zone was also present in our experiment, mainly in the top 10 cm of the substrate.
The observed stable marsh platform aligns with past observations of hurricanes (Katrina and Rita) that eroded 527 km2 of mainly brackish marshes in the Louisiana coastal plain.
Salt marshes remained stable and largely unchanged21.
The stability of the marsh substrate under extreme conditions is an essential feature for marsh existence in areas in which regular wave attacks may be expected22.
Our experiment shows that this essential feature is also valid for extreme storms, which agrees with past field and flume evidence20,21,23.
Thus, with negligible surface erosion and largely intact below-ground vegetation biomass throughout all experimental runs, our experiment suggests that marsh platforms are able to contribute to wave attenuation irrespective of the short-term damage to above-ground biomass, as long as there is no lateral retreat due to seaward cliff initiation and erosion24,25.
We therefore focus hereafter on progressive vegetation damage reducing wave attenuation over time.

Wave attenuation and vegetation damage
Salt marsh vegetation breaks under prolonged wave exposure5,13,26. Consequently, the above-ground biomass that contributes to wave attenuation decreases. The experimental runs are clustered into three distinct groups of repeating wave height and water depth combinations. In the first two groups, continuous wave exposure caused progressively increasing damage to the above-ground vegetation, whereas the above-ground vegetation was removed in the last group (Methods and Supplementary Table 1). This allowed us to explicitly quantify wave attenuation by vegetation as a result of progressive damage of the above-ground biomass.
The above-ground biomass present in the flume before the experiment started did not statistically differ from the vegetation found in the field during the same period (Mann–Whitney U test; P > 0.
05) (Fig.
2).
Initially, after the first experimental run, above-ground biomass and vegetation stem length largely decreased by 33% (from 831 g m–2 to 558 g m–2) and 19% (from 56 cm to 45 cm), respectively (Fig.
3a,b).
Although vegetation damage increased with exposure duration, the above-ground biomass and stem length did not change significantly across the experimental runs with different wave forcing, apart from biomass during the last experimental run with a significant wave height of 2 m (t-test for normal and Mann–Whitney U test for not normal distributed samples; Benjamini–Hochberg FDR P-value correction; P > 0.
05; Supplementary Table 2).

articles.title: Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11183-2The use of zeolites with an appropriate pore structure combined with a high CO/olefin ratio is shown to catalyse olefin carbonylation and produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Carbonylation is an important process used to produce aldehydes, carboxylic acids and esters1,2,3,4,5 that is usually catalysed by homogeneous metal complexes with ligands and iodide promoters6,7,8,9,10,11,12.
Koch has reported that protons of mineral acids can also catalyse carbonylation13.
Previous studies have demonstrated that Brønsted acidic zeolites can act as a heterogeneous, Koch-type catalyst for carbonylation of alcohols and olefins, but the products in this case are limited to tertiary carboxylic acids14,15,16,17,18.
Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation.
We report that, with FER zeolite and a CO/olefin ratio of 360, olefin carbonylation can produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products; ethylene carbonylation to propanoic acid (PA) is achieved with 80% selectivity over 100 h and propylene carbonylation to isobutyric acid (IBA) is achieved with 95% selectivity over 750 h.
The propylene and ethylene carbonylation selectivities decrease to 61% and 57%, respectively, as the CO/olefin ratio decreases to 24 and 90, respectively.
Experiments in combination with theoretical calculations suggest that T2-O5 in eight-membered ring (8-MR) cavities of FER zeolite are the primary active sites for ethylene carbonylation and T3-O1 in ten-membered rings (10-MRs) are the primary active sites for propylene carbonylation.
Our findings open new directions for olefin carbonylation and provide critical insights into the prerequisites for developing new zeolite-based carbonylation processes.

articles.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11152-9A multi-tissue signalling system links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species1,2,3, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear.
Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans.
Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).
BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1.
BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan.
This BH2–BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing.
Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures.
In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington’s disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.
