Main
Emerging evidence demonstrates that moderately cold temperatures delay ageing and promote health across species1. Lowering body temperature extends lifespan in both poikilotherms, including C. elegans, Drosophila melanogaster and various fish species, and homeotherms, including rodents1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8. In adult C. elegans, a shift from standard (20 °C) to moderately low temperature (15 °C) markedly extends lifespan2,9,10,11,12. In rodents, a mild decrease in body temperature by only around 0.5 °C prolongs lifespan, whereas a comparable increase shortens it3,4. Lower body temperature also correlates with longevity in humans13,14. Notably, average human body temperature has declined since the Industrial Revolution, raising the possibility that changes in body temperature may have contributed to increased longevity over recent decades13. Together, these findings suggest that moderate cold engages evolutionarily conserved programs that promote longevity.
Despite being recognized for more than a century15, the mechanisms by which moderate cold temperature promotes longevity remain largely unclear. Historically, cold-induced lifespan extension was interpreted as a consequence of passive thermodynamic effects, including reduced metabolic rate and slower biochemical reaction kinetics. However, studies in C. elegans revealed that cold-induced longevity is an actively regulated process2,9,10,11,12. For example, the temperature-sensitive TRPA-1 ion channel promotes longevity at 15–20 °C but not at warmer temperatures, indicating that low temperature is sensed and transduced into longevity mechanisms11,12. Moreover, cold temperature induces transcriptional programs that enhance proteostasis2,9.
Despite these advances, a fundamental question remains of what systemic signals coordinate cold-induced responses across tissues. Small metabolites are ideally suited for this role because they can act as rapidly diffusible regulators integrating metabolism, enzymatic activity and intertissue signalling. We therefore hypothesized that cold temperature induces metabolite-based signals that coordinate metabolic, proteostatic and longevity pathways across tissues. We further hypothesized that such metabolites could function as temperature-independent effectors capable of recapitulating the beneficial effects of cold temperature even at higher temperatures.
Here we identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into the bioactive enzymatic cofactor BH4 constitute a multi-tissue regulatory system that promotes longevity and maintains proteostasis across tissues. Through metabolomic, genetic and physiological analyses, we find that elevated BH2 synthesis in muscle and its conversion to BH4 in distal tissues promotes tyrosine synthesis, thereby mediating key aspects of cold-induced longevity. This pathway can be leveraged to confer longevity and proteostasis benefits at normal and elevated temperatures in both C. elegans and human cells.
Cold temperature increases BH2 levels
Exposure of C. elegans to moderately low temperature (15 °C) after development induces a considerable extension of lifespan2,10,11,12. To assess metabolic changes associated with this effect, we raised wild-type worms at the standard temperature (20 °C) until adulthood and subsequently transferred them to 15 °C, 20 °C or 25 °C. Untargeted metabolomics analysis on day 5 of adulthood identified 64 metabolites that were significantly increased at 15 °C relative to both 20 °C and 25 °C (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). An independent experiment confirmed 45 of these metabolites, with strong concordance between datasets (Extended Data Fig. 1a–d and Supplementary Table 2).
Among the 45 reproducibly cold-induced metabolites, several were linked to BH4 synthesis and its function as an enzymatic cofactor, including GTP, BH2, tryptophan, phenylalanine and tyrosine (Fig. 1a,b). As BH2 was among the most strongly induced metabolites at cold temperature (Fig. 1a), we focused subsequent analyses on this metabolite. Cold exposure after development increased BH2 levels from day 1 of adulthood, and BH2 remained elevated at 15 °C relative to age-matched animals at 20 °C until at least day 10 (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 3). BH2 induction was not a general consequence of longevity, as reduced insulin signalling, a distinct longevity pathway, did not increase BH2 levels at 20 °C (Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4).
Loss of the temperature-sensitive trpa-1 channel shortens lifespan under both standard and cold temperatures11. However, worms still exhibit substantially extended lifespan at 15 °C compared with at 20 °C, indicating that cold-induced longevity is not solely mediated by TRPA-1-dependent pathways. Loss of trpa-1 did not reduce BH2 levels at cold temperature (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 1), demonstrating that elevated BH2 synthesis is induced independently of canonical TRPA-1 temperature sensing.
We next examined whether BH2 reflects a regulated pathway rather than a passive metabolic consequence of reduced temperature. Quantitative proteomics identified GTP cyclohydrolase I (GCH1 in humans, CAT-4 in C. elegans), the first and rate-limiting enzyme in BH2 synthesis16,17, as one of the most strongly induced proteins at 15 °C (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 5). Cold temperature also increased cat-4 mRNA amounts, indicating that CAT-4 induction occurs, at least in part, at the transcriptional level (Extended Data Fig. 2a). MED15 (human)/MDT-15 (C. elegans), a key transcriptional regulator of metabolic responses, is required for cold-induced longevity9. Importantly, knockdown of mdt-15 reduced cat-4 transcript levels at 15 °C (Extended Data Fig. 2b), indicating that cold-induced CAT-4 expression is part of a regulated transcriptional program.
BH2 is required for cold-induced longevity
Although BH2 is an inactive metabolite, it functions as a key intermediate in the synthesis and intertissue transport of its reduced, bioactive form, BH416,17. As BH4 is chemically unstable and readily oxidized, the more-stable BH2 form serves as a major organismal reservoir of this bioactive metabolite16,17. Consequently, cat-4-mutant worms are severely depleted of BH418. Consistent with the essential role of BH4 as a cofactor for multiple enzymes, these worms exhibit increased fragility compared with wild-type worms18. Accordingly, cat-4-mutant worms were short lived under both cold and standard temperatures (Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). Knockdown of cat-4 from early development also shortened lifespan at both 15 °C and 20 °C, although the effect was more pronounced under cold temperatures (Extended Data Fig. 2f).
As cold temperature during adulthood was sufficient to induce CAT-4 expression, BH2 synthesis and lifespan extension, we next examined the effects of cat-4 knockdown after development. As BH4 could not be detected by metabolomics because of its chemical instability, we quantified BH4 using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Cold temperature induced a significant but modest increase in BH4 levels (Fig. 1f), consistent with BH2 serving as the major intermediate reservoir for this metabolite16,17. Knockdown of cat-4 after development decreased BH4 levels under both standard and cold temperatures, although this reduction was moderate (Fig. 1f). Importantly, cat-4 RNA interference (RNAi) decreased BH4 at cold temperature only to levels comparable to those observed at standard temperature without knockdown (Fig. 1f). Thus, BH4 levels remained within a physiological range, enabling us to determine whether elevated CAT-4 activity during adulthood is required for cold-induced longevity. Notably, knockdown of cat-4 after development diminished the lifespan extension induced by cold temperature, but had no significant effect on lifespan at 20 °C or 25 °C (Fig. 1g).
To further dissect the adult-specific requirement for elevated CAT-4 in cold-induced longevity, we generated an auxin-inducible degron (AID) strain enabling conditional degradation of CAT-4 protein in somatic tissues (Extended Data Fig. 2g). CAT-4 degradation from early development substantially reduced lifespan at 20 °C (Extended Data Fig. 2h). By contrast, degradation of CAT-4 after development did not affect lifespan at 20 °C, but specifically shortened longevity a

articles.title: WEE1 opposes APC/C<sup>CDH1</sup> activity to promote S phase entry
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11188-xExperimental and modelling data indicate that WEE1 promotes re-entry of quiescent cells into the cell cycle, potentially explaining the toxic side effects of WEE1 inhibitors in cancer therapies.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
WEE1 phosphorylates and inhibits the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases to prevent mitotic entry and establish a G2 DNA damage checkpoint1,2,3. Consequently, WEE1 inhibitors have been developed to be synthetically lethal in TP53-mutated tumours that become reliant on this WEE1-mediated checkpoint, and such inhibitors are undergoing clinical trials. However, WEE1 inhibitors also have efficacy in TP53-wild-type tumours, and many trials have been terminated owing to high levels of toxic side effects, suggesting that WEE1 has unknown functions. Here we show that WEE1 promotes cell cycle re-entry from quiescence (G0) by opposing the activity of the E3 ubiquitin ligase, anaphase-promoting complex–cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/CCDH1). WEE1 phosphorylates CDH1 (FZR1) at key residues that mediate the interaction between CDH1 and APC/C. Cells with loss of function of WEE1 during G0/G1 have delayed S phase entry, impaired G1/S transition, abnormal S phase accumulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21Cip1/Kip1 and a p21-dependent G2 arrest. Reduced expression of APC/CCDH1 or p21 renders cells more sensitive to acute WEE1 inhibition, and both pathways are downregulated in cells with acquired WEE1 inhibitor resistance. These results reveal a mechanism of cell cycle control that has implications for how WEE1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) control passage through the eukaryotic cell cycle. WEE1 (ref. 4) is a tyrosine kinase that inhibits CDK1 by phosphorylating Tyr15 (refs. 1,2,3). Late in G2, CDC25 phosphatases dephosphorylate Tyr15, promoting mitotic entry1,5,6,7,8. This mechanism forms a G2 DNA damage checkpoint, which becomes vital in TP53-mutated cancer cells9. Thus, WEE1 inhibitors (WEE1i) have been developed to be synthetically lethal in TP53-mutated cancers and are being trialled across several indications10,11. However, toxic side effects of unknown origin11 have led to trial suspensions. WEE1 also inhibits CDK2, a key driver of G1/S progression and proliferative commitment. Consistently, non-phosphorylatable CDK2T14A;Y15F knock-in mutant mice and human colorectal cancer cells enter S phase faster when returning to the cycle from quiescence12,13. However, no direct cellular evidence of the impact of WEE1 on CDK2 is available14, and exogenous WEE1 expression in IMR90 human fibroblasts has no effect on G1/S timing15. Therefore, we sought to clarify the function of WEE1 in early cell cycle control. We demonstrate a role for WEE1 in suppressing the anaphase-promoting complex–cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/CCDH1), a key antagonist of G1/S progression, to promote timely cell cycle re-entry following release from quiescence. We identify CDH1 (FZR1) as a WEE1 substrate relevant to cell cycle control. Our findings shed light on the pleiotropic impact of WEE1i in cells.
WEE1 promotes efficient S phase entry
To understand the potential roles of WEE1 in regulation of CDK2 activity during G1 and S phase entry, we constructed an influence diagram describing the known interactions of WEE1 with the G1/S regulatory network (Fig. 1a). WEE1 inhibits cyclin E–CDK2 and cyclin A–CDK2 (ref. 16). We converted this influence diagram to a series of ordinary differential equations and parametrized the model to reproduce the known dynamics of the G1/S regulatory network (Fig. 1b). We simulated the depletion of WEE1 levels to 50% of baseline and observed that CDK2 was activated earlier and S phase entry was faster than in the presence of 100% WEE1 activity.
To experimentally test whether we could observe accelerated S phase entry in cells when WEE1 activity was reduced, we used AZD1775, a WEE1i previously used in clinical trials (Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). To investigate the role of WEE1 in S phase entry while avoiding confounding effects from WEE1 perturbation during the preceding G2 phase, we synchronized hTert-RPE1 mRuby–PCNA cells in early G0/G1 phase with a CDK4–CDK6 inhibitor (CDK4/6i) (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Labelling of PCNA at the endogenous locus with mRuby generates a robust marker to define the G1/S transition (Methods). Subsequently, we washed out the CDK4/6i, releasing cells into G1, in the presence or absence of WEE1i and quantified G1 length by time-lapse imaging of mRuby-labelled PCNA (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Contrary to our model predictions, WEE1 inhibition increased both G1 length and the fraction of cells that did not enter S phase during the 48 h imaging period (Fig. 1c). To confirm that this was not an artefact of CDK4/6i treatment, we also arrested cells in G0 by contact inhibition, followed by serum starvation (Extended Data Fig. 1f), then replated cells at low density, releasing the cells into G1 in the presence or absence of WEE1i, and again performed time-lapse imaging. Again, we observed increased G1 length and an increased fraction of cells not entering S phase after WEE1 inhibition (Extended Data Fig. 1g).
As kinase inhibitors can have off-target effects, we depleted WEE1 from CDK4/6i-arrested G0/G1 cells using short interfering RNA (siRNA) (Extended Data Fig. 1h), then released the cells back into the cell cycle and quantified G1 length by time-lapse imaging. WEE1 depletion had a more severe impact than WEE1 inhibition, with very few cells entering S phase over the 48 h imaging period compared with control-depleted cells and those that did so having an increased G1 length (Fig. 1d). To be certain that the delay in entering S phase was due to loss of WEE1 function, we generated a cell line with an inducible WEE1–GFP degron (Extended Data Fig. 2) to remove endogenous WEE1 in a highly specific manner. We validated WEE1–GFP localization and normal growth of this cell line and showed that WEE1 could be degraded within 1 h of addition of doxycycline and indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) (Extended Data Fig. 2b,d,e). Degradation of endogenous WEE1 upon release from CDK4/6i-mediated G0/G1 arrest again led to most cells not entering S phase; of those that did enter S phase, the length of G1 was significantly longer in the absence of WEE1 (Fig. 1e).
These data show that, contrary to our predictions and previous understanding of the functions of WEE1, WEE1 inhibition does not accelerate S phase entry. Instead, WEE1 is required for timely S phase entry in cells returning to proliferation from quiescence.
WEE1 couples CDK2 activity to G1/S
Our model (Fig. 1a,b) predicted an earlier and more rapid increase in CDK2 activity upon WEE1 inhibition. To test this, we used an exogenously expressed fluorescent live-cell reporter (CDK2L–GFP) that measures cyclin E–CDK2 activity in real time during G1 (ref. 17) (Fig. 2a). hTert-RPE1 mRuby–PCNA CDK2L–GFP cells were released from CDK4/6i G0/G1 arrest in the presence or absence of WEE1i, and CDK2 activity was tracked by time-lapse imaging. We used a WEE1i to perturb WEE1, as it was a clinically relevant drug, and because a higher fraction of cells entered S phase with this approach compared with siRNA or degron approaches, allowing us to make statistically meaningful comparisons. When WEE1 was inhibited, CDK2 activity started to increase earlier during G1 and reached a higher activity than in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated cells (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Video 1). Cells treated with WEE1i therefore entered S phase at a higher level of CDK2 activity. The observation that cells could remain in G1 with high CDK2 activity was surprising; we repeated the experiment using a similar, shorter version of the CDK2 sensor (DHB–mCherry) and observed the same result18 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b).
Two key events drive the G1/S transition: an increase in CDK2 activity and inhibition of APC/CCDH1 E3 ubiquitin ligase activity19 (Fig.
1b).
CDK2 can phosphorylate CDH1 and inhibit APC/CCDH1 activity20,21,22.
Therefore, we tested whether there was any change in the timing and/or rate of APC/CCDH1 inactivation relative to the G1/S transition in WEE1i-treated cells that had abnormally high CDK2 activity in G1.
We used hTert-RPE1 cells expressing mCherry–geminin(1–110), constitutively expressed from an exogenous promoter, as a live-cell reporter of APC/CCDH1 activity21.
Geminin is very effectively degraded by APC/CCDH1 during G1, and geminin protein only starts to accumulate after the G1/S transition (Extended Data Fig.
3c).
Therefore, mCherry–geminin, together with coexpressed mTurquoise2–PCNA (under the control of an exogenous promoter), is a useful reporter for determining the timing and rate of APC/CCDH1 inactivation relative to the G1/S transition.
Using this reporter, we identified that in cells released from CDK4/6i G0/G1 arrest, APC/CCDH1 activity was switched off just after the G1/S transition in WEE1i-treated cells, with timing and rate indistinguishable from those observed in DMSO-treated cells (Fig.
2c and Extended Data Fig.
3c).
Our data suggest that upon WEE1 inhibition, CDK2 activity increases to a higher level in G1, but the timing of APC/CCDH1 inactivation relative to the G1/S transition remains similar to that in DMSO-treated cells (Fig.
2d).
Consequently, APC/CCDH1 inactivation is more important than reaching a threshold of CDK2 activity with respect to establishing the timing of S phase entry.

articles.title: A single archaeon couples long-chain fatty acid oxidation to methanogenesis
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11207-xMethanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75 is a thermophilic archaeon isolated from a Chinese petroleum reservoir that converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, and uses saturated and unsaturated fatty acids to produce methane.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Anaerobic degradation of complex organic compounds to methane and carbon dioxide is common in the deep subsurface biosphere and has long been considered to require syntrophic cooperation, with methanogens confined to the terminal use of simple C1 and C2 substrates.
Thermodynamic considerations, multi-omics analyses and microcosm experiments suggest that archaeal lineages are capable of methanogenic degradation of complex substrates1,2,3,4,5,6.
However, experimental validation in pure culture was lacking.
Here we report the isolation of a thermophilic archaeon, Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75, affiliated with Archaeoglobi, from a Chinese petroleum reservoir.
Strain AA-75 not only converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, but also uses saturated fatty acids varying from C7:0 to C18:0 and unsaturated fatty acids including C16:1, C18:1 and C18:2 to produce methane.
We term the latter lipotrophic methanogenesis, which integrates β-oxidation of fatty acids with the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway and the canonical methyl-tetrahydromethanopterin:coenzyme M methyltransferase and methyl-coenzyme M reductase complexes, together with an intracellular electron transfer system.
A formaldehyde-methanol branch probably functions as an auxiliary route for C1 metabolism during methanogenesis.
Methane produced from stearate is moderately 13C-enriched (δ13C–CH4 = −40.
0‰ to −36.
3‰), distinct from the strong 13C depletion characteristic of canonical methanogenic pathways.
These findings demonstrate that methanogens can function as primary degraders of complex organic matter, challenging the classical syntrophic paradigm and calling for refinement of current models of carbon cycling in the deep subsurface biosphere.

articles.title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11179-yAn environment-regulated state is identified across multiple cell types at the root tip, revealing a shared dichotomy between cells with and without this state.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions.
Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions.
Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory1.
Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping.
One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling.
This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity.
It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity.
Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions.
Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions.
These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types.

Main
The root of Arabidopsis thaliana is a valuable model for studying cell differentiation in plants. Cell types are arranged in concentric layers around a central vascular bundle and arise from distinct stem cell populations maintained near the root tip in the meristem1. As stem cells divide, their descendants are displaced shootward and progressively differentiate, which creates developmental trajectories in which the spatial arrangement of cells recapitulates the temporal dynamics of differentiation (Fig. 1a).
Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has refined the transcriptional signatures of Arabidopsis root cell types and enabled high-resolution reconstruction of these developmental trajectories2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Although these studies have identified transient cell states in individual lineages, they have largely analysed each lineage independently, which may overlook transcriptional states shared across multiple cell types irrespective of developmental identity. Whether such shared transcriptional states exist and how they contribute to root cell identity remain largely unexplored.
A dichotomy in root cell lineages
To characterize cell states during root development, here we generated a high-resolution scRNA-seq (10x Genomics) atlas of the A. thaliana Col-0 root tip (Fig. 1b). After filtering low-quality cells, doublets and genes significantly affected by protoplast isolation, batch integration generated a reference atlas comprising 87,056 cells from 9 replicates, with a total of 25,784 detected genes (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1).
We identified 27 transcriptionally distinct clusters and assigned their identities by combining differential expression with optimized whole-mount hybridization chain reaction (HCR)10 and tissue clearing11 to spatially map the expression of the 15 most specific marker genes (Fig. 1b–d). This process resolved all known cell types, including distinct root cap subpopulations (early, tip and lateral) (Fig. 1b–d). One cluster located between the root cap and epidermis could not be assigned directly by marker expression. However, on the basis of its position and developmental origin of these tissues, it was annotated as ‘epidermis–meristem’ (Fig. 1b).
Cells were grouped according to their developmental lineages (epidermis, root cap, cortex, endodermis, xylem pole pericycle (XPP), phloem pole pericycle (PPP), procambium, phloem and xylem), which confirmed that ontogenic programs remain the dominant determinant of root cell identity (Fig. 1b,e). Cells from each lineage were analysed independently to reconstruct developmental trajectories. A meristematic score, derived from genes enriched in the meristematic epidermis cluster, was calculated for each lineage, and the cell with the highest score was defined as the trajectory starting point (t = 0). Trajectory topology was inferred using partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA), and developmental progression was ordered by diffusion pseudotime from t = 0 (Fig. 1e–g).
The root cap lineage exhibited the most complex topology and recapitulated known developmental events. That is, the split of lateral and tip populations and their convergence with columella cells to form the sloughing border-like cells12 (Fig. 1g). These trajectories were supported by stage-specific marker genes13,14,15 (Extended Data Fig. 1a), which further validated the inferred developmental trajectories.
Although some lineages are anticipated to be composed of distinct cell subtypes, such as phloem and xylem, which are made of metaphloem and protophloem and metaxylem and protoxylem, respectively, and the epidermis, which subdivides into root hairs and non-root hairs, each is expected to follow a single developmental trajectory from undifferentiated to differentiated states. Notably, PAGA revealed that all cell types and subcell types instead exhibit two branches (branch 1 and branch 2) that diverge at an early pseudotime point (Fig. 1g). Only the epidermis contained cells preceding this bifurcation and a clearly identifiable meristematic population. In most other lineages, branching occurred directly from t = 0, which probably reflects the difficulty in capturing the rarer inner-layer meristematic cells during protoplasting.
To independently validate the inferred topology, whole-mount HCR was used to detect early and late markers in epidermis, endodermis and XPP (Extended Data Fig. 1b–e). In all three lineages, genes predicted to be expressed near t = 0 were detected closer to the meristem than predicted late markers. Consistent with this finding, lineage-specific meristem, elongation and maturation gene signatures obtained from a previous study8 progressed as expected along pseudotime. This result provides support for the robustness of our t = 0 assignment and inferred developmental ordering (Extended Data Fig. 2a).
Independent trajectory inference using Monocle also recovered the bifid topology (Extended Data Fig. 2b–d). Cell ordering in both branches was highly correlated with diffusion pseudotime and supported by RNA velocity analyses (Extended Data Fig. 2e–g).
Together, these data show that in addition to developmental progression, cells in most cell types exhibit two alternative transcriptional states. This result therefore reveals the existence of an additional, previously unrecognized, level of complexity in cell identity.
A shared transcriptional program
To identify transcriptional programs associated with cell type, developmental progression and branch identity, we performed high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA). Of the 6,649 genes assigned to 25 identified co-expression modules (Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Table 3), most were enriched in specific cell types, groups of cell types or developmental stages. By contrast, modules 20 and 21 were specifically enriched in branch 1 across all lineages. This result demonstrates that there is a transcriptional program shared across multiple cell types independently of developmental identity.
Across all cell types, branch 1 cells consistently contained more detected genes and higher unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts than branch 2 cells (Fig. 2c), which indicated greater overall transcriptional activity. Modules 20 and 21 were also among the largest co-expression modules identified (320 and 615 genes, respectively; Fig. 2d), which showed that this transcriptional asymmetry involves a broad coordinated gene expression program. Although the PAGA analysis did not resolve two branches in non-hair cells, enrichment of the branch-specific modules and increased transcript abundance suggest that both populations are also present in this lineage.
Given the unexpected transcriptional differences between the two branches of the same cell type, we next sought to exclude possible experimental or analytical artefacts that might have created spurious trajectory bifurcations. Branch separation was not explained by cell cycle phase, experimental batches or genes affected by protoplast isolation (Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). Because roots grown on the surface of agar experience distinct agar-facing and air-facing microenvironments, we also profiled root tips from plants grown fully embedded in agar. The bifid trajectories remained clearly detectable across all cell types, which therefore ruled out these growth microenvironments as a contributing factor (Extended Data Fig. 3f–h).
Another possibility was that the lower UMI branch (branch 2) reflected damaged cells from which fewer transcripts were captured, despite these cells not exhibiting elevated mitochondrial or chloroplastic transcript content (Extended Data Fig. 3i–j). If so, lowly expressed genes would be preferentially detected in the higher UMI branch 1, whereas highly expressed genes would be shared between both branches. Using the XPP, we found that depletion of branch-1-specific genes in branch 2 substantially exceeded that expected from expression level alone (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). Likewise, branch separation persisted after randomly downsampling branch 1 cells to match the UMI distribution of their branch 2 counterparts and reprocessing the dataset in three independent replicates (Extended Data Fig. 4d–g). articles.title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11186-zCD51+ astrocytes promote synapse formation in the developing cortex, circuit plasticity in the hippocampus and circuit remodelling after stroke.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes1,2. Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes3; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies4, we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51+ and CD51− astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51+ astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51+ astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51+ astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Cellular diversity is an operational necessity of all organ systems, in which diverse cell types participate in a division of labour that orchestrates essential physiological activities.
Astrocytes are the most abundant type of glial cell in the central nervous system (CNS) and have vital roles in all facets of brain physiology, including neurotransmission, synaptogenesis, circuit function, metabolic support and maintenance of the blood–brain barrier, along with responses to injury and degeneration1,5,6,7.
Advances in single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) technologies have facilitated the identification of several prospective astrocyte subpopulations, suggesting that these diverse roles may be conducted by subsets of distinct astrocytes8.
However, whether specialized astrocytes are capable of executing a subset of these diverse functions remains very poorly defined, as experimentally examining the extent to which molecular heterogeneity reflects functionally distinct subtypes of astrocytes in active neural circuits remains a major challenge.
While several previous studies identified astrocyte populations that express unique markers and demonstrated roles for these specific genes in astrocytes in the context of neural circuits, whether these populations have unique functional properties remains unclear9,10.
Unambiguous demonstration of functionally distinct astrocyte subpopulations at the cellular level requires a direct comparison of the functional properties between two populations in vivo.
Critically, tools that enable selective labelling and manipulation of defined subsets of astrocytes, which would facilitate the direct comparison between different subpopulations of astrocytes, do not exist.
Thus, whether functionally distinct subtypes of astrocytes exist in neural circuits has remained unresolved.
Here we identify CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes as subpopulations with distinct properties and diverse functions in regulating neural circuits across postnatal cortical development, learning and memory, and brain repair.

Distinct cellular properties
Using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-based approaches in the adult mouse brain, our previous studies identified CD51, the αV integrin subunit encoded by Itgav, as a cell surface marker capable of subdividing subsets of astrocytes with unique molecular properties4.
Whether CD51-expressing astrocytes are endowed with unique properties in vivo in functioning neural circuits remains unclear.
We therefore generated a mouse line that enables the selective targeting of CD51+ astrocytes in the mouse brain.
To achieve this, we engineered a CD51-FLP BAC (bacterial artificial chromosome) mouse line and intercrossed the CD51-FLP founder line with Rosa-FSF-tdTomato mice (where FSF denotes FRT-stop-FRT), such that the reporter is expressed in the presence of FLP activity (CD51-FLP;Rosa-FSF-tdTomato) (Fig.
1a).
Analysis of this mouse line revealed expression of CD51 protein in tdTomato-expressing cells, indicating successful targeting of this population (Extended Data Fig.
1c–e).
tdTomato expression was also evident in a subset of endothelial cells, but rarely in other cells types (Extended Data Fig.
2a,b).
Importantly, tdTomato expression in astrocytes was highly concordant with immunoreactivity to an anti-CD51 antibody (Extended Data Figs.
1c–e and 2c,d).
To assess the extent to which the CD51-FLP;Rosa-FSF-tdTomato line targets astrocytes in the brain of 8-week-old mice, we co-stained for the pan-astrocyte marker SOX9 and evaluated the constituency of CD51+ (tdTomato+SOX9+) and CD51− (tdTomato−SOX9+) astrocytes across a host of brain regions (Fig.
1b,c and Extended Data Fig.
1a,b).
This analysis revealed the presence of CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes in varying proportions throughout the brain, with CD51+ astrocytes representing approximately 19% of hippocampal astrocytes, 13% of olfactory bulb astrocytes and 38% of cortical astrocytes (Fig.
1c).
Notably, our finding that 19% of astrocytes in the hippocampus are CD51+ is consistent with publicly available scRNA-seq data from the adult mouse hippocampus11 (Extended Data Fig.
1f).
These data indicate that the CD51-FLP mouse can distinguish CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes in the adult brain.

We next sought to assess the cellular properties of CD51+ and CD51− astrocyte populations in the cortex and hippocampus, focusing on cell morphology and Ca2+ activity.
The CD51-FLP mouse line allows us to use the FLP-FRT system to conditionally express reporters using intersectional viral approaches in CD51+ or CD51− astrocytes12,13.
Combining these FLP-based viral tools with the CD51-FLP mouse, we can label CD51+ and CD51− astrocyte subpopulations with tdTomato (Fig.
1d).
Accordingly, we injected the cortex or hippocampus of 4-week-old CD51-FLP mice, collected mouse tissue at 8 weeks of age and assessed expression of the conditional tdTomato reporter.
Using the tdTomato reporter to assess morphology, we found that CD51+ astrocytes in the cortex exhibit enhanced morphological complexity compared with CD51− astrocytes; by contrast, CD51+ astrocytes in the hippocampus exhibited comparatively decreased complexity (Fig.
1e,f).
Using similar approaches, we generated conditional adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) that enabled us to selectively target CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes with GCaMP6, an optical sensor that reliably reports Ca2+ activity14 (Fig.
1g).
Using the same workflow as described above, we used two-photon imaging to measure Ca2+ activity in ex vivo slices from the cortex or hippocampus and found that CD51+ astrocytes in the cortex exhibit enhanced spontaneous Ca2+ activity compared with CD51− astrocytes (Fig.
1h,i).
By contrast, in the hippocampus, CD51− astrocytes exhibited elevated spontaneous Ca2+ activity compared with CD51+ astrocytes (Fig.
1j,k).
Together, these studies indicate that CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes are endowed with unique morphological and physiological properties within and across the cortex and hippocampus.

Emergence of CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes
The identification of unique properties for CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes in the adult brain led us to next examine whether they also exhibit unique developmental characteristics, such as proliferation and timelines of expansion.
Using postnatal cortical development as a model, in conjunction with the CD51-FLP;Rosa-FSF-tdTomato mouse line, we evaluated the constituency of CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes during the postnatal day 1 (P1) to P28 developmental interval when astrocytogenesis occurs in the cortex15,16,17.
This analysis revealed a steady increase in the proportion of CD51+ astrocytes between P1 and P21, with the relative number of tdTomato+SOX9+ astrocytes peaking at about 40% by P21 (Fig.
1l–n).
This finding was conserved across individual cortical layers (Extended Data Fig.
2e).
These observations suggest that CD51+ cells undergo a proliferative expansion during this interval.
Given that around 50% of cortical astrocytes are generated by local proliferation outside the germinal zones and in the brain parenchyma between P1 and P21 (refs.
15,16,18), we next assessed the relative proliferation rates of these populations.
Using EdU-labelling approaches (Fig.
1l), we found that CD51− astrocytes are highly proliferative at P1, which is followed by enhanced proliferation of CD51+ astrocytes at P7–21 (Fig.
1m–o).
Immunostaining for the cell cycle markers Ki-67 and phosphorylated histone H3 yielded the same pattern of results (Extended Data Fig.
2f–k).
These data are consistent with our observation of increased numbers of CD51+ astrocytes during this interval, indicating that CD51+ astrocytes proliferate and expand in the brain parenchyma during the P1–21 interval.
By contrast, CD51− astrocytes appear to be predominantly generated earlier in development and exhibit less proliferative capacity during the later stages of the P1–21 interval.

We next sought to understand the origin of CD51+ astrocytes.
Analysis of developing astrocyte RNA-seq data19 revealed that expression of Itgav emerged after birth in astrocyte lineage cells (Extended Data Fig.
3a).
Concordantly, using CD51-FLP;Rosa-FSF-tdTomato mice, we found that SOX2+ precursors within the ventricular/subventricular zone did not express tdTomato (CD51) at the onset of cortical gliogenesis at embryonic day 16.
5 (E16.
5), but a subset was tdTomato positive at P1 (Extended Data Fig.
3c–e).
These data suggest that CD51+ astrocytes are specified after the onset of gliogenesis.

articles.title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11165-4Genetic and proteomic analyses in human neurons and mouse models of Angelman syndrome (AS) show that loss of the ubiquitin ligase UBE3A leads to an overabundance of asparagine synthetase, and that this is linked with many AS phenotypes.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Angelman syndrome (AS) occurs in 1:20,000 births and is characterized by intellectual disability, developmental delay, epilepsy, microcephaly, dysmorphic facial features and a unique behavioural profile1,2. It is caused by deletion or mutation of the maternally inherited copy of UBE3A, a gene also linked to mood disorders7,8, autism4,5,7 and cancer9,10. It is widely accepted that phenotypes in AS arise due to the dysregulation of UBE3A substrates during development. However, although numerous substrates have been proposed3, establishing their link to AS phenotypes has proved difficult, limiting researchers’ mechanistic understanding of this disorder.
UBE3A is the founding member of the HECT (homologous to E6-AP C terminus) domain family of E3 ubiquitin ligases, all of which have a conserved HECT domain that contains the necessary biochemical machinery to accept activated ubiquitin from E2 enzymes and to transfer it to target proteins9. UBE3A expression is imprinted specifically in neurons such that only the maternally inherited allele is expressed, with the paternal allele being epigenetically silenced11. This imprinting mechanism, along with many disease-related phenotypes, is conserved in AS model mice that lack a maternal copy of Ube3a (Ube3am−/p+)12. These phenotypes include motor and behavioural deficits, and microcephaly, the most prominent neuroanatomical deficit in AS13. Microcephaly is not present at birth in mice but is acquired postnatally, driven by a failure of neuronal growth that results in shorter and simplified dendritic arbors and smaller-diameter axons14,15.
The integrated stress response (ISR) is a conserved pathway that helps maintain cellular homeostasis in response to noxious stimuli, including proteotoxic stress, nutrient deprivation, viral infection and oxidative stress16. These stimuli are sensed by four specialized kinases (PERK, GCN2, PKR and HRI) that converge on phosphorylation of the α-subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 (p-eIF2α) to suppress global protein synthesis and initiate compensatory transcription programs. Asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a conserved metabolic enzyme that is induced by the ATF4 transcription factor in response to amino acid deprivation17. ASNS catalyses the ATP-dependent synthesis of asparagine and glutamate from aspartate and glutamine, but its role in neuronal development remains poorly understood.
Proteomics identifies UBE3A substrates
To identify substrates of UBE3A, we used cell lines expressing gain-of-function (GOF) and loss-of-function (LOF) mutants4,5 and subjected them to stable isotype labelling by amino acids in cell culture (SILAC), tryptic remnant immunoaffinity enrichment (di-Gly purification) and mass spectrometry18 (Fig. 1a). We performed this experiment in quadruplicate and identified proteins whose ubiquitination levels were enriched by at least 20% in cells expressing a hyperactivating mutation in UBE3A (Supplementary Table 1). Because of technical issues in this experiment (see Methods for details), the total numbers of detected proteins varied across replicates. However, comparing unique proteins across replicates allowed us to compile a list of 23 proteins that could serve as potential substrates (Fig. 1b). Within this list were novel substrates, as well as many proteins that are known to bind to or become ubiquitinated by UBE3A (Fig. 1c).
To validate these candidates, first we compared protein abundance by western blot analysis in HEK293T cells expressing (1) wild-type (WT) or ligase-dead UBE3A (C820A; UBE3A(LD)), and (2) WT UBE3A or the GOF UBE3A(T485A) mutant5. In both experiments, the abundance of the catalytic subunit of DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PKc), ASNS and the ribosomal protein RPL3 was affected by UBE3A in a manner consistent with these proteins being substrates of UBE3A (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1a–d). Second, we generated knockdown (KD) cells stably expressing a short hairpin RNA (shRNA) targeting UBE3A (UBE3A KD), and analysed candidate substrate abundance. A moderate reduction of UBE3A (25%) increased the abundance of ASNS, DNA-PKc and RPL3 in these cells (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Third, we treated cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (15 μM, 12 h) to test proteasome dependence. MG132 reversed the effect of WT UBE3A on DNA-PKc and ASNS abundance but had no effect on RPL3, suggesting that the UBE3A-elicited changes in RPL3 were proteasome independent (Extended Data Fig. 1g,h).
We next compared the results of our screen with the findings of a previous co-immunoprecipitation experiment using UBE3A(LD) overexpressed in HEK293T cells18. Fifteen of the 23 candidates, including ASNS and DNA-PKc, were also identified as binding partners in this previous experiment (Fig. 1f). Finally, we compared a list of 55 proposed UBE3A substrates, including ASNS and DNA-PKc, with a previously reported dataset of upregulated proteins identified in two independent patient-derived AS neuron lines6 (Supplementary Table 2). Of the 532 proteins that were commonly upregulated in both lines, only 4 proposed substrates were on this list, including annexin A119, peroxiredoxin 120, PEG106 and ASNS (Fig. 1g). Because every validation step pointed to ASNS, we expanded our analysis of this protein.
ASNS is a direct substrate of UBE3A
ASNS is composed of a glutamine hydrolysing domain and an asparagine synthase domain, reflecting its two catalytic activities (Extended Data Fig. 2a). We first performed co-immunoprecipitation experiments and found that overexpressed UBE3A co-purifies with endogenous ASNS in HEK293T cells, consistent with our previous mass-spectrometry results18 (Extended Data Fig. 2b). We next reconstituted an in vitro ubiquitin reaction consisting of recombinant human ASNS, UBE1 (E1), UBCH7 (E2), UBE3A, ubiquitin and ATP. We found that UBE3A was required to catalyse the time-dependent formation of high-molecular-weight ubiquitin chains on ASNS while simultaneously reducing the level of unmodified ASNS (Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). Finally, we examined ASNS ubiquitination in UBE3A-KD cells expressing HA-tagged ASNS and Flag-tagged ubiquitin and treated with MG132 (30 μM) for 1 h. A modest decrease in UBE3A produced a proportional 25% decrease in ASNS ubiquitination (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g), suggesting that UBE3A is the principal E3 enzyme targeting ASNS for proteasomal degradation in these cells.
Our proteomics experiment identified five candidate ubiquitination sites on ASNS: K83 and K168, which are poorly conserved and located in the glutamine hydrolysing domain; and K467, K478 and K504, which are more highly conserved and are found in the ASNS domain (Extended Data Fig. 2h). To confirm UBE3A-dependent ubiquitination at these sites, we generated ASNS lysine-to-arginine (KR) mutants and co-transfected them with Flag-tagged ubiquitin and UBE3A into HEK293T cells. Whereas ubiquitination of the K83R and K168R mutants resembled what was observed with WT ASNS, it was reduced or altered for the K467R, K478R and K504R mutants (Extended Data Fig. 2i). In steady-state experiments, WT UBE3A reduced the abundance of WT ASNS and the K83R and K168R mutants, but no changes were observed for the K467R, K478R and K504R mutants (Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). Because degradative ubiquitination is rarely directed by a single lysine, we cannot rule out changes in cooperativity, ubiquitination linkage or ubiquitination kinetics arising from K467R, K478R and K504R mutations. Nonetheless, these results strongly suggest that ubiquitination in the asparagine synthase domain is crucial for ASNS degradation.
We next assessed UBE3A-mediated ASNS regulation in vivo by analysing ASNS protein levels and ubiquitination in the brains of Ube3am−/p+ mice (referred to as Angelman mice). In hippocampal tissue, immunoprecipitated ASNS showed a reduction in ubiquitination of about 50% in Angelman mice, compared with WT controls (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Similarly, ASNS abundance was increased in the hippocampus (130.63 ± 3.92% above WT) and cortex (114.55 ± 3.60%) with a trend in the midbrain, but not in cerebellar samples (Extended Data Fig. 3c). These changes were not due to an increase in Asns transcription, because quantitative PCR (qPCR) of hippocampal RNA showed that there was no difference in Asns mRNA levels (Extended Data Fig. 3d). Finally, ASNS protein levels in hippocampal lysates from mice with an equivalent maternal GOF T485A mutation in UBE3A (mT503A in mice21) showed a subtle but consistent decrease (Extended Data Fig. 3e,f). Altogether, our biochemical experiments show that UBE3A ubiquitinates ASNS both in vitro and in vivo.

articles.title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11184-1The structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike defines the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms—occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike.

Main
Hantaviruses are a large and globally distributed family of viruses associated with severe zoonotic disease in humans. The New World hantaviruses (NWHs) ANDV and Sin Nombre virus (SNV) cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in South and North America, respectively, with high case-fatality rates that can approach 40%. Cardiogenic shock and respiratory failure are hallmarks of HCPS. Old World hantaviruses (OWHs) are endemic in Europe and Asia or globally distributed in some cases (Seoul virus (SEOV)). The OWH Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) are associated with severe zoonotic disease and considerable mortality. Although hantaviruses are typically transmitted to humans through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, ANDV appears uniquely capable of human-to-human transmission2,3, raising its global public health significance and epidemic potential. This risk was underscored by the recent ANDV outbreak on a cruise ship departing Ushuaia, Argentina4. No US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- or European Medicines Agency (EMA)-approved medical countermeasures are available to prevent or treat hantaviral infections.
Hantavirus glycoprotein spikes are formed by two glycoproteins, Gn and Gc, which are organized into a partial lattice at the surface of the virion. Each spike consists of four Gn molecules that form a central stabilizing core surrounded by four Gc molecules at the periphery. Gc mediates the interspike contacts that stabilize the lattice. Gn consists of a head (GnH) and a base (GnB) domain. GnH is exposed at the viral surface and is thought to participate in receptor binding, whereas GnB is buried within the spike and mediates most of the intraspike interactions. Gc consists of three domains that drive membrane fusion. At neutral pH, GnH interacts with Gc, forming a pre-fusion complex that prevents premature fusion. After exposure to acidic pH, the Gn–Gc complex dissociates, allowing Gc to insert three hydrophobic loops into the host cell membrane and undergo conformational rearrangements that drive fusion of viral and cellular membranes. Structural studies have reported the structures of GnH, GnB, Gc, the GnH–Gc complex and the Gn–Gc spike from several hantaviruses5,6,7,8,9,10.
Understanding how hantaviruses recognize their cellular receptors is a critical step toward the rational development of therapies and vaccines.
Previous studies have identified several cell-surface molecules as candidate entry host factors, including integrins β1–3 (refs.
11,12,13,14), decay accelerating factor (DAF, encoded by CD55)15,16, complement factors (gC1qR)17 and the cadherin-superfamily protein PCDH1 (ref.
1).
However, only PCDH1 has been shown to directly recognize the ANDV Gn–Gc spike1,18 and to be required for infection of human endothelial cells—major targets of hantavirus infection1,19.
Furthermore, PCDH1 is critical for ANDV infection in vivo and for disease pathogenesis in a lethal hamster model of ANDV challenge1,18.
PCDH1 is a type I membrane protein expressed in human airway epithelial and endothelial cells.
It contains seven extracellular cadherin-repeat (EC) domains that extend into the extracellular space.
Binding studies have shown that PCDH1 does not recognize soluble monomeric glycoproteins but instead binds to the tetrameric glycoprotein spikes displayed on the viral surface1,18.
Monoclonal antibodies targeting the first EC repeat (EC1) inhibited entry of a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) pseudotyped with Gn–Gc from multiple NWHs1, and point mutations at the tip of EC1 prevented PCDH1’s interaction with Gn–Gc of rVSVs bearing the glycoproteins of ANDV (rVSV-ANDV)1,18.
Together, these findings indicate that NWHs infect host cells by engaging the EC1 domain of PCDH1.
However, the structural determinants of this interaction remain unclear.
Here we sought to determine the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV Gn–Gc spike.

PCDH1 stabilizes the (Gn–Gc)4 spike
PCDH1 binds to viral particles but not to the soluble GnH–Gc heterodimer1,18, suggesting that the receptor-binding site is presented only on viral spikes.
To elucidate the structural basis for PCDH1 recognition, we designed a soluble version of the ANDV spike tetramer by adding a hetero-octamerization domain at the C-terminal end of the Gn and Gc ectodomains (Fig.
1a).
The octamerization sequence was derived from HALC4_136, a de novo tetramerization domain comprising three antiparallel helices per protomer20.
We split this scaffold by fusing the first two helices to Gn and the third helix to Gc, so that co-expression of Gn and Gc would reconstitute a hetero-oligomeric assembly with the stoichiometry of the native spike (Extended Data Fig.
1a).
We cloned both genes into a bicistronic plasmid, purified the complex from the supernatants of stably transfected Drosophila melanogaster S2 cells using affinity and size-exclusion chromatography and confirmed that it interacts with a truncated PCDH1 construct consisting of wild-type EC domains 1 to 4 (sEC1–4WT) using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA; Fig.
1b).
As a negative control, we used a construct containing the substitutions Y81A and F83A (sEC1–4MUT), which are known to abrogate virus binding18.
We also confirmed that incubation of the soluble spike with an excess of soluble sEC1WT, but not sEC1MUT, prevented the binding to sEC1–4WT (Fig.
1c).
Furthermore, we used biolayer interferometry (BLI) to demonstrate specific spike–EC1 binding.
Specifically, sEC1–4WT or sEC1–4MUT were immobilized on sensors, which were then dipped into solutions containing increasing concentrations of soluble spike (Fig.
1d).
BLI assays performed in the opposite orientation corroborated these findings (Extended Data Fig.
1b).

To verify that the soluble spike proteins fold like the spikes observed on the viral surface, we performed cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). We observed a few two-dimensional (2D) classes compatible with Gn–Gc tetramers (Extended Data Fig. 1c). However, a low-resolution three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction obtained from them was not compatible with the known ANDV spike structure5 (Extended Data Fig. 1d), suggesting that, in the absence of lateral contacts between spikes and the transmembrane regions, the intersubunit contacts within the spike are not sufficiently stable to maintain the intact eight-subunit assembly. We next hypothesized that prolonged incubation of the two proteins might help to stabilize the spike in its receptor-binding conformation. To test this hypothesis, we co-transfected S2 cells with the plasmids encoding sEC1–4WT and the soluble spike and purified the complex using double-affinity and size-exclusion chromatography. We performed cryo-EM studies and observed many new 2D classes showing tetramers (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Extended Data Table 1). Using particles from these classes, we reconstructed a map at a resolution of 2.4 Å, and we used the map to build a model of the spike that closely resembles the tetramers observed on viral particles5. The only notable differences between the two models are a slight rotation of the GnH domains relative to GnB and the poorly resolved density for domain III in the soluble spikes (Extended Data Fig. 3).
PCDH1 binds to a central spike pocket
The cryo-EM map of the complex revealed an additional density at the centre of the spike, consistent in size with a single EC domain of PCDH1.
However, as the map was processed using C4 symmetry, and the symmetry axis passes through the centre of the spike, we were unable to model this residual density.
We reprocessed the map by combining a masked 3D classification with a non-uniform refinement using a pseudo-C4 symmetry.
This approach yielded a new map at a resolution of 2.
6 Å (Fig.
1e), in which we modelled PCDH1 EC1 at the centre of the spike (Fig.
1f,g).
The final model showed the EC1 domain deeply inserted into a pocket formed by four protomers of Gn, establishing contacts with two neighbouring protomers (660 and 200 Å2, respectively) and sparse contacts with the other two (80 Å2 and 35 Å2).
This mode of interaction, whereby one receptor molecule interacts with four viral glycoproteins, represents a binding mode that to our knowledge has not been observed in any enveloped virus, and explains why PCDH1 binds to viral particles but not to soluble GnH–Gc heterodimers.
In the model, EC1 loops BCEC1 and FGEC1 interact with the AB and CD loops of GnH and the DE loop of GnB from two neighbouring protomers (Fig.
1g and Extended Data Fig.
4a).

articles.title: GRP75-dependent SIMPA mediates inter-organellar quality control
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10733-yProteotoxic stress drives formation of GRP75-dependent protein aggregates that signal through mitochondria–ER contact sites to activate targeted quality-control pathways, enabling selective clearance of damaged proteins and preserving mitochondrial integrity.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Mitochondria are bound by a double membrane and are semiautonomous organelles, rendering them highly vulnerable to global and internal proteostatic stress1.
Multiple surveillance mechanisms at proteostatic and inter-organellar levels have evolved to maintain mitochondrial integrity and cellular health2,3,4,5,6,7.
However, the precise mechanisms by which proteostatic damage relays stress signals across organelles and how the quality surveillance machinery coordinates these functions remain unknown.
Here we report that under proteostatic stress, damaged mitochondrial proteins are sequestered to form stress-induced mitochondrial protein aggregates (SIMPAs) that activate specific quality control mechanisms in a spatially confined manner without perturbing the mitochondrial network.
Quantitative proteomic and correlative light–electron microscopy analysis revealed that SIMPA mediates inter-organellar communication via mitochondria–endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes.
Mechanistically, GRP75 coordinates SIMPA biogenesis and focally activates endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response pathways via mitochondria–endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes for the targeted clearance of SIMPAs.
Functionally, in both cellular and liver disease models, we found that a GRP75-dependent SIMPA signalling cascade attenuates mitochondrial stress and preserves mitochondrial integrity under proteotoxic stress.
Overall, we show that SIMPAs, functioning as protein condensates, serve as a central cross-compartment communication hub for mitochondrial quality control, supporting cellular and organismal fitness.

articles.title: Octupole-driven spin torque switching of antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11172-5All-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions can display both a large TMR and a reciprocal switching effect, octupole-driven spin-transfer torque, enabling nanoscale magnetic memory and potentially room-temperature terahertz spintronic devices.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Magnetic tunnel junctions based on ferromagnets are canonical devices in spintronics, with wide-ranging applications in data storage, computing and sensing.
They simultaneously exhibit mechanisms for electrical detection and control of magnetic order through the tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR)1,2,3,4,5 and spin-transfer torque6,7,8,9 effects, respectively.
It was long assumed that neither of these effects could be sizeable in all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions (AATJs), considering that they have no net magnetization.
However, it was recently shown that AATJs based on chiral antiferromagnets do exhibit TMR due to their non-relativistic momentum-dependent spin polarization and cluster magnetic octupole moment, which are manifestations of their spin–split band structure10,11,12,13.
However, the reciprocal effect, that is, the antiferromagnetic counterpart of spin–transfer torque, has been assumed non-existent due to the total electric current being spin-neutral.
Here we report nanoscale AATJs that display this reciprocal effect, which we term octupole-driven spin-transfer torque (OTT).
We demonstrate current-induced OTT switching of PtMn3|MgO|PtMn3 AATJs, with a TMR value of 363% at room temperature and switching current densities of the order of 10 MA cm–2.
Our theoretical modelling explains the origin of OTT in terms of the imbalance between intra- and inter-sublattice spin currents across the AATJ, and, equivalently, in terms of the non-zero net cluster octupole polarization of each PtMn3 layer.
This work establishes a new materials platform for antiferromagnetic spintronics and provides a pathway towards deeply scaled magnetic memory and room-temperature terahertz technologies.

articles.title: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11168-1Fifteen years of atmospheric CO2 measurements show that the Amazon carbon sink is weakening, with fires, deforestation and climate stress driving increasingly high carbon emissions.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation1,2,3,4,5, rising tree mortality6,7,8 and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest9,10,11.
Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions1,2,3,4,11,12.
Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable1,9,13.
Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts9,14,15,16,17.
Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO2 measurements.
We determine a carbon balance of 0.
32 ± 0.
08 PgC yr−1, with fires acting as the dominant source (0.
40 ± 0.
07 PgC yr−1) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions.
Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups.
Group 1 (2011–2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.
11 ± 0.
08 PgC yr−1) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation.
Group 2 (2019–2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.
43 ± 0.
13 PgC yr−1) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress.
Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.
49 ± 0.
07 PgC yr−1) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning.

Main
Amazonia, the largest tropical forest in the world, has lost substantial carbon stocks due to large-scale deforestation and other land-use changes. Remaining forests in the region have offset some of this carbon loss through carbon sequestration processes. However, this capacity is declining, primarily because of increased tree mortality6,7,8,18 and changes in regional climatic conditions modified by deforestation1,3,9,13. The Amazon forest stores approximately 123 ± 23 billion tonnes of carbon (PgC) in vegetation and soils19,20. The interactions among the forest ecosystem, hydrological cycle and regional climate are complex, with atmospheric moisture recycling by evapotranspiration accounting for up to half of precipitation16. Direct human activities within Amazonia, including deforestation, forest degradation and biomass burning, have profoundly altered the carbon balance of the region and climate11. Forest loss reduces precipitation, raises temperatures and lengthens the dry season, delaying the onset of the wet season1,3,4,14,16. During periods of extreme climatic variability, such as El Niño or anomalously high Tropical North Atlantic (TNA) sea-surface temperatures (SSTs), these impacts are amplified through the interaction of accumulated forest loss, global warming, changing circulation and large-scale anomalies9,14,16.
Many questions remain about the main drivers of carbon emissions and variability in Amazonia. Studies based on modelling and bottom-up techniques show increased emissions during extreme climate (warm and dry) years, pointing to extreme events as the reason for increased carbon emissions. However, our direct atmospheric measurements show a more complex situation. Here, we use our 15-year history of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO2 measurements to answer important questions about the main factors driving increased carbon emissions and variability in the Amazon and whether they are caused by global extreme climate events or direct human activities (deforestation, biomass burning and degradation) in the Amazon.
Historic land use change
In 2000, deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon represented a total area of 474,770 km2 (12.5% of the Brazilian Amazon, 3.8 × 106 km2). The Brazilian Amazon represents 58% of the Pan-Amazonia region (Fig. 1). By 2004, the PRODES programme21 of Brazil for monitoring native vegetation had recorded cumulative deforestation of 612,225 km2 across the Legal Amazon, equivalent to 15.5% of the original forest cover of the region. Between 2004 and 2012, the annual rate of deforestation fell 84% as a result of public policies designed to curb clearing22,23, reaching a cumulative loss of 697,319 km2 (18.4% of the total forest area). The rate began to rise again from 2013 to 2018, when total forest loss reached 19.5%, and accelerated sharply after 2019, reaching 791,835 km2 (20.9%) in 2022. Although the annual rate of deforestation declined strongly in 2023 and 2024 (30% and 47%, respectively) relative to the 2019–2022 period, cumulative forest loss still reached 807,301 km2 (21.3%). From 2010 to 2024, pasture area expanded by 19%, soybean plantation area by 193% and mining by 272% (ref. 24) to estimated values of 561,416 km2, 59,368 km2 and 3,956 km2, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 1).
Amazon precipitation and temperature changes
We present precipitation and temperature time series from 1979 to 2024 in Extended Data Fig. 1. To assess the impact of the past six years, during which deforestation accelerated sharply between 2019 and 2022, on precipitation and temperature, we compared the previously studied period1 (1979–2018) with the current period from 1979 to 2024, using the same database for both periods (Methods). From 1979 to 2018, the changes in annual precipitation were not statistically significant (27 ± 69 mm); however, from 1979 to 2024, there was a reduction of 174 ± 69 mm, representing an 8% decrease. During the dry-season peak period (August–October), from 1979 to 2018, precipitation decreased by 17% (64 ± 19 mm), and from 1979 to 2024, by 20% (83 ± 18 mm). The increase in annual temperature from 1979 to 2018 was 0.93 ± 0.13 °C, and from 1979 to 2024 was 1.13 ± 0.13 °C, representing a 0.20 °C increase over 6 years. During the dry-season peak period, the increase in temperature was 1.51 ± 0.17 °C from 1979 to 2018 and 1.81 ± 0.18 °C from 1979 to 2024, representing a 0.30 °C increase over 6 years. Between 2018 and 2024, Amazonia lost an additional 60,964 km2 of primary forest and 564,532 km2 of burned area, representing a significant increase in human activity impacting the region since 2019. Further discussion of changes in climatic conditions in Amazonia and the studied regions is provided in Extended Data Fig. 1, Extended Data Table 1 and Supplementary Discussion 1.
Regional analyses show that the most pronounced temperature increase occurred in the southeast region (ALF), with warming of 2.19 ± 0.21 °C during the dry-season peak and 1.37 ± 0.15 °C in the annual mean between 1979 and 2024. From 2018 to 2024, this region lost 37,930 km2 (62% of the total deforestation of the Brazilian Amazon) of primary forest. The most intense decline in precipitation happened in the northeast region (SAN). From 1979 to 2024, annual precipitation decreased by 304 ± 150 mm (12%), and during the dry-season peak, it declined by 37% (77 ± 23 mm). Over the same six-year period, SAN lost 15,023 km2 (25% of the total deforestation) of primary forest. More details are presented in Extended Data Fig. 1, Extended Data Table 1 and Supplementary Discussion 3.
Annual mean vertical profiles
This study includes 1,017 vertical profiles conducted between 2010 and 2024 at four Amazonian sites, whose upwind areas of influence represent nearly the entirety of Amazonia (Fig.
1 and Extended Data Fig.
2).
Vertical profiles were typically performed twice per month, from 4.
4 km above sea level (a.
s.
l.
) to near the surface (about 0.
3 km a.
s.
l.
), sampling air at 12 heights in a descending helical trajectory at each of the four sites between 12:00 and 13:00 local time.
Air samples were analysed for CO2 and CO at the Greenhouse Gas Laboratory (LaGEE/INPE), São José dos Campos, Brazil.
The Amazon exhibits a dominant lower-tropospheric circulation pattern, with air masses originating over the tropical Atlantic Ocean, crossing the Amazon towards the Andes, then to the southern regions, and returning to the Atlantic in the southern regions.
This circulation enables integration of both natural and anthropogenic processes by computing atmospheric mass balance across vertical profiles of sites.
Here, we present Amazonian annual mean CO2 vertical profiles (VP; Fig.
2a), and the profiles differenced from the CO2 background (∆VP; Fig.
2b) for 2010–2024, calculated from the annual mean profiles at each site (Extended Data Fig.
3), using the same weighting methodology used for Amazonia carbon balance calculations1,13 (Methods).
Most years show a positive ∆VP near the surface (Fig.
2b), indicating that Amazonia is a net carbon source rather than a sink and cannot offset regional anthropogenic emissions.

Carbon flux from column budget technique
Carbon fluxes were calculated using the atmospheric column budget technique1 for each vertical profile and site over a 15-year study period. Total carbon flux (TCF), fire carbon flux (FCF) and net biome exchange (NBE) monthly mean carbon fluxes (TCF subtracted by FCF = NBE) for each site were derived from the two vertical profiles collected per month, and Amazonia-wide monthly and annual mean fluxes were computed using a weighted mean approach that accounts for regional contributions1,13 (Methods). Figure 3 shows the Amazon carbon balance over 15 years, alongside some climatic and anthropogenic drivers. Examining the annual mean vertical profiles (Fig. 2) and the annual carbon balance (Fig. 3, blue bars) shows strong variability over the 15-year period.
