articles.title: The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11132-zDenisovans from the Xujiayao and other East Asian sites are morphologically distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
The taxonomy and phylogeny of late Middle Pleistocene hominins in East Asia remain highly debated1.
Xujiayao, a key representative assemblage with many fossils and a clear stratigraphy dating to around 199–138 thousand years ago, has been extensively studied, but its evolutionary position remains uncertain.
Here, to clarify this, we analysed Xujiayao material through both palaeoproteomic analysis and morphological comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo.
Proteomic analysis of two specimens identified 18 endogenous proteins, and the Denisova-specific COL1A2-996 R>K mutation strongly supported their affiliation with the Denisovan lineage.
Extended analysis identifies a set of shared morphological traits between Denisovan fossils (Xujiayao and Harbin) and other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo (such as Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong), indicating that they all belong to the Denisovan lineage.
This analysis provides a comprehensive view of Denisovan features, showing both traits reminiscent of Homo erectus (such as a thick cranial vault) and those characteristic of modern humans (for example, a strongly arched temporal squama).
They also share features with late Neanderthals, such as the structure of the temporal labyrinth and the presence of a suprainiac fossa.
Notably, Denisovans are distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism.

Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Late Middle Pleistocene Homo systematics in eastern Eurasia remain poorly defined compared with the better-established evolutionary scenarios in western Eurasia, with East Asian hominins variously classified as archaic Homo sapiens, archaic Homo, China archaics or archaic humans2,3,4,5.
Recent studies have revealed greater morphological diversity in this group than previously known, prompting their assignment to distinct species1.
Homo longi, defined by the Harbin cranium (about 309–146 thousand years ago (ka)) and now classified as Denisovan, is characterized by a massive, long, low cranium; a low, flat face with a shallow canine fossa, reduced alveolar prognathism; a relatively rounded occipital contour with weak torus; a robust supraorbital torus overhanging near-square orbits; and a large, forwardly and inwardly inclined mastoid process, clustering phylogenetically with Jinniushan, Dali, Hualongdong and Xiahe6,7,8,9.
However, despite some primitive traits, Hualongdong has been designated as a transitional form from archaic hominins to H.
sapiens on the basis of derived facial morphologies, mainly including a small size, flattened malar region, weak prognathism, a well-developed anterior nasal spine and a parabolic dental arcade with an anteriorly displaced incisive foramen10.
Another lineage, characterized by an exceptionally large cranium, has been proposed as Homo juluensis, encompassing Xujiayao/Xuchang crania and the Denisovan-affiliated Xiahe and Penghu mandibles, identified through palaeoproteomic analyses1,11,12.
Beyond the Denisovan hypothesis, competing phylogenetic hypotheses proposed these hominins as ancestral to either H.
sapiens or another sister group, further obscuring the evolutionary scenarios in late Middle Pleistocene eastern Eurasia6,13,14.

The Xujiayao assemblage, dated to around 199–138 ka through combined uranium series and electron-spin-resonance methods15, comprises 20 hominin cranial, mandibular and dental fossils excavated between 1976 and 1979 from a well-defined stratigraphic context in the Nihewan Basin, northern China16,17.
This assemblage, recovered alongside abundant artifacts (dominated by scrapers and spheroids) and faunal remains, represents one of the most extensive collections among East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo18,19 (Fig.
1 and Supplementary Text 1).
Initial analyses identified a thick cranial vault, large cerebral fossa relative to the cerebellar fossa, moderate occipital torus, an anterior nasal spine, reduced inion–endinion distance and Neanderthal-like dental morphology, leading to classification as Homo sapiens neanderthalensis, early H.
sapiens or archaic H.
sapiens3,16,17.
To circumvent taxonomic disputes when sapiens lacks consensus, terms such as archaic Homo were temporarily adopted4.
Recent analysis of Xujiayao 6, comprising parietal, temporal and occipital bones, revealed an exceptionally large endocranial capacity of 1,700 ml, designating Xujiayao as the holotype of H.
juluensis20,21.
Shared dental traits between Xujiayao and Altai Denisovans, including large crown size, complex occlusal surface and highly divergent molar roots, have been proposed to support their taxonomic affinity22.
Altai Denisovans and Xujiayao were then grouped under H.
juluensis, alongside the Penghu and Xiahe mandibles, Xuchang crania and the Tam Ngu Hao 2 tooth due to their close morphological affinity1,23.
This lineage is thought to be distinct from H.
longi (Harbin, Dali and Jinniushan), archaic Homo (Hualongdong) and a potential Neanderthal-like Maba lineage1.
As an abundant fossil assemblage with a clear stratigraphic context and linked to nearly all classifications of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo, a confirmed taxonomy of Xujiayao would be critical to resolving the evolutionary relationships of other Middle Pleistocene Homo in East Asia through palaeoproteomic analysis and morphological comparisons.

Here we implemented a palaeoproteomic analysis to explore Xujiayao’s taxonomic classification and assess its genetic population affinity. Subsequently, we conducted a systematic morphological comparison between Xujiayao and other members of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene within a broader evolutionary framework of genus Homo to investigate their morphological affinities to the Xujiayao population. The palaeoproteomic results revealed Xujiayao hominins as Denisovans, and their morphological similarities with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo (such as Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong) indicate that they all belong to the Denisovan lineage.
Recovery of endogenous ancient proteome
Molecular evidence was sought to determine the phylogenetic placement of the Xujiayao hominin samples, on the basis of the positive result of animal samples from the same site (Supplementary Text 2). Ancient proteins were successfully extracted from two bone fragments, including one right parietal bone (PA1490, XJY-6) and one mandible (right ramus, PA1497, XJY-14). To maximize protein yields, we extracted proteins from bone samples by sequential fractionation, resulting in one acid-soluble fraction (>3 kDa) and two acid-insoluble fractions for each sample (Methods and Supplementary Table 1). The preservation of peptides in both Xujiayao hominin samples was first confirmed through the identification of collagen peptide markers24,25,26 in matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) (Supplementary Text 2), and the proteomic data were then further analysed using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) analysis.
To obtain protein sequences from the Xujiayao hominin samples, LC–MS/MS data of the samples were searched on PEAKS Online against the Harbin database8, which includes bone proteins of published archaic individuals and the proteome of present-day humans. The PEAKS search yielded 102,029 peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) and 15,194 unique peptides across the two samples (Fig. 2, Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1). We also searched the data on MaxQuant for confirmation, and the search yielded 3,526 unique peptides across the 2 samples (Supplementary Fig. 2).
To differentiate endogenous ancient proteins from modern contamination, Gln and Asn deamination characteristics of ancient proteins were calculated for each protein.
Proteins with neither Gln nor Asn residues were excluded from the analyses, as the deamination rates of those proteins cannot be assessed.
For proteins that contain at least two peptides with Gln or Asn, we calculated deamidation rates for 41 proteins containing both or one of those Gln/Asn residues.

articles.title: Functional architecture of the human insula
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11175-2A functional architecture of the human insula links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood.
Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7,8,9,10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal–posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral–posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior–polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode.
Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception.
Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

articles.title: Touch-sensing digital pixel fibre enables interactive garment GUI
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11128-9Multifunctional digital fibres integrate display, touch sensing, computation and multimodal input–output, enabling flexible, washable garments with interactive graphical interfaces and wireless multimedia capabilities.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Wearable computing promises to transform human interaction with information, yet conventional graphical user interfaces (GUIs) rely on planar, rigid displays incompatible with textiles, which are composed of one-dimensional fibres.
Despite recent progress1,2 in flexible and fibre-based displays, bridging this fundamental dimensional mismatch remains challenging because existing approaches do not naturally provide the digitally addressable, high-throughput, information-rich interfaces required for interactive GUIs.
Here we present a digital pixel fibre integrating addressable pixels, a common propagation-axis interconnection for scalable in-fibre circuitry and a coaxial sensing layer for fibre-level touch localization.
Microelectronic components and a touch-gated resistive path system form a linear circuit that acts as both an interactive display backbone and a computational bus, while peripheral multimodal fibre sensors and actuators enable physiological, inertial, optical, and acoustic input and output.
We integrate these fibres into the forearm portion of a garment sleeve to realize a GUI with a 96 × 54-pixel display, 30-frame-per-second refresh rate and 8-bit colour depth.
It supports dynamic graphics, integrated audio–video playback, wireless data exchange and interactive computing functions, while maintaining the flexibility, washability, breathability and mechanical robustness of everyday textiles.
By merging display, sensing and computation within a single fibre, this work establishes a scalable platform for intrinsically interactive textiles, opening pathways toward garments that operate as fully integrated computational systems.

articles.title: Drought and disease trigger novel interactions among top predators
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11194-zClimate-driven drought and prey decline triggered lynx predation on raptors, reducing raptor fitness and abundance and producing cascading effects across lower trophic levels.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Interactions among species are increasingly recognized as key determinants of climate change impacts on ecosystems1,2,3,4,5.
However, we know little about how climatic perturbations affect interactions among top vertebrate predators.
Here we show that, when an emergent disease caused the decline of shared prey (rabbits), after decades of neutral co-existence a mammalian carnivore (lynx) started to prey heavily on a top predatory raptor (kites).
These predation bouts occurred exclusively under drought conditions and when lynx found rabbit remains under the raptor nests, consistent with the removal of a potential competitor.
Drought-induced lynx predation depressed lifetime reproductive success and triggered territory abandonment and dispersal by the raptor, suggestive of a new arms race among predators.
A reduction in raptor abundance was associated with an increase in an insectivorous bird (a small owl), showing that the new interaction had the potential to reach lower trophic levels.
These results underline the importance of diet flexibility and mobility as important mediators of resilience to stressors.
In the future, synergistic effects of multiple anthropogenic stressors may reshape the interactions and ecological roles of many apex predators, with potential cascading consequences for whole ecosystems.
A key to forecasting the future impact of global change may reside in understanding how behavioural flexibility and interacting keystone species respond to interacting shocks.

Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Species interactions, such as pollination or herbivory, are increasingly recognized as key drivers of climate impacts on biodiversity1,2,3,4,5. Climate change can profoundly alter biotic interactions—which in turn can reshape its impact—thus constraining species distribution6,7, imposing population declines8, driving extinctions9,10,11 and modifying food web structure, function and stability12,13. Understanding the relation between climate and biotic interactions is therefore considered an essential prerequisite for anticipating the ecosystem effects of climatic perturbations2,3. However, despite many recent advances for certain taxa and ecosystems14,15,16, we have scarce knowledge of the interplay between climate and several key interactions.
From a broader point of view, species interactions are likely to mediate a wide range of multiple interacting stressors, such as climate extremes, habitat degradation, environmental contamination, overhunting by humans or introduction of non-native species and pathogens17,18. Animals facing such stressors can either succumb (for example, decline to extinction19) or enact coping strategies that allow them to resist the stressor impact20,21. Resistance is usually attained through phenotypic plasticity and altered use of resources, such as food or habitats22,23, which may change or broaden the realized niche of a species. Such niche-rewiring has produced some recent, striking examples of species using new, unexpected foods, with positive consequences in terms of their abundance and resilience23,24,25,26. In turn, these niche alterations are likely to reshape the network of ecological interactions in which a species is embedded, with potential consequences for its supporting community. This will be particularly expected for species already involved in large networks of key interactions, such as top predators. Thus, there is a need for studies that examine how the response to multiple stressors by keystone predators repercusses on their interactions with other predators, with potential indirect consequences for lower-trophic level species.
One common interaction among predators is intraguild predation, which is the killing and consumption of species that compete for the same resource27. Intraguild predation is considered ubiquitous in food webs, widespread in guilds of top vertebrate predators28,29, and a common driver of population dynamics and community structure30,31,32. Intraguild predation is an ideal candidate for research on the interface between climate and biotic interactions, because it integrates competition and predation, both of which are affected by climate change and in turn modulate its impact3,4,5,7,11. However, knowledge on the interplay between climate change and intraguild predation is based almost exclusively on warming experiments on invertebrates13,33,34, with little research on vertebrate predators. This is despite two recent studies showing that climate change will probably increase the encounter rates among intraguild predation killers and victims35,36. Such a lack of information is particularly striking given that top predatory vertebrates: receive a large amount of management and research; are highly interactive species; can structure whole food webs through top-down forcing; are especially sensitive to climate change; and are considered ideal biotic multipliers, capable of amplifying the impact of climate change on their communities32,37,38,39.
Another less studied form of intraguild predation is represented by killings among taxonomically distant predators, such as mammalian carnivores and birds of prey. Such cross-taxonomic intraguild predation has proven difficult to investigate, probably due to the extreme difficulty of detection of rare events involving distantly related taxa typically studied by independent research specialists40. As such, research has been devoted to the sole description of individual casualties41,42,43. Knowledge is limited to a handful of studies that quantified the predation rate, or tested its impact on the victim abundance or behaviour44,45,46. The relation between cross-taxonomic intraguild predation and climate change remains uncertain.
Here we study an intraguild predation module composed of a mammalian carnivore (the Iberian lynx Lynx pardinus) and a raptorial bird (the black kite Milvus migrans) that share the same main prey (the European rabbit Oryctolagus cuniculus) (Fig. 1). These kinds of community modules are considered ideal study systems for gaining the necessary mechanistic understanding of interactions that are simultaneously vulnerable to climate and key determinants of community function and structure—an essential prerequisite for predicting community responses to climate change2. The Iberian lynx (hereafter lynx) is a medium-sized solitary felid (with a body mass of 9–13 kg and a longevity of up to 11 years) considered as a rabbit specialist and mainly active at night and twilight47. The black kite (hereafter kite) is a medium-sized, diurnal, long-lived, opportunistic raptor (with a body mass of 0.8–1 kg, a wingspan of about 1.5 m and a longevity of up to 30 years) that preys heavily on rabbits when these are abundant48. The European rabbit (hereafter rabbit) is a small herbivore (around 1.1 kg) and a keystone prey for over 30 Mediterranean predators49.
We monitored the predatory interaction between lynx and kites for three decades within a 10-km2 sector of Doñana National Park—a wetland in southern Spain that inundates seasonally, but is periodically affected by year-round drought (Extended Data Figs.
1 and 2) that severely curtails prey availability for most predators (for example, 4–5-fold reductions in prey50).
Climate models forecast a substantial increase in drought frequency for this region over the next 30–100 years51,52,53, which makes this predator-rich ecosystem an ideal candidate to explore the interplay between climatic forcing and interactions among top predatory vertebrates.
The study plot supported a relatively stable population of 4–6 adult lynxes (2–3 males and 2–3 females)47 and 105–223 kite pairs, representing 82–90% of the local raptor assemblage.
These two species can therefore be considered the main diurnal (kite) and nocturnal (lynx) top predators of the ecosystem.
In this area, lynx diet is dominated by rabbits (70–90% of the diet), but expands during periods of rabbit scarcity to include alternative prey, mainly in the form of waterbirds from the marshes, especially ducks54,55.
During these prey troughs, lynx can also depredate tree nests of large birds such as raptors and storks (Extended Data Fig.
3).
Similarly, kite diet is dominated by rabbits when these are abundant (up to 80% of the diet, with a mean of 58% before the current rabbit crash) and broadens when these are less available to include birds, fish, reptiles and crayfish mainly captured in the marshes48.
Kites are capable of killing adult rabbits, which are usually dismembered and taken to the nest in two-to-three sequential deliveries.

In 2013, the local rabbit population started to decline severely (by over 70%) owing to a new variant of the rabbit haemorrhagic disease56. The virus originated from a breeding farm in France and spread rapidly from farm to farm, and to surrounding wild populations throughout the Iberian Peninsula56, thus representing a form of anthropogenic, global change impact. The crash in main rabbit prey and the predators’ dietary overlap over alternative marshland prey—which is in turn affected by drought—offered a unique opportunity to study how top predators interact under increasing competition imposed by a global change driver and multiple bouts of drought. Below, we use the term ‘intraguild predation’ interchangeably with ‘lynx predation on kites’.
Data from 1,624 kite nests cumulatively monitored over three decades showed that intraguild predation was strongly tied to the interaction between the availability of shared prey and drought (R2 = 0.
87, Fig.

In particular, lynx and kites basically acted neutrally towards each other for two decades (Fig.

articles.title: Additive manufacturing of ultralong and architected single crystals
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11185-0A free-form additive manufacturing method that uses alternating and pulsed heat inputs is described for fabricating metre-tall, centimetre-diameter single crystals of Ti-6Al-4V, as well as hard-to-process refractory metals, including W, Mo, Nb and MoNb alloys.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Single-crystal materials are indispensable for high-performance applications, yet their deployment remains constrained by conventional manufacturing techniques that depend on strict quasi-steady thermal conditions1.
This requirement fundamentally conflicts with the intense cyclic thermal fluctuations inherent to additive manufacturing2, historically preventing the 3D printing of large or architected single crystals.
Here we present a free-form additive manufacturing approach that resolves this contradiction by using delicately controlled alternating and pulsed heat inputs to govern and direct single-crystal growth.
Using this method, we demonstrate the fabrication of metre-tall, centimetre-diameter single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V alongside, to our knowledge, the first single-crystal lattice structures containing complex zigzag ligaments, effectively eliminating theoretical size constraints for single-crystal components.
The resulting bulk single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V exhibits an order-of-magnitude increase in creep resistance over standard grain-size scaling predictions, driven by the synergistic elimination of grain boundaries and an additive manufacturing-induced hierarchical α/β-architecture that regulates dislocation density, mobility and void evolution.
Furthermore, we demonstrate the broad applicability of this technique by printing single crystals of hard-to-process refractory metals, including W, Mo, Nb and MoNb alloys.
Our work introduces a large-scale method for single-crystal additive manufacturing, expanding the accessible materials library and enabling high-performance, complex geometries previously unattainable by classical methods.

articles.title: Enzyme-embedded polyesters for accelerated biodegradation in the deep sea
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11192-1Near-complete deep-sea degradation of enzyme-embedded compostable polyesters shows that thermal enzyme embedding greatly accelerates breakdown across marine environments while preserving material performance, offering a promising strategy to mitigate persistent ocean plastic pollution.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
The accumulation of persistent plastics in the ocean is causing wide-ranging environmental problems1,2,3.
Some commercially available compostable plastics4,5,6,7, developed to address these issues, degrade efficiently under industrial composting conditions; however, their degradation in marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, remains limited8,9,10.
Here we demonstrate that thermally embedding enzymes into compostable polyesters (poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT)) significantly accelerates their degradation in both coastal and deep-sea environments from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m.
Enzyme-embedded polyesters achieved near-complete degradation at a deep-sea depth of 757 m within 5 months.
Furthermore, moderate biodegradation of enzyme-embedded polyesters was observed under extreme conditions on deep-sea floors of 5,503 m.
In coastal seawater, films embedded with trace amounts (0.
1 wt%) of enzyme underwent rapid degradation.
The mechanical properties of enzyme-embedded polyesters were similar to those of enzyme-free polyesters.
Chemical analysis confirmed the formation of low-molecular-mass degradation products and biochemical oxygen demand measurements supported the mineralization of the enzyme-embedded polyesters.
The enzyme-embedding strategy enables enhanced marine degradation of compostable polyesters and represents a potential solution to marine plastic pollution.

Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Plastics are indispensable in many areas of modern life, but their accumulation in marine environments has emerged as a global environmental issue1,2,3. Biodegradable plastics have been considered a promising mitigation strategy4,5,6. Most commercially available biodegradable plastics are compostable4,5,7, meaning that their degradation is optimized for industrial composting conditions characterized by elevated temperatures, high microbial activity and humidity. However, some compostable polyesters have shown limited degradation and may therefore persist in these environments8,9,10. In marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, low temperatures and lack of viable microorganisms capable of degrading these plastics can substantially limit polyester degradation8,9,10,11,12,13, raising concerns about their environmental persistence.
Recent studies have demonstrated that embedding specialized enzymes directly into polymers can enhance their biodegradation14,15,16,17,18,19,20,21,22. However, these demonstrations have been confined to laboratory or closed-system incubations, and whether enzyme-embedded polyesters can achieve efficient degradation in situ under natural marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, remains unknown. At the same time, practical deployment requires enhanced biodegradability without compromising the mechanical properties needed for use.
In this study, thermally embedding Candida antarctica lipase B (CaLB) or Humicola insolens cutinase (HiC) in various compostable polyester films and microbeads, including PBS, PBSA, PCL and PBAT, has been shown to significantly accelerate their degradation in coastal and deep-sea environments, ranging from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1a–c). CaLB and HiC were selected for their broad hydrolytic activity towards aliphatic and aromatic–aliphatic polyesters23,24,25,26,27. Their high thermal stability in freeze-dried form enabled retention of catalytic activity during thermal embedding16,18,28.
Here we demonstrate that certain compostable polyesters that are widely regarded as persistent in the ocean can undergo substantial biodegradation with enzyme embedding in marine environments, including under extreme deep-sea conditions. Notably, efficient degradation was achieved using trace enzyme loadings while preserving initial mechanical properties resembling those of enzyme-free materials, supporting their practical applicability. This study demonstrates that the enzyme-embedding strategy enables marine degradation of such compostable polyesters while maintaining material performance, thereby broadening the range of candidate biodegradable materials with potential to address persistent plastic accumulation in marine environments.
Enzyme-embedded polyester design
To evaluate the feasibility of the enzyme-embedding strategy in various marine environments, we developed a series of enzyme-embedded compostable polyesters (PBS, PBSA, PCL and PBAT) (Fig. 1a,b). Building on the previously reported thermal stability of freeze-dried CaLB and HiC16,18, we embedded two different enzymes into polymer matrices by twin-screw extrusion at temperatures ranging from 90 °C to 130 °C (processing temperatures in Supplementary Table 1a). The final melt-processing approach yielded both thin films (100–300 μm) and microbeads (20–300 μm in diameter) (Extended Data Fig. 1), representative of common plastic waste forms and microplastic pollutants.
A comprehensive environmental degradation study was subsequently conducted in environments ranging from coastal seawater (2–6 m) to deep-sea floor (757–5,503 m) (Fig. 1c–e). Deployment sites were strategically selected to encompass various ecological conditions (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 1b), including one coastal site (port of JAMSTEC Yokosuka Headquarters (PJM)), three bathyal sites (off Misaki Port (BMS; depth = 757 m), off Hatsushima Island (BHT; depth = 855 m) and Myojin Knoll (BMJ; depth = 1,292 m)) and one abyssal site (Kuroshio Extension Observatory (AKR); depth = 5,503 m). Deep-sea deployment and recovery of the samples were performed aboard the human-occupied vehicle (HOV) Shinkai 6500 using a robotic arm (Fig. 1d), and follow-up evaluation of samples was carried out in the laboratory (Fig. 1e).
To account for the lower temperature, high pressure and distinct microbial activity in deep-sea environments, enzyme loading was increased from 0.1 wt% for coastal seawater deployments (PJM) to 3 wt% for deep-sea deployments (BMS, BMJ, BHT and AKR).
Film degradation at different depths
Enzyme-embedded polymer films were deployed across several distinct deep-sea floors (BMS, BMJ, BHT and AKR) at water depths ranging from 757 to 5,503 m (Fig.
1c).
These sites exhibited contrasting temperatures, water pressures and microbial community compositions10.
The decreases in mass of the films after 1 month of immersion in coastal seawater (PJM) and 18 months on deep-sea floors (BMS, BMJ and AKR) are presented in Fig.
2a.
Notably, even after long-term immersion on the deep-sea floor, enzyme-free compostable PBS, PBSA, PCL and PBAT films exhibited little to no loss of mass (0.
4–12.
9%).
Consistent with these results, no signs of degradation were observed in images of the films (Extended Data Fig.
2) and in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images (Extended Data Fig.
3) except PCL film.
Additionally, enzyme-free compostable PBS, PBSA, PCL and PBAT films placed at a coastal seawater site (PJM) exhibited a substantially faster degradation rate compared with those placed on deep-sea floors (BMS, BMJ and AKR) (Extended Data Fig.
4a and Supplementary Tables 2–5).
Based on our previous studies10, the slower biodegradation of these compostable polyesters in deep-sea environments compared to coastal seawater can be attributed to several factors, including lower temperatures, higher hydrostatic pressure and reduced microbial abundance and diversity.
By contrast, polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) such as poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (P3HB) demonstrate efficient degradation in diverse deep-sea environments (Fig.
2a).
Their microbial origin and intrinsic biodegradability distinguish this family of materials from other synthetic polyesters29.
Although PHAs demonstrate excellent biodegradability, their production volume is still low and their cost remains too high to meet the diverse demands of various applications30.

Embedding 3 wt% CaLB markedly enhanced the degradation of aliphatic compostable polyesters across diverse marine environments (Fig. 2a). This was exemplified at BMS (757 m depth), where CaLB-embedded PBSA and PCL films exhibited substantial mass losses of 57.3% and 99.0%, respectively, after 18 months (Fig. 2a), whereas enzyme-free control polyesters showed negligible degradation (Extended Data Fig. 4a). The substantial mass loss, accompanied by relatively large variability for films deployed at BMJ, is likely to be associated with the dynamic and heterogeneous sea floor conditions near hydrothermal vents, which may introduce greater environmental variability31,32. Finally, CaLB-embedded PBSA and PCL films also demonstrated significant mass losses of 30.5% and 7.7%, compared with 1.6% and 3.4% for enzyme-free PBSA and PCL films, respectively, after 18 months of immersion at AKR, located at a depth of 5,503 m (Fig. 2a). SEM observations (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3) revealed the formation of surface holes on CaLB-embedded films after immersion, consistent with localized enzymatic degradation promoted by the embedded enzyme.
Laboratory pressure-vessel experiments conducted at 0.1 MPa, 10 MPa and 25 MPa (equivalent to atmospheric pressure, hydrostatic pressure at 1,000 m and hydrostatic pressure at 2,500 m) using a 100 lipase units (LU; 1 LU is the amount of enzyme that liberates 1 μmol of titratable butyric acid per minute from glycerol tributyrate under standard conditions) per ml CaLB solution prepared from autoclaved BMS deep-sea water further corroborate that enzymatic hydrolysis of PBSA and PCL occurs even under high pressures (Fig. 2b). This provides additional evidence that the mass loss observed in enzyme-embedded compostable polyester is directly attributable to enzymatic degradation. Although a decrease in the degree of degradation was observed for PBSA above 10 MPa and for PCL at 25 MPa, CaLB has been confirmed to remain effective under 25 MPa high

articles.full_text:
Research: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust
        This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation.
With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems.
My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone:

Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly

This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built:

Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README
Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension
Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial

This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't (or won't) invest the necessary time to understand what it can do?
